paragraphs: Membership in an online social-network community can reveal sensitive information about a user. This paper studies how to obscure a given community structure by making limited changes to the network. The objective, called community structure deception, balances keeping modifications small with making the original communities difficult for detection algorithms to uncover.

The authors approach this problem through information theory. They define a community-based structural entropy intended to express how much information a community structure reveals. This quantity provides the basis for residual entropy minimization, or REM, an efficient procedure for carrying out the deception objective. It turns the task into one guided by an explicit measure of structural information.

Experiments cover nine real-world networks and six community detection algorithms. Across these evaluations, REM is very effective at obscuring communities compared with other benchmark methods. The results support structural entropy as a useful guide for modifying networks to conceal affiliations. The demonstrated outcome is reduced visibility of community structure to detection methods, addressing the stated route by which sensitive attributes may be inferred.
summary.tldr: REM uses a structural-entropy objective to efficiently modify social networks so that their community affiliations become harder to detect.

title: REM: From Structural Entropy to Community Structure Deception

abstract: Regularization is typically understood as improving generalization by altering the landscape of local extrema to which the model eventually converges. Deep neural networks (DNNs), however, challenge this view: We show that removing regularization after an initial transient period has little effect on generalization, even if the final loss landscape is the same as if there had been no regularization. In some cases, generalization even improves after interrupting regularization. Conversely, if regularization is applied only after the initial transient, it has no effect on the final solution, whose generalization gap is as bad as if regularization never happened. This suggests that what matters for training deep networks is not just whether or how, but when to regularize. The phenomena we observe are manifest in different datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, ImageNet), different architectures (ResNet-18, All-CNN), different regularization methods (weight decay, data augmentation, mixup), different learning rate schedules (exponential, piece-wise constant). They collectively suggest that there is a "critical period'' for regularizing deep networks that is decisive of the final performance. More analysis should, therefore, focus on the transient rather than asymptotic behavior of learning.

paragraphs: Regularization is often explained through how it changes the solutions a model eventually reaches. This paper examines a different part of that story: when regularization is applied during training. The authors find that early training can determine its effect on generalization, challenging an explanation focused only on the final loss landscape.

In their experiments, removing regularization after an initial transient period has little effect on generalization, and sometimes improves it. Applying regularization only after that early period does not change the final solution in the observed settings; its generalization gap remains as poor as without regularization. Thus, the same eventual loss landscape can be associated with different outcomes depending on training history.

The observations span multiple datasets, architectures, regularization methods, and learning-rate schedules, including weight decay, data augmentation, and mixup. Collectively, they suggest a critical early period during which regularization strongly influences final performance. The authors consequently argue for more analysis of transient learning dynamics, since behavior near convergence alone does not explain the experimental patterns they report.
summary.tldr: Experiments suggest that regularization’s effect on generalization is concentrated in an early training period, with little benefit from introducing it late.

title: Time Matters in Regularizing Deep Networks: Weight Decay and Data Augmentation Affect Early Learning Dynamics, Matter Little Near Convergence

abstract: To analyze a collection of interconnected documents, relational topic models (RTMs) have been developed to describe both the link structure and document content, exploring their underlying relationships via a single-layer latent representation with limited expressive capability. To better utilize the document network, we first propose graph Poisson factor analysis (GPFA) that constructs a probabilistic model for interconnected documents and also provides closed-form Gibbs sampling update equations, moving beyond sophisticated approximate assumptions of existing RTMs. Extending GPFA, we develop a novel hierarchical RTM named graph Poisson gamma belief network (GPGBN), and further introduce two different Weibull distribution based variational graph auto-encoders for efficient model inference and effective network information aggregation. Experimental results demonstrate that our models extract high-quality hierarchical latent document representations, leading to improved performance over baselines on various graph analytic tasks.

paragraphs: A collection of linked documents contains information both in its text and in the connections between documents. Relational topic models analyze those sources together, but a single layer of hidden representations can limit what they express. This paper develops a hierarchical probabilistic approach intended to capture richer relationships within such document networks.

The starting point is graph Poisson factor analysis, which models interconnected documents and supplies closed-form Gibbs sampling updates. The authors then extend it into a graph Poisson gamma belief network, introducing a hierarchy of latent document representations. This progression moves from a basic relational model toward a deeper representation of document content and connectivity.

To make inference efficient and aggregate network information, the paper also introduces two variational graph autoencoders based on Weibull distributions. Experiments show that the resulting models extract high-quality hierarchical representations and improve performance over baselines on several graph analysis tasks. The stated benefit is therefore practical as well as representational: jointly modeling links and content through a hierarchy yields useful features for downstream graph analysis.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical probabilistic topic model combines document content and links to learn representations that improve graph analysis tasks.

title: Deep Relational Topic Modeling via Graph Poisson Gamma Belief Network

abstract: Classical optimal transport problem seeks a transportation map that preserves the total mass between two probability distributions, requiring their masses to be equal. This may be too restrictive in some applications such as color or shape matching, since the distributions may have arbitrary masses and/or only a fraction of the total mass has to be transported. In this paper, we address the partial Wasserstein and Gromov-Wasserstein problems and propose exact algorithms to solve them. We showcase the new formulation in a positive-unlabeled (PU) learning application. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of optimal transport in this context and we first highlight that partial Wasserstein-based metrics prove effective in usual PU learning settings. We then demonstrate that partial Gromov-Wasserstein metrics are efficient in scenarii in which the samples from the positive and the unlabeled datasets come from different domains or have different features.

paragraphs: Classical optimal transport matches distributions while preserving all their mass, which requires equal total mass on both sides. Some applications need only part of one distribution matched to another, or involve unequal masses. This paper develops partial transport formulations that accommodate those situations, covering both Wasserstein and Gromov–Wasserstein problems.

The authors propose exact algorithms for these partial problems and apply them to positive-unlabeled learning. In that setting, the available data include known positive examples and examples whose labels are unknown. Partial matching is relevant because the goal does not require treating the whole unlabeled collection as corresponding to the positive collection.

The reported results distinguish two useful settings. Partial Wasserstein-based metrics work effectively in usual positive-unlabeled learning scenarios. Partial Gromov–Wasserstein metrics are effective when the positive and unlabeled datasets come from different domains or have different features. The contribution therefore combines algorithms for matching only selected distributional mass with an application demonstrating how the two formulations address different relationships between the available datasets.
summary.tldr: Exact partial transport algorithms support positive-unlabeled learning, including cases where the two datasets have different domains or features.

title: Partial Optimal Tranport with applications on Positive-Unlabeled Learning

abstract: Conformal inference, cross-validation+, and the jackknife+ are hold-out methods that can be combined with virtually any machine learning algorithm to construct prediction sets with guaranteed marginal coverage. In this paper, we develop specialized versions of these techniques for categorical and unordered response labels that, in addition to providing marginal coverage, are also fully adaptive to complex data distributions, in the sense that they perform favorably in terms of approximate conditional coverage compared to alternative methods. The heart of our contribution is a novel conformity score, which we explicitly demonstrate to be powerful and intuitive for classification problems, but whose underlying principle is potentially far more general. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate the practical value of our theoretical guarantees, as well as the statistical advantages of the proposed methods over the existing alternatives.

paragraphs: A classifier can express uncertainty by returning a set of possible labels. This paper develops methods for constructing such sets when labels are categorical and have no natural ordering. It specializes conformal inference, cross-validation+, and jackknife+, techniques that can work with virtually any machine learning algorithm and provide guarantees about how often prediction sets contain the correct answer.

The central contribution is a new conformity score, which determines how well a candidate label agrees with the information used to build a prediction set. The authors design this score specifically for classification. Their methods preserve guaranteed marginal coverage, a guarantee averaged across the data distribution, while adapting to complex distributions.

The adaptation claim concerns favorable approximate conditional coverage compared with alternatives: coverage that better reflects different parts of the distribution. It does not replace the marginal guarantee with an exact conditional one. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the practical usefulness of the guarantees and show statistical advantages over existing methods.
summary.tldr: A new classification conformity score produces prediction sets with guaranteed marginal coverage and improved adaptation to complex data distributions.

title: Classification with Valid and Adaptive Coverage

abstract: Recent advances in neural architecture search inspire many channel number search algorithms~(CNS) for convolutional neural networks. To improve searching efficiency, parameter sharing is widely applied, which reuses parameters among different channel configurations. Nevertheless, it is unclear how parameter sharing affects the searching process. In this paper, we aim at providing a better understanding and exploitation of parameter sharing for CNS. Specifically, we propose affine parameter sharing~(APS) as a general formulation to unify and quantitatively analyze existing channel search algorithms. It is found that with parameter sharing, weight updates of one architecture can simultaneously benefit other candidates. However, it also results in less confidence in choosing good architectures. We thus propose a new strategy of parameter sharing towards a better balance between training efficiency and architecture discrimination. Extensive analysis and experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed strategy in channel configuration against many state-of-the-art counterparts on benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Channel-number search chooses how many channels to use in a convolutional network. To make this search cheaper, many methods reuse parameters across candidate configurations. This paper examines how that reuse changes the search itself, focusing on the relationship between efficient training and the ability to distinguish promising architectures.

The authors introduce affine parameter sharing as a common formulation for existing channel-search algorithms. It enables quantitative analysis of a shared mechanism: updating the weights of one candidate can benefit other candidates at the same time. That cross-candidate benefit improves training efficiency, but the analysis also finds reduced confidence in selecting good architectures.

Based on this tradeoff, the paper proposes a parameter-sharing strategy that seeks a better balance between training candidates efficiently and discriminating among them. Extensive analysis and benchmark experiments show superior channel configurations compared with many state-of-the-art alternatives. The contribution is both an explanatory framework and a revised search strategy. It makes clear why the way candidates share training progress matters to the quality of the architecture ultimately selected.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis of parameter sharing motivates a channel-search strategy that better balances training efficiency and reliable architecture selection.

title: Revisiting Parameter Sharing for Automatic Neural Channel Number Search

abstract: Patch adversarial attacks on images, in which the attacker can distort pixels within a region of bounded size, are an important threat model since they provide a quantitative model for physical adversarial attacks. In this paper, we introduce a certifiable defense against patch attacks that guarantees for a given image and patch attack size, no patch adversarial examples exist. Our method is related to the broad class of randomized smoothing robustness schemes which provide high-confidence probabilistic robustness certificates. By exploiting the fact that patch attacks are more constrained than general sparse attacks, we derive meaningfully large robustness certificates against them. Additionally, in contrast to smoothing-based defenses against L_p and sparse attacks, our defense method against patch attacks is de-randomized, yielding improved, deterministic certificates. Compared to the existing patch certification method proposed by (Chiang et al., 2020), which relies on interval bound propagation, our method can be trained significantly faster, achieves high clean and certified robust accuracy on CIFAR-10, and provides certificates at ImageNet scale. For example, for a 5-by-5 patch attack on CIFAR-10, our method achieves up to around 57.6% certified accuracy (with a classifier with around 83.8% clean accuracy), compared to at most 30.3% certified accuracy for the existing method (with a classifier with around 47.8% clean accuracy). Our results effectively establish a new state-of-the-art of certifiable defense against patch attacks on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

paragraphs: Patch attacks alter pixels within a region of bounded size. This paper develops a defense that can certify, for a given image and attack size, that no such adversarial patch exists. The spatial restriction is central: a patch attacker has less freedom than an attacker who can modify scattered pixels anywhere in an image.

The method builds on smoothing-based robustness approaches but exploits that restriction to obtain larger certificates. It also removes randomization, producing deterministic certificates instead of high-confidence probabilistic ones. The authors report substantially faster training than the existing patch-certification approach based on interval bound propagation, along with certificates at ImageNet scale.

For a 5-by-5 patch on CIFAR-10, the method reaches around 57.6% certified accuracy with around 83.8% clean accuracy. The comparison method reaches at most 30.3% certified accuracy with around 47.8% clean accuracy. These results show improved ordinary classification and certified protection in the reported comparison; the guarantee remains tied to the specified image and bounded patch size.
summary.tldr: A deterministic smoothing defense exploits patch geometry to improve certified robustness and scale certification to ImageNet.

title: (De)Randomized Smoothing for Certifiable Defense against Patch Attacks

abstract: Reasoning over an instance composed of a set of vectors, like a point cloud, requires that one accounts for intra-set dependent features among elements. However, since such instances are unordered, the elements' features should remain unchanged when the input's order is permuted. This property, permutation equivariance, is a challenging constraint for most neural architectures. While recent work has proposed global pooling and attention-based solutions, these may be limited in the way that intradependencies are captured in practice. In this work we propose a more general formulation to achieve permutation equivariance through ordinary differential equations (ODE). Our proposed module, Exchangeable Neural ODE (ExNODE), can be seamlessly applied for both discriminative and generative tasks. We also extend set modeling in the temporal dimension and propose a VAE based model for temporal set modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our method over strong baselines.

A model must capture those relationships while ensuring that reordering the inputs simply reorders the corresponding element features. This requirement is permutation equivariance, and it places a structural constraint on the architecture.

The paper proposes Exchangeable Neural ODE, or ExNODE, which uses ordinary differential equations to achieve this property. The authors present it as a more general formulation for modeling dependencies within sets than existing pooling and attention approaches may capture in practice. The same module can be applied to both discriminative tasks and generative tasks.

The work also extends set modeling across time through a model based on a variational autoencoder. This brings changing sets into the framework alongside individual unordered instances. Extensive experiments report effectiveness against strong baselines. The stated contribution is therefore both architectural and practical: differential equations provide a way to respect unordered structure while learning dependencies for several kinds of set modeling.
summary.tldr: ExNODE uses ordinary differential equations to model relationships within unordered sets while preserving permutation equivariance.

title: Exchangeable Neural ODE for Set Modeling

abstract: Many modern data analyses benefit from explicitly modeling dependence structure in data -- such as measurements across time or space, ordered words in a sentence, or genes in a genome. A gold standard evaluation technique is structured cross-validation (CV), which leaves out some data subset (such as data within a time interval or data in a geographic region) in each fold. But CV here can be prohibitively slow due to the need to re-run already-expensive learning algorithms many times. Previous work has shown approximate cross-validation (ACV) methods provide a fast and provably accurate alternative in the setting of empirical risk minimization. But this existing ACV work is restricted to simpler models by the assumptions that (i) data across CV folds are independent and (ii) an exact initial model fit is available. In structured data analyses, both these assumptions are often untrue. In the present work, we address (i) by extending ACV to CV schemes with dependence structure between the folds. To address (ii), we verify -- both theoretically and empirically -- that ACV quality deteriorates smoothly with noise in the initial fit. We demonstrate the accuracy and computational benefits of our proposed methods on a diverse set of real-world applications.

Structured cross-validation evaluates models by withholding meaningful subsets, such as an interval or region. This can be expensive because each withheld subset ordinarily requires another run of an already costly learning procedure.

Approximate cross-validation offers a faster alternative, but earlier approaches assumed independence across folds and an exact initial model fit. Both assumptions can fail when analyzing structured data. This paper extends approximate cross-validation to schemes in which dependencies remain between folds, bringing the approximation closer to the evaluation settings these models actually require.

The authors also study what happens when the initial fit is imperfect. Their theoretical and empirical results show that approximation quality degrades smoothly as noise in that fit increases. This matters because an exact fit need not be available before evaluation begins. Across diverse real applications, the proposed methods demonstrate accuracy and computational benefits, supporting their use for evaluating dependent-data models without repeatedly paying the full cost of fitting.
summary.tldr: The paper extends fast approximate cross-validation to dependent data and shows that imperfect initial fits degrade its quality smoothly.

title: Approximate Cross-Validation for Structured Models

abstract: We study bandit model selection in stochastic environments. Our approach relies on a master algorithm that selects between candidate base algorithms. We develop a master-base algorithm abstraction that can work with general classes of base algorithms and different type of adversarial master algorithms. Our methods rely on a novel and generic smoothing transformation for bandit algorithms that permits us to obtain optimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ model selection guarantees for stochastic contextual bandit problems as long as the optimal base algorithm satisfies a high probability regret guarantee. We show through a lower bound that even when one of the base algorithms has $O(\log T)$ regret, in general it is impossible to get better than $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ regret in model selection, even asymptotically. Using our techniques, we address model selection in a variety of problems such as misspecified linear contextual bandits \citep{lattimore2019learning}, linear bandit with unknown dimension \citep{Foster-Krishnamurthy-Luo-2019} and reinforcement learning with unknown feature maps. Our algorithm requires the knowledge of the optimal base regret to adjust the master learning rate. We show that without such prior knowledge any master can suffer a regret larger than the optimal base regret.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose among learning algorithms while interacting with a stochastic bandit environment. A master algorithm selects between candidate base algorithms, allowing model selection to happen during learning. The authors develop an abstraction that accommodates general base algorithms and different adversarial master algorithms, rather than requiring one particular pairing.

A generic smoothing transformation enables an optimal regret guarantee growing as the square root of the number of rounds, provided the optimal base algorithm has a high-probability regret guarantee. A matching lower bound shows that this square-root cost is unavoidable in general, even when one candidate alone would achieve logarithmic regret. Selecting a good learner can therefore be fundamentally harder than running it with advance knowledge.

The framework applies to misspecified linear contextual bandits, unknown linear dimension, and reinforcement learning with unknown feature maps. A consequential requirement is that the proposed algorithm needs the optimal base regret to set the master's learning rate. The authors also show that, without this prior knowledge, any master can incur regret exceeding that of the optimal base.
summary.tldr: A smoothing-based master algorithm achieves optimal square-root bandit model-selection regret under stated guarantees and knowledge of the optimal base regret.

title: Model Selection in Contextual Stochastic Bandit Problems

abstract: Partial observations of continuous time-series dynamics at arbitrary time stamps exist in many disciplines. Fitting this type of data using statistical models with continuous dynamics is not only promising at an intuitive level but also has practical benefits, including the ability to generate continuous trajectories and to perform inference on previously unseen time stamps. Despite exciting progress in this area, the existing models still face challenges in terms of their representational power and the quality of their variational approximations. We tackle these challenges with continuous latent process flows (CLPF), a principled architecture decoding continuous latent processes into continuous observable processes using a time-dependent normalizing flow driven by a stochastic differential equation. To optimize our model using maximum likelihood, we propose a novel piecewise construction of a variational posterior process and derive the corresponding variational lower bound using trajectory re-weighting. Our ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of our contributions in various inference tasks on irregular time grids. Comparisons to state-of-the-art baselines show our model's favourable performance on both synthetic and real-world time-series data.

paragraphs: Many time series contain only partial observations, recorded at irregular times. A model with continuous dynamics can represent what happens between observations and support inference at times absent from the recorded data. This paper addresses two challenges in such models: expressing sufficiently rich dynamics and constructing effective variational approximations for inference.

Continuous latent process flows connect a continuous hidden process to a continuous observable process. The architecture uses a time-dependent normalizing flow driven by a stochastic differential equation. This provides the model's mechanism for decoding latent dynamics into observations while retaining a continuous-time formulation.

The paper also develops a piecewise construction of the variational posterior process. Through trajectory reweighting, the authors derive a variational lower bound for likelihood-based training. Their ablation studies support the usefulness of these contributions across inference tasks on irregular time grids. Comparisons with state-of-the-art baselines show favorable performance on synthetic and real-world time series. Together, the architecture and inference procedure address both what continuous-time dynamics the model can represent and how it can learn from incomplete observations.
summary.tldr: Continuous latent process flows combine stochastic dynamics, normalizing flows, and variational inference to model irregularly observed time series.

title: Continuous Latent Process Flows

abstract: It was estimated that the world produced $59 ZB$ ($5.9 \times 10^{13} GB$) of data in 2020, resulting in the enormous costs of both data storage and transmission. Fortunately, recent advances in deep generative models have spearheaded a new class of so-called "neural compression" algorithms, which significantly outperform traditional codecs in terms of compression ratio. Unfortunately, the application of neural compression garners little commercial interest due to its limited bandwidth; therefore, developing highly efficient frameworks is of critical practical importance. In this paper, we discuss lossless compression using normalizing flows which have demonstrated a great capacity for achieving high compression ratios. As such, we introduce iFlow, a new method for achieving efficient lossless compression. We first propose Modular Scale Transform (MST) and a novel family of numerically invertible flow transformations based on MST. Then we introduce the Uniform Base Conversion System (UBCS), a fast uniform-distribution codec incorporated into iFlow, enabling efficient compression. iFlow achieves state-of-the-art compression ratios and is $5 \times$ quicker than other high-performance schemes. Furthermore, the techniques presented in this paper can be used to accelerate coding time for a broad class of flow-based algorithms.

paragraphs: Neural compression methods can achieve strong compression ratios, but their processing speed can hinder practical use. iFlow addresses this problem for lossless compression based on normalizing flows. Its objective is to preserve the compression advantages of these generative models while making the coding process substantially faster.

The method has two main components. First, the authors introduce the Modular Scale Transform and use it to construct a family of numerically invertible flow transformations. Numerical invertibility matters to lossless compression because decoding must recover the original data exactly. Second, they introduce the Uniform Base Conversion System, a fast codec for uniform distributions that becomes part of the iFlow compression framework.

summary.tldr: iFlow combines numerically invertible transformations with a fast uniform codec to deliver efficient lossless neural compression.

title: iFlow: Numerically Invertible Flows for Efficient Lossless Compression via a Uniform Coder

abstract: As a basic component of SE(3)-equivariant deep feature learning, steerable convolution has recently demonstrated its advantages for 3D semantic analysis. The advantages are, however, brought by expensive computations on dense, volumetric data, which prevent its practical use for efficient processing of 3D data that are inherently sparse. In this paper, we propose a novel design of Sparse Steerable Convolution (SS-Conv) to address the shortcoming; SS-Conv greatly accelerates steerable convolution with sparse tensors, while strictly preserving the property of SE(3)-equivariance. Based on SS-Conv, we propose a general pipeline for precise estimation of object poses, wherein a key design is a Feature-Steering module that takes the full advantage of SE(3)-equivariance and is able to conduct an efficient pose refinement. To verify our designs, we conduct thorough experiments on three tasks of 3D object semantic analysis, including instance-level 6D pose estimation, category-level 6D pose and size estimation, and category-level 6D pose tracking. Our proposed pipeline based on SS-Conv outperforms existing methods on almost all the metrics evaluated by the three tasks. Ablation studies also show the superiority of our SS-Conv over alternative convolutions in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Our code is released publicly at https://github.com/Gorilla-Lab-SCUT/SS-Conv.

paragraphs: Steerable convolutions learn 3D features that transform consistently when objects rotate or translate. Their computational cost on dense volumes can make them poorly suited to inherently sparse 3D data. This paper introduces Sparse Steerable Convolution, or SS-Conv, to accelerate this processing while strictly retaining SE(3)-equivariance, the required consistency under rigid spatial transformations.

SS-Conv operates with sparse tensors and serves as the foundation for an object-pose estimation pipeline. A Feature-Steering module exploits the equivariant features to refine pose efficiently. The contribution connects the mathematical transformation property with a practical refinement operation, making that property useful throughout the estimation process rather than only in feature extraction.

Experiments cover instance-level pose estimation, category-level pose and size estimation, and category-level pose tracking. The pipeline outperforms existing methods on almost all evaluated metrics across these tasks. Ablation studies also favor SS-Conv over alternative convolutions in both accuracy and efficiency. These findings support sparse computation as a way to make equivariant 3D processing more practical without surrendering its defining transformation behavior.
summary.tldr: SS-Conv accelerates equivariant 3D feature learning on sparse data and supports accurate, efficient object-pose estimation and tracking.

title: Sparse Steerable Convolutions: An Efficient Learning of SE(3)-Equivariant Features for Estimation and Tracking of Object Poses in 3D Space

abstract: As predictive models are increasingly being deployed in high-stakes decision making (e.g., loan approvals), there has been growing interest in post-hoc techniques which provide recourse to affected individuals. These techniques generate recourses under the assumption that the underlying predictive model does not change. However, in practice, models are often regularly updated for a variety of reasons (e.g., dataset shifts), thereby rendering previously prescribed recourses ineffective.To address this problem, we propose a novel framework, RObust Algorithmic Recourse (ROAR), that leverages adversarial training for finding recourses that are robust to model shifts. To the best of our knowledge, this work proposes the first ever solution to this critical problem. We also carry out theoretical analysis which underscores the importance of constructing recourses that are robust to model shifts: 1) We quantify the probability of invalidation for recourses generated without accounting for model shifts. 2) We prove that the additional cost incurred due to the robust recourses output by our framework is bounded. Experimental evaluation on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed framework.

paragraphs: Algorithmic recourse tells someone what changes could lead to a favorable prediction, such as approval of a loan application. Such advice is often computed as though the predictive model will remain fixed. In practice, models are updated, and a change that would satisfy today’s model may fail under its replacement.

The paper proposes RObust Algorithmic Recourse, or ROAR, to account for model shifts when constructing advice. It uses adversarial training to find recourses that are robust to those shifts. This makes the stability of the recommendation part of the optimization problem, addressing the possibility that someone acts on advice whose predictive basis later changes.

The theoretical analysis quantifies the probability that recourse generated without considering model shifts becomes invalid. It also proves a bound on the additional cost of robust recourses produced by the framework. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. Together, the results examine both sides of the problem: the risk of fragile advice and the extra cost associated with making advice more robust.
summary.tldr: ROAR uses adversarial training to produce recourse that is robust to model shifts and provides a bound on its additional cost.

title: Towards Robust and Reliable Algorithmic Recourse

abstract: In the paper, we study the underdamped Langevin diffusion (ULD) with strongly-convex potential consisting of finite summation of $N$ smooth components, and propose an efficient discretization method, which requires $O(N+d^\frac{1}{3}N^\frac{2}{3}/\varepsilon^\frac{2}{3})$ gradient evaluations to achieve $\varepsilon$-error (in $\sqrt{\mathbb{E}{\lVert{\cdot}\rVert_2^2}}$ distance) for approximating $d$-dimensional ULD. Moreover, we prove a lower bound of gradient complexity as $\Omega(N+d^\frac{1}{3}N^\frac{2}{3}/\varepsilon^\frac{2}{3})$, which indicates that our method is optimal in dependence of $N$, $\varepsilon$, and $d$. In particular, we apply our method to sample the strongly-log-concave distribution and obtain gradient complexity better than all existing gradient based sampling algorithms. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world data show that our new method consistently outperforms the existing ULD approaches.

Moreover, we prove a lower bound of gradient complexity as $\Omega(N+d^\frac{1}{3}N^\frac{2}{3}/\varepsilon^\frac{2}{3})$, which indicates that our method is optimal in dependence of $N$, $\varepsilon$, and $d$. paragraphs: This paper studies how efficiently a discrete algorithm can approximate underdamped Langevin diffusion. The potential is assumed to be strongly convex and composed of a finite sum of N smooth components. Within that setting, the authors design a discretization method and measure its computational cost through the number of gradient evaluations needed for a specified approximation accuracy.

For dimension d and error ε, the method requires O(N + d^(1/3)N^(2/3)/ε^(2/3)) gradient evaluations in the stated root-mean-square Euclidean distance. A matching lower bound shows that this dependence on component count, dimension, and accuracy is optimal for the analyzed approximation problem. The optimality claim is therefore tied to those quantities and assumptions.

The authors also apply the method to sampling strongly log-concave distributions, obtaining better gradient complexity than existing gradient-based sampling algorithms. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data consistently outperform existing underdamped Langevin approaches. The work combines a matching theoretical cost bound with empirical evidence that the proposed discretization improves the tested sampling procedures.
summary.tldr: A new underdamped Langevin discretization achieves matching upper and lower gradient-complexity bounds under strongly convex finite-sum assumptions.

title: Optimal Underdamped Langevin MCMC Method

abstract: The objective of change point detection (CPD) is to detect significant and abrupt changes in the dynamics of the underlying system of interest through multivariate time series observations. In this work, we develop and analyze an algorithm for CPD that is inspired by a variant of the classical singular spectrum analysis (SSA) approach for time series by combining it with the classical cumulative sum (CUSUM) statistic from sequential hypothesis testing. In particular, we model the underlying dynamics of multivariate time series observations through the spatio-temporal model introduced recently in the multivariate SSA (mSSA) literature. The change point in such a setting corresponds to a change in the underlying spatio-temporal model. As the primary contributions of this work, we develop an algorithm based on CUSUM-statistic to detect such change points in an online fashion. We extend the analysis of CUSUM statistics, traditionally done for the setting of independent observations, to the dependent setting of (multivariate) time series under the spatio-temporal model. Specifically, for a given parameter $h > 0$, our method achieves the following desirable trade-off: when a change happens, it detects it within $O(h)$ time delay on average, while in the absence of change, it does not declare false detection for at least $\exp(\Omega(h))$ time length on average. We conduct empirical experiments using benchmark and synthetic datasets. We find that the proposed method performs competitively or outperforms the state-of-the-art change point detection methods across datasets.

paragraphs: Change point detection aims to recognize abrupt shifts in a system from streams of observations. This paper considers multiple time series whose values have dependencies across both variables and time. It represents their dynamics using a spatio-temporal model from multivariate singular spectrum analysis, with a change point corresponding to a change in that model.

The proposed online algorithm combines this representation with a cumulative-sum statistic that accumulates evidence of change. A central theoretical contribution extends analysis of that statistic from independent observations to dependent time series under the stated model. This directly addresses the temporal dependence built into the problem formulation.

Thus the analysis gives an explicit trade-off between prompt detection and false alarms. Experiments on benchmark and synthetic datasets find performance competitive with, or better than, state-of-the-art methods across the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: An online change detector combines multivariate time-series structure with cumulative evidence and proves a delay–false-alarm trade-off under its model.

title: Change Point Detection via Multivariate Singular Spectrum Analysis

abstract: Probabilistic numerics casts numerical tasks, such the numerical solution of differential equations, as inference problems to be solved. One approach is to model the unknown quantity of interest as a random variable, and to constrain this variable using data generated during the course of a traditional numerical method. However, data may be nonlinearly related to the quantity of interest, rendering the proper conditioning of random variables difficult and limiting the range of numerical tasks that can be addressed. Instead, this paper proposes to construct probabilistic numerical methods based only on the final output from a traditional method. A convergent sequence of approximations to the quantity of interest constitute a dataset, from which the limiting quantity of interest can be extrapolated, in a probabilistic analogue of Richardson’s deferred approach to the limit. This black box approach (1) massively expands the range of tasks to which probabilistic numerics can be applied, (2) inherits the features and performance of state-of-the-art numerical methods, and (3) enables provably higher orders of convergence to be achieved. Applications are presented for nonlinear ordinary and partial differential equations, as well as for eigenvalue problems—a setting for which no probabilistic numerical methods have yet been developed.

paragraphs: Probabilistic numerics treats a numerical computation as an inference problem: the unknown answer is represented probabilistically and informed by numerical evidence. One established approach uses data produced inside a conventional numerical method. That becomes difficult when the internal data have a nonlinear relationship to the answer, because conditioning the probability model can be challenging.

This paper instead uses only the final outputs of conventional numerical methods. A convergent sequence of approximations becomes the dataset, and a probabilistic model extrapolates the quantity those approximations approach. The idea is a probabilistic counterpart of Richardson extrapolation. Working with outputs allows the approach to retain the features and performance of existing numerical solvers without modeling their internal calculations.

The authors show that this construction can achieve provably higher orders of convergence and substantially broaden the tasks accessible to probabilistic numerics. Applications include nonlinear ordinary and partial differential equations, along with eigenvalue problems. The key prerequisite in the construction is a convergent approximation sequence: its outputs supply the evidence for estimating the limiting answer.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic extrapolation of conventional solver outputs broadens probabilistic numerics and can achieve higher convergence orders.

title: Black Box Probabilistic Numerics

abstract: The importance of aggregated count data, which is calculated from the data of multiple individuals, continues to increase. Collective Graphical Model (CGM) is a probabilistic approach to the analysis of aggregated data. One of the most important operations in CGM is maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference of unobserved variables under given observations. Because the MAP inference problem for general CGMs has been shown to be NP-hard, an approach that solves an approximate problem has been proposed. However, this approach has two major drawbacks. First, the quality of the solution deteriorates when the values in the count tables are small, because the approximation becomes inaccurate. Second, since continuous relaxation is applied, the integrality constraints of the output are violated. To resolve these problems, this paper proposes a new method for MAP inference for CGMs on path graphs. Our method is based on the Difference of Convex Algorithm (DCA), which is a general methodology to minimize a function represented as the sum of a convex function and a concave function. In our algorithm, important subroutines in DCA can be efficiently calculated by minimum convex cost flow algorithms. Experiments show that the proposed method outputs higher quality solutions than the conventional approach.

paragraphs: Collective graphical models analyze counts aggregated across many individuals. One important task is inferring the most probable values of unobserved variables given observed counts. This maximum a posteriori inference problem is NP-hard for general collective graphical models, motivating methods that replace the original problem with an approximation.

The paper identifies two weaknesses in an existing approximation. It becomes inaccurate when count-table entries are small, reducing solution quality, and its continuous relaxation can produce outputs that violate integer-count requirements. The authors develop a method for models on path graphs that addresses these issues by working with a discrete formulation.

Their approach uses the difference of convex algorithm, which handles an objective expressed through convex and concave components. Key subroutines can be computed efficiently using minimum convex cost flow algorithms. Experiments produce higher-quality solutions than the conventional approach. The contribution concerns avoiding the stated approximations for path-structured models; the reported result does not assert a general solution to the NP-hard inference problem across arbitrary graphs.
summary.tldr: A discrete optimization method improves collective graphical model inference on path graphs while addressing small-count approximation errors and integer constraints.

title: Non-approximate Inference for Collective Graphical Models on Path Graphs via Discrete Difference of Convex Algorithm

abstract: We present Native Chinese Reader (NCR), a new machine reading comprehension MRC) dataset with particularly long articles in both modern and classical Chinese. NCR is collected from the exam questions for the Chinese course in China’s high schools, which are designed to evaluate the language proficiency of native Chinese youth. Existing Chinese MRC datasets are either domain-specific or focusing on short contexts of a few hundred characters in modern Chinese only. By contrast, NCR contains 8390 documents with an average length of 1024 characters covering a wide range of Chinese writing styles, including modern articles, classical literature and classical poetry. A total of 20477 questions on these documents also require strong reasoning abilities and common sense to figure out the correct answers. We implemented multiple baseline models using popular Chinese pre-trained models and additionally launched an online competition using our dataset to examine the limit of current methods. The best model achieves 59% test accuracy while human evaluation shows an average accuracy of 79%, which indicates a significant performance gap between current MRC models and native Chinese speakers.

abstract: With the rapid emergence of graph representation learning, the construction of new large-scale datasets are necessary to distinguish model capabilities and accurately assess the strengths and weaknesses of each technique. By carefully analyzing existing graph databases, we identify 3 critical components important for advancing the field of graph representation learning: (1) large graphs, (2) many graphs, and (3) class diversity. To date, no single graph database offers all of these desired properties. We introduce MalNet , the largest public graph database ever constructed, representing a large-scale ontology of malicious software function call graphs. MalNet contains over 1.2 million graphs, averaging over 15k nodes and 35k edges per graph, across a hierarchy of 47 types and 696 families. Compared to the popular REDDIT-12K database, MalNet offers 105x more graphs, 44x larger graphs on average, and 63x more classes. We provide a detailed analysis of MalNet, discussing its properties and provenance, along with the evaluation of state-of-the-art machine learning and graph neural network techniques. The unprecedented scale and diversity of MalNet offers exciting opportunities to advance the frontiers of graph representation learning--enabling new discoveries and research into imbalanced classification, explainability and the impact of class hardness. The database is publicly available at www.mal-net.org.

The authors argue that existing graph databases do not bring all three together, restricting how researchers can distinguish the strengths and weaknesses of different methods.

The scale and category diversity also create opportunities to investigate uneven class representation, explainability, and differences in classification difficulty; these are research possibilities enabled by the dataset.
summary.tldr: MalNet combines over 1.2 million large software graphs with diverse hierarchical labels to broaden evaluation of graph learning methods.

title: A Large-Scale Database for Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Recent advances in Natural Language Processing (NLP), and specifically automated Question Answering (QA) systems, have demonstrated both impressive linguistic fluency and a pernicious tendency to reflect social biases. In this study, we introduce Q-Pain, a dataset for assessing bias in medical QA in the context of pain management, one of the most challenging forms of clinical decision-making. Along with the dataset, we propose a new, rigorous framework, including a sample experimental design, to measure the potential biases present when making treatment decisions. We demonstrate its use by assessing two reference Question-Answering systems, GPT-2 and GPT-3, and find statistically significant differences in treatment between intersectional race-gender subgroups, thus reaffirming the risks posed by AI in medical settings, and the need for datasets like ours to ensure safety before medical AI applications are deployed.

Pain treatment is the specific decision-making setting in which the dataset makes those concerns available for systematic study.

The contribution includes an evaluation framework and a sample experimental design for measuring potential bias in treatment decisions. This gives researchers both material to evaluate and a proposed structure for conducting the evaluation. The focus is on whether treatment responses differ across social groups, connecting model behavior to a consequential medical use case.

The authors demonstrate the framework with GPT-2 and GPT-3 and find statistically significant treatment differences across subgroups defined jointly by race and gender. These results provide evidence of disparities in the evaluated systems and setting. They support the authors’ call for targeted bias assessment before medical deployment, with Q-Pain offered as a resource for that assessment.
summary.tldr: Q-Pain evaluates bias in pain-management question answering and finds significant treatment differences across race-gender subgroups in GPT-2 and GPT-3.

title: Q-Pain: A Question Answering Dataset to Measure Social Bias in Pain Management

abstract: Hierarchical clustering over graphs is a fundamental task in data mining and machine learning with applications in many domains including phylogenetics, social network analysis, and information retrieval. Specifically, we consider the recently popularized objective function for hierarchical clustering due to Dasgupta~\cite{Dasgupta16}, namely, minimum cost hierarchical partitioning. Previous algorithms for (approximately) minimizing this objective function require linear time/space complexity. In many applications the underlying graph can be massive in size making it computationally challenging to process the graph even using a linear time/space algorithm. As a result, there is a strong interest in designing algorithms that can perform global computation using only sublinear resources (space, time, and communication). The focus of this work is to study hierarchical clustering for massive graphs under three well-studied models of sublinear computation which focus on space, time, and communication, respectively, as the primary resources to optimize: (1) (dynamic) streaming model where edges are presented as a stream, (2) query model where the graph is queried using neighbor and degree queries, (3) massively parallel computation (MPC) model where the edges of the graph are partitioned over several machines connected via a communication channel.We design sublinear algorithms for hierarchical clustering in all three models above. At the heart of our algorithmic results is a view of the objective in terms of cuts in the graph, which allows us to use a relaxed notion of cut sparsifiers to do hierarchical clustering while introducing only a small distortion in the objective function. Our main algorithmic contributions are then to show how cut sparsifiers of the desired form can be efficiently constructed in the query model and the MPC model. We complement our algorithmic results by establishing nearly matching lower bounds that rule out the possibility of designing algorithms with better performance guarantees in each of these models.

This enables the use of a relaxed form of cut sparsifier, a reduced representation that preserves enough cut information to keep distortion of the clustering objective small. The authors develop sublinear algorithms across all three models, with efficient sparsifier construction in the query and massively parallel models forming major contributions.

The results show how a global clustering objective can be approached without paying the previously required linear resource costs in the relevant models. The paper also establishes nearly matching lower bounds for each model. Those bounds complement the algorithms by showing that substantially better performance guarantees are ruled out within the studied computational settings.
summary.tldr: Relaxed cut sparsifiers enable hierarchical graph clustering with sublinear resources across streaming, query, and massively parallel models.

title: Sublinear Algorithms for Hierarchical Clustering

abstract: An interactive mechanism is an algorithm that stores a data set and answers adaptively chosen queries to it. The mechanism is called differentially private, if any adversary cannot distinguish whether a specific individual is in the data set by interacting with the mechanism. We study composition properties of differential privacy in concurrent compositions. In this setting, an adversary interacts with $k$ interactive mechanisms in parallel and can interleave its queries to the mechanisms arbitrarily. Previously, Vadhan and Wang [2021] proved an optimal concurrent composition theorem for pure-differential privacy. We significantly generalize and extend their results. Namely, we prove optimal parallel composition properties for several major notions of differential privacy in the literature, including approximate DP, Renyi DP, and zero-concentrated DP. Our results demonstrate that the adversary gains no advantage by interleaving its queries to independently running mechanisms. Hence, interactivity is a feature that differential privacy grants us for free.Concurrently and independently of our work, Vadhan and Zhang [2022] proved an optimal concurrent composition theorem for f-DP [Dong et al., 2022], which implies our result for the approximate DP case.

paragraphs: An interactive private mechanism holds a dataset and answers queries that can depend on previous answers. Differential privacy limits what this interaction can reveal about an individual's participation. The paper asks how privacy guarantees combine when an adversary can interact with several independently running mechanisms and freely alternate queries among them.

This concurrent setting allows information obtained from one mechanism to shape questions sent to another. The authors prove optimal composition results for approximate differential privacy, Rényi differential privacy, and zero-concentrated differential privacy. Their theorems extend earlier work that established an optimal concurrent composition result for pure differential privacy.

The central conclusion is that interleaving queries gives the adversary no additional advantage in the studied composition setting. Consequently, accounting for the combined privacy cost does not require an extra penalty simply because these independent mechanisms support interactivity. The abstract also identifies concurrent independent work on another privacy framework that implies the approximate-privacy case, while this paper establishes results across the other named notions.
summary.tldr: Optimal composition theorems show that interleaving queries to independently running private mechanisms adds no privacy cost under several major privacy notions.

title: Composition Theorems for Interactive Differential Privacy

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of networked multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), where a number of agents are deployed as a partially connected network and each interacts only with nearby agents. Networked MARL requires all agents to make decisions in a decentralized manner to optimize a global objective with restricted communication between neighbors over the network. Inspired by the fact that sharing plays a key role in human's learning of cooperation, we propose LToS, a hierarchically decentralized MARL framework that enables agents to learn to dynamically share reward with neighbors so as to encourage agents to cooperate on the global objective through collectives. For each agent, the high-level policy learns how to share reward with neighbors to decompose the global objective, while the low-level policy learns to optimize the local objective induced by the high-level policies in the neighborhood. The two policies form a bi-level optimization and learn alternately. We empirically demonstrate that LToS outperforms existing methods in both social dilemma and networked MARL scenarios across scales.

paragraphs: This paper studies cooperation among agents arranged in a partially connected network. Each agent interacts and communicates only with nearby agents, yet the group must optimize a global objective. The challenge is to make decentralized decisions serve that collective objective despite the restrictions on who can exchange information.

LToS introduces two levels of policy for each agent. The high-level policy learns how to share reward with neighbors, shaping the local objectives pursued across the network. The low-level policy learns actions that optimize the objective induced by reward-sharing policies in its neighborhood. These policies are trained alternately as a two-level optimization problem.

Reward sharing is therefore something agents learn dynamically, rather than merely a fixed rule supplied before action learning begins. This provides a mechanism for encouraging local cooperation in support of the global goal. Experiments in social dilemmas and networked multi-agent settings across scales show LToS outperforming existing methods. The evidence supports learned reward allocation as a useful component of decentralized cooperation in the evaluated scenarios.
summary.tldr: LToS learns how neighboring agents share rewards and choose actions to improve decentralized cooperation.

title: Learning to Share in Networked Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Two-sample tests are important in statistics and machine learning, both as tools for scientific discovery as well as to detect distribution shifts.This led to the development of many sophisticated test procedures going beyond the standard supervised learning frameworks, whose usage can require specialized knowledge about two-sample testing. We use a simple test that takes the mean discrepancy of a witness function as the test statistic and prove that minimizing a squared loss leads to a witness with optimal testing power. This allows us to leverage recent advancements in AutoML. Without any user input about the problems at hand, and using the same method for all our experiments, our AutoML two-sample test achieves competitive performance on a diverse distribution shift benchmark as well as on challenging two-sample testing problems.

paragraphs: A two-sample test asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. This matters both for scientific comparisons and for detecting changes in the data a machine-learning system encounters. The paper seeks to make these tests easier to use by connecting them to familiar supervised learning tools, reducing the need for specialized choices about testing procedures.

The method learns a witness function: a function whose average output can differ between the two samples. That difference becomes the test statistic. The central theoretical result shows that minimizing a squared loss leads to a witness with optimal testing power. This connection makes automated machine learning relevant: AutoML can supply the learning machinery for constructing the witness.

The authors apply the same automated method across a diverse distribution-shift benchmark and challenging testing problems, without user input specific to each problem. They report competitive performance. The finding supports a practical route to two-sample testing in which advances in automated prediction can also improve the construction of statistical tests.
summary.tldr: A squared-loss formulation lets AutoML learn powerful two-sample tests that perform competitively without problem-specific user input.

title: AutoML Two-Sample Test

abstract: Placement and routing are two critical yet time-consuming steps of chip design in modern VLSI systems. Distinct from traditional heuristic solvers, this paper on one hand proposes an RL-based model for mixed-size macro placement, which differs from existing learning-based placers that often consider the macro by coarse grid-based mask. While the standard cells are placed via gradient-based GPU acceleration. On the other hand, a one-shot conditional generative routing model, which is composed of a special-designed input-size-adapting generator and a bi-discriminator, is devised to perform one-shot routing to the pins within each net, and the order of nets to route is adaptively learned. Combining these techniques, we develop a flexible and efficient neural pipeline, which to our best knowledge, is the first joint placement and routing network without involving any traditional heuristic solver. Experimental results on chip design benchmarks showcase the effectiveness of our approach, with code that will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Chip design requires placing components and routing the connections between them, both of which can be time-consuming. This paper develops a neural pipeline that handles both stages. Its placement approach combines reinforcement learning for mixed-size macros with GPU-accelerated, gradient-based placement for standard cells.

The macro-placement model differs from learning-based placers that represent macros through coarse grid masks. For routing, the authors introduce a conditional generative model that connects the pins within each net in one shot. It combines a generator that adapts to input size with a two-discriminator design, while the order in which nets are routed is learned adaptively.

Together, these components form a joint placement-and-routing network without a traditional heuristic solver. The authors qualify their novelty claim as the first such network to their knowledge. Chip-design benchmark experiments demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. The contribution is the integrated use of learned and gradient-based components across both design stages, including learned routing order and direct generation of within-net connections.
summary.tldr: The paper combines reinforcement-learning placement, gradient-based cell placement, and generative routing into a joint neural chip-design pipeline.

title: The Policy-gradient Placement and Generative Routing Neural Networks for Chip Design

abstract: This is the first attempt at considering human influence in the reinforcement learning control of a robotic lower limb prosthesis toward symmetrical walking in real world situations. We propose a collaborative multi-agent reinforcement learning (cMARL) solution framework for this highly complex and challenging human-prosthesis collaboration (HPC) problem. The design of an automatic controller of the robot within the HPC context is based on accessible physical features or measurements that are known to affect walking performance. Comparisons are made with the current state-of-the-art robot control designs, which are single-agent based, as well as existing MARL solution approaches tailored to the problem, including multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG) and counterfactual multi-agent policy gradient (COMA). Results show that, when compared to these approaches, treating the human and robot as coupled agents and using estimated human adaption in robot control design can achieve lower stage cost, peak error, and symmetry value to ensure better human walking performance. Additionally, our approach accelerates learning of walking tasks and increases learning success rate. The proposed framework can potentially be further developed to examine how human and robotic lower limb prosthesis interact, an area that little is known about. Advancing cMARL toward real world applications such as HPC for normative walking sets a good example of how AI can positively impact on people’s lives.

This paper treats that interaction as a collaborative control problem, with symmetrical walking as the objective. Its reinforcement-learning framework represents the human and prosthesis as coupled agents and incorporates estimated human adaptation into the robot's controller.

The controller uses accessible physical measurements or features known to affect walking performance. The authors compare their collaborative approach with single-agent robot controllers and with adaptations of two existing multi-agent methods, MADDPG and COMA. These comparisons examine whether explicitly accounting for the coupled human response improves control beyond the alternative approaches considered.

The reported results show lower stage cost, peak error, and symmetry value, which the authors associate with better walking performance. The framework also learns walking tasks faster and achieves a higher learning success rate. Beyond these findings, the authors identify a possible future role in studying human-prosthesis interaction. That broader scientific use remains a potential development of the proposed framework.
summary.tldr: Modeling a person and robotic prosthesis as collaborating agents improves reported walking-control outcomes and learning success.

title: Human-Robotic Prosthesis as Collaborating Agents for Symmetrical Walking

abstract: In zero-sum games, an NE strategy tends to be overly conservative confronted with opponents of limited rationality, because it does not actively exploit their weaknesses. From another perspective, best responding to an estimated opponent model is vulnerable to estimation errors and lacks safety guarantees. Inspired by the recent success of real-time search algorithms in developing superhuman AI, we investigate the dilemma of safety and opponent exploitation and present a novel real-time search framework, called Safe Exploitation Search (SES), which continuously interpolates between the two extremes of online strategy refinement. We provide SES with a theoretically upper-bounded exploitability and a lower-bounded evaluation performance. Additionally, SES enables computationally efficient online adaptation to a possibly updating opponent model, while previous safe exploitation methods have to recompute for the whole game. Empirical results show that SES significantly outperforms NE baselines and previous algorithms while keeping exploitability low at the same time.

paragraphs: In a zero-sum game, a Nash-equilibrium strategy can be conservative against an opponent whose weaknesses could be exploited. Directly optimizing against an estimated opponent model introduces a different problem: mistakes in that estimate can leave the player vulnerable. This paper studies how to improve performance against such opponents while retaining control over that vulnerability.

Safe Exploitation Search is a real-time search framework that continuously interpolates between these strategy-refinement extremes. The authors provide a theoretical upper bound on exploitability and a lower bound on evaluation performance. These bounds make the safety–exploitation tradeoff explicit, rather than treating either pure equilibrium play or an unrestricted response to the opponent model as the only option.

SES also supports efficient online adaptation as the opponent model changes, whereas previous safe-exploitation methods require recomputation across the whole game. Experiments report substantially better performance than equilibrium baselines and previous algorithms while maintaining low exploitability. Here, safety means bounded strategic vulnerability within the game, alongside the ability to capitalize on an opponent's weaknesses.
summary.tldr: Safe Exploitation Search adapts to opponent weaknesses through real-time refinement while providing bounds on exploitability and evaluation performance.

title: Safe Opponent-Exploitation Subgame Refinement

abstract: This paper studies a simple extension of image-based Masked Autoencoders (MAE) to self-supervised representation learning from audio spectrograms. Following the Transformer encoder-decoder design in MAE, our Audio-MAE first encodes audio spectrogram patches with a high masking ratio, feeding only the non-masked tokens through encoder layers. The decoder then re-orders and decodes the encoded context padded with mask tokens, in order to reconstruct the input spectrogram. We find it beneficial to incorporate local window attention in the decoder, as audio spectrograms are highly correlated in local time and frequency bands. We then fine-tune the encoder with a lower masking ratio on target datasets. Empirically, Audio-MAE sets new state-of-the-art performance on six audio and speech classification tasks, outperforming other recent models that use external supervised pre-training. Our code and models is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AudioMAE.

paragraphs: Audio-MAE adapts masked autoencoding from images to audio spectrograms, which organize sound information across time and frequency. The self-supervised learning task is to reconstruct a spectrogram after hiding many of its patches. This lets the model learn representations from the structure of audio itself.

A Transformer encoder processes only the visible patches, using a high masking ratio during this stage. The decoder restores their ordering, inserts tokens for the missing patches, and reconstructs the input. The authors find that local-window attention improves the decoder, matching the strong relationships among nearby time and frequency regions in spectrograms.

For downstream classification, the encoder is fine-tuned using a lower masking ratio. Audio-MAE achieves reported state-of-the-art results on six audio and speech classification tasks, outperforming recent models that use external supervised pretraining. These empirical findings show that masked spectrogram reconstruction can produce useful audio representations. They also identify a concrete adaptation to audio’s local structure within an otherwise straightforward extension of the image-based method.
summary.tldr: Audio-MAE learns audio representations by reconstructing heavily masked spectrograms, achieving strong results across six classification tasks.

title: Masked Autoencoders that Listen

abstract: Unlike existing knowledge distillation methods focus on the baseline settings, where the teacher models and training strategies are not that strong and competing as state-of-the-art approaches, this paper presents a method dubbed DIST to distill better from a stronger teacher. We empirically find that the discrepancy of predictions between the student and a stronger teacher may tend to be fairly severer. As a result, the exact match of predictions in KL divergence would disturb the training and make existing methods perform poorly. In this paper, we show that simply preserving the relations between the predictions of teacher and student would suffice, and propose a correlation-based loss to capture the intrinsic inter-class relations from the teacher explicitly. Besides, considering that different instances have different semantic similarities to each class, we also extend this relational match to the intra-class level. Our method is simple yet practical, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it adapts well to various architectures, model sizes and training strategies, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using predictions from a teacher. This paper examines a problem that can arise when the teacher is especially strong: the student's predictions may differ substantially from the teacher's, and forcing an exact match through KL divergence can disrupt training. The authors report this as an empirical motivation for changing the distillation objective.

Their method, DIST, asks the student to preserve relationships within predictions instead of matching every predicted value exactly. A correlation-based loss captures relationships between classes in the teacher's outputs. The method also matches relationships within each class across different instances, reflecting that examples can have different semantic similarities to that class.

Experiments show that DIST adapts to different architectures, model sizes, and training strategies, with consistently state-of-the-art results reported for image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. The findings support relational matching as a practical way to learn from stronger teachers. They show that useful teacher information can be transferred without requiring exact agreement between teacher and student predictions.
summary.tldr: DIST improves distillation from strong teachers by matching prediction relationships through correlation-based losses.

title: Knowledge Distillation from A Stronger Teacher

abstract: Representations learned by pre-training a neural network on a large dataset are increasingly used successfully to perform a variety of downstream tasks. In this work, we take a closer look at how features are encoded in such pre-trained representations. We find that learned representations in a given layer exhibit a degree of diffuse redundancy, ie, any randomly chosen subset of neurons in the layer that is larger than a threshold size shares a large degree of similarity with the full layer and is able to perform similarly as the whole layer on a variety of downstream tasks. For example, a linear probe trained on $20\%$ of randomly picked neurons from the penultimate layer of a ResNet50 pre-trained on ImageNet1k achieves an accuracy within $5\%$ of a linear probe trained on the full layer of neurons for downstream CIFAR10 classification. We conduct experiments on different neural architectures (including CNNs and Transformers) pre-trained on both ImageNet1k and ImageNet21k and evaluate a variety of downstream tasks taken from the VTAB benchmark. We find that the loss \& dataset used during pre-training largely govern the degree of diffuse redundancy and the "critical mass" of neurons needed often depends on the downstream task, suggesting that there is a task-inherent redundancy-performance Pareto frontier. Our findings shed light on the nature of representations learned by pre-trained deep neural networks and suggest that entire layers might not be necessary to perform many downstream tasks. We investigate the potential for exploiting this redundancy to achieve efficient generalization for downstream tasks and also draw caution to certain possible unintended consequences. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/nvedant07/diffused-redundancy}.
