paragraphs: A pretrained network's useful information may be distributed broadly enough that many subsets of its neurons retain similar capabilities. This paper studies that phenomenon as diffuse redundancy. The authors find that randomly selected subsets above a threshold size can resemble the full layer's representation and perform similarly on downstream tasks.

One example uses the penultimate layer of an ImageNet1k-pretrained ResNet50. A linear probe trained on a random 20% of its neurons achieves CIFAR10 accuracy within 5% of a probe using the entire layer. Broader experiments include convolutional networks and Transformers, two pretraining datasets, and multiple downstream tasks from VTAB.

The amount of redundancy depends substantially on the pretraining loss and dataset, while the number of neurons needed often depends on the downstream task. This suggests a task-dependent tradeoff between retained representation size and performance. The findings motivate exploring more efficient transfer using only part of a layer, without establishing that the same fraction will suffice for every network or task.
summary.tldr: Pretrained layers often distribute useful information redundantly, allowing sufficiently large random neuron subsets to retain substantial downstream performance.

title: Diffused Redundancy in Pre-trained Representations

abstract: Generative Models (GMs) have attracted considerable attention due to their tremendous success in various domains, such as computer vision where they are capable to generate impressive realistic-looking images. Likelihood-based GMs are attractive due to the possibility to generate new data by a single model evaluation. However, they typically achieve lower sample quality compared to state-of-the-art score-based Diffusion Models (DMs). This paper provides a significant step in the direction of addressing this limitation. The idea is to borrow one of the strengths of score-based DMs, which is the ability to perform accurate density estimation in low-density regions and to address manifold overfitting by means of data mollification. We propose a view of data mollification within likelihood-based GMs as a continuation method, whereby the optimization objective smoothly transitions from simple-to-optimize to the original target. Crucially, data mollification can be implemented by adding one line of code in the optimization loop, and we demonstrate that this provides a boost in generation quality of likelihood-based GMs, without computational overheads. We report results on real-world image data sets and UCI benchmarks with popular likelihood-based GMs, including variants of variational autoencoders and normalizing flows, showing large improvements in FID score and density estimation.

paragraphs: Likelihood-based generative models are attractive because they can produce new data with a single model evaluation, but their sample quality often trails leading score-based diffusion models. This paper borrows data mollification, a smoothing idea associated with diffusion models, to improve how likelihood-based generators are optimized.

The authors interpret mollification as a continuation method. Training begins with an objective that is easier to optimize and gradually transitions toward the original target. The motivation includes improving density estimation in low-density regions and addressing manifold overfitting. This connects a change in the training data’s treatment to a smoother progression through the optimization problem.

The proposed modification can be added with one line in the optimization loop, and the authors report improved generation quality without computational overhead. Tests on real-world image datasets and UCI benchmarks include variants of variational autoencoders and normalizing flows, showing large improvements in FID and density estimation. The findings support a lightweight training change as a useful way to improve the evaluated likelihood-based models.
summary.tldr: Gradually smoothing the training objective through data mollification improves tested likelihood-based generators with a one-line training change.

title: One-Line-of-Code Data Mollification Improves Optimization of Likelihood-based Generative Models

abstract: Adaptive optimization methods are well known to achieve superior convergence relative to vanilla gradient methods. The traditional viewpoint in optimization, particularly in convex optimization, explains this improved performance by arguing that, unlike vanilla gradient schemes, adaptive algorithms mimic the behavior of a second-order method by adapting to the *global* geometry of the loss function. We argue that in the context of neural network optimization, this traditional viewpoint is insufficient. Instead, we advocate for a *local* trajectory analysis. For iterate trajectories produced by running a generic optimization algorithm OPT, we introduce $R^{\text{OPT}}\_{\text{med}}$, a statistic that is analogous to the condition number of the loss Hessian evaluated at the iterates. Through extensive experiments on language models where adaptive algorithms converge faster than vanilla gradient methods like SGD, we show that adaptive methods such as Adam bias the trajectories towards regions where $R^{\text{Adam}}_{\text{med}}$ is small, where one might expect faster optimization. By contrast, SGD (with momentum) biases the trajectories towards regions where $R^{\text{SGD}}\_{\text{med}}$ is comparatively large. We complement these empirical observations with a theoretical result that provably demonstrates this phenomenon in the simplified setting of a two-layer linear network. We view our findings as evidence for the need of a new explanation of the success of adaptive methods, one that is different than the conventional wisdom.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers are often explained as adjusting to the overall geometry of a loss function, resembling methods that use second-order information. This paper argues that this account is insufficient for neural networks. It instead examines the local regions encountered along an optimizer’s path, asking whether different algorithms steer training into differently conditioned parts of the loss landscape.

The authors introduce a trajectory statistic analogous to the condition number of the loss Hessian at successive iterates. In language-model experiments where adaptive methods converge faster, Adam tends to visit regions with smaller values of this statistic. Momentum SGD tends to visit regions with comparatively larger values, where optimization might be expected to proceed less easily.

A theoretical result demonstrates the phenomenon in a simplified two-layer linear network. Together, the experiments and analysis support examining how an optimizer shapes its trajectory, alongside how it responds to geometry. The paper presents this as evidence for a revised explanation of adaptive optimization’s success, with the formal demonstration limited to the simplified network setting.
summary.tldr: Experiments and a simplified theoretical result suggest that adaptive optimizers favor training paths through more favorably conditioned local regions.

title: How Does Adaptive Optimization Impact Local Neural Network Geometry?

abstract: Combinatorial optimization (CO) problems are often NP-hard and thus out of reach for exact algorithms, making them a tempting domain to apply machine learning methods. The highly structured constraints in these problems can hinder either optimization or sampling directly in the solution space.On the other hand, GFlowNets have recently emerged as a powerful machinery to efficiently sample from composite unnormalized densities sequentially and have the potential to amortize such solution-searching processes in CO, as well as generate diverse solution candidates.In this paper, we design Markov decision processes (MDPs) for different combinatorial problems and propose to train conditional GFlowNets to sample from the solution space. Efficient training techniques are also developed to benefit long-range credit assignment.Through extensive experiments on a variety of different CO tasks with synthetic and realistic data, we demonstrate that GFlowNet policies can efficiently find high-quality solutions.Our implementation is open-sourced at https://github.com/zdhNarsil/GFlowNet-CombOpt.

paragraphs: Combinatorial optimization involves searching among discrete candidate solutions, often under tightly structured constraints. Many such problems are NP-hard, making exact solution methods difficult to use at scale. This paper investigates whether GFlowNets can learn to generate useful candidates efficiently while accommodating the structure of different graph optimization problems.

The authors formulate different combinatorial problems as Markov decision processes and train conditional GFlowNets to sample solutions. This provides a sequential construction process for candidates rather than requiring direct search across the full solution space. They also develop training techniques for long-range credit assignment, helping connect decisions made during construction with the eventual quality of a completed solution.

The motivation includes reusing a learned policy across solution searches and generating diverse candidates. Experiments across multiple combinatorial tasks, using synthetic and realistic data, show that the resulting policies can efficiently find high-quality solutions. These findings establish practical promise for learned sequential sampling in constrained optimization. They concern solution quality and efficiency in the tested problems, without claiming that the approach produces exact optima.
summary.tldr: Conditional GFlowNets learn sequential solution-generation policies that efficiently find high-quality candidates for graph combinatorial optimization problems.

title: Let the Flows Tell: Solving Graph Combinatorial Problems with GFlowNets

abstract: In this paper, we take a new look at real-world image super-resolution (real-SR) from a multi-task learning perspective. We demonstrate that the conventional formulation of real-SR can be viewed as solving multiple distinct degradation tasks using a single shared model. This poses a challenge known as task competition or task conflict in multi-task learning, where certain tasks dominate the learning process, resulting in poor performance on other tasks. This problem is exacerbated in the case of real-SR, due to the involvement of numerous degradation tasks. To address the issue of task competition in real-SR, we propose a task grouping approach. Our approach efficiently identifies the degradation tasks where a real-SR model falls short and groups these unsatisfactory tasks into multiple task groups. We then utilize the task groups to fine-tune the real-SR model in a simple way, which effectively mitigates task competition and facilitates knowledge transfer. Extensive experiments demonstrate our method achieves significantly enhanced performance across a wide range of degradation scenarios.

paragraphs: Real-world image super-resolution must restore images affected by many different degradation processes. This paper views those processes as distinct learning tasks handled by one shared model. From that perspective, uneven restoration quality can arise because some tasks dominate training and interfere with learning the others.

The authors propose grouping tasks to address this competition. Their method identifies degradation tasks on which the super-resolution model performs poorly, organizes those tasks into several groups, and uses the groups to fine-tune the model. The approach targets weaknesses in the existing model while aiming to make knowledge transfer between tasks more effective.

Experiments show significantly improved performance across a wide range of degradation scenarios. The finding supports treating the organization of restoration tasks as an important part of training. A model’s challenge is not simply encountering numerous degradations; it must also learn them without allowing some to overwhelm others. The proposed grouping method provides a practical way to reduce that conflict through targeted fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: Grouping poorly learned degradation tasks for fine-tuning reduces task competition and improves real-world image super-resolution.

title: Real-World Image Super-Resolution as Multi-Task Learning

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of localizing and inferring multiple change points, in non-parametric multivariate time series settings. Specifically, we consider a multivariate time series with potentially short-range dependence, whose underlying distributions have Hölder smooth densities and can change over time in a piecewise-constant manner. The change points, which correspond to the times when the distribution changes, are unknown. We present the limiting distributions of the change point estimators under the scenarios where the minimal jump size vanishes or remains constant. Such results have not been revealed in the literature in non-parametric change point settings. As byproducts, we develop a sharp estimator that can accurately localize the change points in multivariate non-parametric time series, and a consistent block-type long-run variance estimator. Numerical studies are provided to complement our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to locate multiple times when the probability distribution of a multivariate time series changes. The observations may have short-range dependence, so nearby measurements need not be independent. Rather than specifying a fixed parametric family, the analysis assumes distributions with Hölder-smooth densities that remain constant within successive time segments.

The main contribution describes the limiting distributions of estimated change times. These results cover both changes whose smallest jump shrinks as the sample grows and changes whose smallest jump stays constant. Characterizing how estimates fluctuate around the true change times supports statistical inference beyond simply reporting a detected boundary.

The analysis also yields an estimator for accurately locating changes and a consistent block-based estimator of long-run variance, which accounts for variability in dependent observations. Numerical studies complement the theoretical results. The findings therefore connect detection and inference in a setting that permits multivariate, nonparametric data, while retaining the stated smoothness, dependence, and piecewise-constant distribution assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper develops change-point estimators and limiting distributions for multivariate time series with smooth densities and short-range dependence.

title: Change point detection and inference in multivariate non-parametric models under mixing conditions

abstract: Machine learning for differential equations paves the way for computationally efficient alternatives to numerical solvers, with potentially broad impacts in science and engineering. Though current algorithms typically require simulated training data tailored to a given setting, one may instead wish to learn useful information from heterogeneous sources, or from real dynamical systems observations that are messy or incomplete. In this work, we learn general-purpose representations of PDEs from heterogeneous data by implementing joint embedding methods for self-supervised learning (SSL), a framework for unsupervised representation learning that has had notable success in computer vision. Our representation outperforms baseline approaches to invariant tasks, such as regressing the coefficients of a PDE, while also improving the time-stepping performance of neural solvers. We hope that our proposed methodology will prove useful in the eventual development of general-purpose foundation models for PDEs.

paragraphs: Machine learning methods for partial differential equations often rely on simulated training data prepared for a particular setting. This paper investigates learning more general representations from heterogeneous data. The motivation is to make useful information available across varied sources, including the broader challenge of observations from dynamical systems that may be messy or incomplete.

The authors apply joint embedding methods for self-supervised learning, bringing a representation-learning framework used successfully in computer vision into the PDE setting. The aim is to learn representations that support multiple uses, instead of making the training objective specific to just one solver task. Lie symmetries provide the paper's stated organizing theme.

The learned representation outperforms baseline approaches on invariant tasks, including estimating PDE coefficients, and improves the time-stepping performance of neural solvers. These findings connect representation quality to both identifying properties of equations and advancing their solutions through time. The authors present the methodology as a possible step toward general-purpose PDE foundation models, leaving that broader goal as a future prospect.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised joint embeddings learn PDE representations from heterogeneous data that improve coefficient estimation and neural-solver time stepping.

title: Self-Supervised Learning with Lie Symmetries for Partial Differential Equations

abstract: Recently, unsupervised adversarial training (AT) has been highlighted as a means of achieving robustness in models without any label information. Previous studies in unsupervised AT have mostly focused on implementing self-supervised learning (SSL) frameworks, which maximize the instance-wise classification loss to generate adversarial examples. However, we observe that simply maximizing the self-supervised training loss with an untargeted adversarial attack often results in generating ineffective adversaries that may not help improve the robustness of the trained model, especially for non-contrastive SSL frameworks without negative examples. To tackle this problem, we propose a novel positive mining for targeted adversarial attack to generate effective adversaries for adversarial SSL frameworks. Specifically, we introduce an algorithm that selects the most confusing yet similar target example for a given instance based on entropy and similarity, and subsequently perturbs the given instance towards the selected target. Our method demonstrates significant enhancements in robustness when applied to non-contrastive SSL frameworks, and less but consistent robustness improvements with contrastive SSL frameworks, on the benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can improve robustness by training models on deliberately perturbed inputs. In self-supervised learning, this must work without class labels. A common approach creates perturbations by maximizing the self-supervised training loss, but the authors observe that a higher loss does not always produce a useful adversarial example.

This problem is particularly pronounced for non-contrastive frameworks, which lack negative examples. The proposed method gives the perturbation a specific target. For each instance, it selects another example that is both similar and confusing, using entropy and similarity to guide the choice. It then perturbs the original instance toward that selected example.

The approach makes target selection part of generating useful challenges for training, rather than relying solely on untargeted loss maximization. On benchmark datasets, it yields substantial robustness improvements for non-contrastive self-supervised frameworks. Contrastive frameworks also improve, though by smaller, consistent amounts. These findings suggest that the usefulness of an adversarial training example depends on how it is constructed and on the self-supervised framework receiving it.
summary.tldr: Selecting similar, confusing targets for adversarial perturbations improves self-supervised robustness, especially in non-contrastive frameworks.

title: Effective Targeted Attacks for Adversarial Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: The success of meta-learning on out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks in the wild has proved to be hit-and-miss.To safeguard the generalization capability of the meta-learned prior knowledge to OOD tasks, in particularly safety-critical applications, necessitates detection of an OOD task followed by adaptation of the task towards the prior. Nonetheless, the reliability of estimated uncertainty on OOD tasks by existing Bayesian meta-learning methods is restricted by incomplete coverage of the feature distribution shift and insufficient expressiveness of the meta-learned prior. Besides, they struggle to adapt an OOD task, running parallel to the line of cross-domain task adaptation solutions which are vulnerable to overfitting.To this end, we build a single coherent framework that supports both detection and adaptation of OOD tasks, while remaining compatible with off-the-shelf meta-learning backbones. The proposed Energy-Based Meta-Learning (EBML) framework learns to characterize any arbitrary meta-training task distribution with the composition of two expressive neural-network-based energy functions. We deploy the sum of the two energy functions, being proportional to the joint distribution of a task, as a reliable score for detecting OOD tasks; during meta-testing, we adapt the OOD task to in-distribution tasks by energy minimization.Experiments on four regression and classification datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposal.

paragraphs: Meta-learning transfers knowledge across tasks, but that transfer can become unreliable when a new task differs from those encountered during training. This paper addresses both recognizing such unfamiliar tasks and adapting them toward the learned task distribution. It identifies limited uncertainty estimates and insufficiently expressive learned priors as obstacles in existing Bayesian approaches.

Energy-Based Meta-Learning, or EBML, represents the training-task distribution through two neural-network energy functions. Their combined score is used to detect tasks outside that distribution. At test time, energy minimization guides adaptation of an unfamiliar task toward in-distribution tasks, linking detection and adaptation through the same learned representation.

The framework is designed to work with existing meta-learning backbones, making it a shared addition rather than a separate backbone for each setting. Experiments on four regression and classification datasets support its effectiveness. The stated contribution is a coherent way to detect and respond to task shift; the reported evaluations do not turn that capability into an unconditional guarantee of safe generalization.
summary.tldr: EBML uses learned energy functions to detect unfamiliar tasks and adapt them toward the meta-training distribution.

title: Secure Out-of-Distribution Task Generalization with Energy-Based Models

abstract: Visual reasoning requires multimodal perception and commonsense cognition of the world. Recently, multiple vision-language models (VLMs) have been proposed with excellent commonsense reasoning ability in various domains. However, how to harness the collective power of these complementary VLMs is rarely explored. Existing methods like ensemble still struggle to aggregate these models with the desired higher-order communications. In this work, we propose Cola, a novel paradigm that coordinates multiple VLMs for visual reasoning. Our key insight is that a large language model (LLM) can efficiently coordinate multiple VLMs by facilitating natural language communication that leverages their distinct and complementary capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our instruction tuning variant, Cola-FT, achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual question answering (VQA), outside knowledge VQA, visual entailment, and visual spatial reasoning tasks. Moreover, we show that our in-context learning variant, Cola-Zero, exhibits competitive performance in zero and few-shot settings, without finetuning. Through systematic ablation studies and visualizations, we validate that a coordinator LLM indeed comprehends the instruction prompts as well as the separate functionalities of VLMs; it then coordinates them to enable impressive visual reasoning capabilities.

Cola explores a language model's role as a coordinator for visual reasoning. It uses natural language communication to bring the separate capabilities of multiple vision-language models into a shared reasoning process.

abstract: With the growing demand for the right to be forgotten, there is an increasing need for machine learning models to forget sensitive data and its impact. To address this, the paradigm of selective forgetting (a.k.a machine unlearning) has been extensively studied, which aims to remove the impact of requested data from a well-trained model without retraining from scratch. Despite its significant success, limited attention has been given to the security vulnerabilities of the unlearning system concerning malicious data update requests. Motivated by this, in this paper, we explore the possibility and feasibility of malicious data update requests during the unlearning process. Specifically, we first propose a new class of malicious selective forgetting attacks, which involves a static scenario where all the malicious data update requests are provided by the adversary at once. Additionally, considering the sequential setting where the data update requests arrive sequentially, we also design a novel framework for sequential forgetting attacks, which is formulated as a stochastic optimal control problem. We also propose novel optimization algorithms that can find the effective malicious data update requests. We perform theoretical analyses for the proposed selective forgetting attacks, and extensive experimental results validate the effectiveness of our proposed selective forgetting attacks. The source code is available in the supplementary material.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove requested data's influence from a trained model without starting training again. This paper examines a security concern within that process: data update requests can themselves be malicious. It studies whether an adversary can use the selective-forgetting interface to mount effective attacks.

The authors consider two ways requests can arrive. In the static setting, the adversary submits all malicious updates together. In the sequential setting, requests arrive over time. They formulate sequential attacks as a stochastic optimal control problem and develop optimization algorithms to find effective malicious requests in the studied settings.

The paper combines theoretical analyses with extensive experiments that validate the proposed attacks' effectiveness. Its contribution is to treat the handling of forgetting requests as a security-relevant part of the learning system. Distinguishing simultaneous from sequential requests also makes the timing of adversarial interaction explicit, broadening the study beyond a single batch of malicious updates.
summary.tldr: The paper develops and analyzes attacks that exploit malicious data update requests during machine unlearning, both in batches and sequentially.

title: Static and Sequential Malicious Attacks in the Context of Selective Forgetting

abstract: Zero-Shot Temporal Action Detection (ZSTAD) aims to classify and localize action segments in untrimmed videos for unseen action categories. Most existing ZSTAD methods utilize a foreground-based approach, limiting the integration of text and visual features due to their reliance on pre-extracted proposals. In this paper, we introduce a cross-modal ZSTAD baseline with mutual cross-attention, integrating both text and visual information throughout the detection process. Our simple approach results in superior performance compared to previous methods. Despite this improvement, we further identify a common-action bias issue that the cross-modal baseline over-focus on common sub-actions due to a lack of ability to discriminate text-related visual parts. To address this issue, we propose Text-infused attention and Foreground-aware Action Detection (Ti-FAD), which enhances the ability to focus on text-related sub-actions and distinguish relevant action segments from the background. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that Ti-FAD outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on ZSTAD benchmarks by a large margin: 41.2\% (+ 11.0\%) on THUMOS14 and 32.0\% (+ 5.4\%) on ActivityNet v1.3. Code is available at: https://github.com/YearangLee/Ti-FAD.

summary.tldr: Ti-FAD uses text-guided attention and foreground modeling to improve localization and recognition of unseen video actions.

title: Text-Infused Attention and Foreground-Aware Modeling for Zero-Shot Temporal Action Detection

abstract: Many structured prediction and reasoning tasks can be framed as program synthesis problems, where the goal is to generate a program in a \emph{domain-specific language} (DSL) that transforms input data into the desired output. Unfortunately, purely neural approaches, such as large language models (LLMs), often fail to produce fully correct programs in unfamiliar DSLs, while purely symbolic methods based on combinatorial search scale poorly to complex problems. Motivated by these limitations, we introduce a hybrid approach, where LLM completions for a given task are used to learn a task-specific, context-free surrogate model, which is then used to guide program synthesis. We evaluate this hybrid approach on three domains, and show that it outperforms both unguided search and direct sampling from LLMs, as well as existing program synthesizers.

paragraphs: Many reasoning tasks can be expressed as finding a program that transforms specified inputs into desired outputs. The program may need to use a specialized domain-specific language. Language models often struggle to produce fully correct programs in unfamiliar languages, while symbolic search can become prohibitively difficult as the space of possible programs grows.

HYSYNTH combines these approaches by using language-model completions to learn a task-specific, context-free surrogate model. That surrogate then guides program synthesis. The language model's suggestions therefore become information for directing the search, allowing the synthesis process to use patterns in those suggestions even when direct generation is unreliable.

The authors evaluate the hybrid approach in three domains. It outperforms unguided search, direct sampling from language models, and existing program synthesizers in those evaluations. These findings support the central design choice: approximating the model's task-specific guidance in a form usable by symbolic search can make program synthesis more effective than either unguided search or direct language-model sampling.
summary.tldr: HYSYNTH turns language-model completions into a task-specific surrogate that guides symbolic program synthesis.

title: HYSYNTH: Context-Free LLM Approximation for Guiding Program Synthesis

abstract: The Spiking Neural Network (SNN) is a biologically inspired neural network infrastructure that has recently garnered significant attention. It utilizes binary spike activations to transmit information, thereby replacing multiplications with additions and resulting in high energy efficiency. However, training an SNN directly poses a challenge due to the undefined gradient of the firing spike process. Although prior works have employed various surrogate gradient training methods that use an alternative function to replace the firing process during back-propagation, these approaches ignore an intrinsic problem: gradient vanishing. To address this issue, we propose a shortcut back-propagation method in the paper, which advocates for transmitting the gradient directly from the loss to the shallow layers. This enables us to present the gradient to the shallow layers directly, thereby significantly mitigating the gradient vanishing problem. Additionally, this method does not introduce any burden during the inference phase.To strike a balance between final accuracy and ease of training, we also propose an evolutionary training framework and implement it by inducing a balance coefficient that dynamically changes with the training epoch, which further improves the network's performance. Extensive experiments conducted over static and dynamic datasets using several popular network structures reveal that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks communicate through binary spikes, supporting energy-efficient computation using additions. Training them directly is difficult because the spike-firing process lacks a usable gradient. Surrogate-gradient methods substitute another function during back-propagation, but the paper highlights a further problem: training signals can vanish before reaching shallow layers.

The proposed shortcut back-propagation method transmits gradients directly from the loss to shallow layers. This gives those layers a more direct learning signal and substantially mitigates gradient vanishing. The modification operates during training and, according to the authors, adds no burden during inference, preserving the attraction of the network's spike-based computation.

The paper also introduces an evolutionary training framework with a balance coefficient that changes over training epochs. This is intended to balance ease of training against final accuracy and further improve performance. Across static and dynamic datasets and several popular network structures, the authors report consistent improvements over compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support addressing gradient transmission alongside the choice of surrogate gradient.
summary.tldr: Direct gradient shortcuts improve spiking-network training by mitigating vanishing gradients without adding inference overhead.

title: Take A Shortcut Back: Mitigating the Gradient Vanishing for Training Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: Novel view acoustic synthesis (NVAS) aims to render binaural audio at any target viewpoint, given a mono audio emitted by a sound source at a 3D scene. Existing methods have proposed NeRF-based implicit models to exploit visual cues as a condition for synthesizing binaural audio. However, in addition to low efficiency originating from heavy NeRF rendering, these methods all have a limited ability of characterizing the entire scene environment such as room geometry, material properties, and the spatial relation between the listener and sound source. To address these issues, we propose a novel Audio-Visual Gaussian Splatting (AV-GS) model. To obtain a material-aware and geometry-aware condition for audio synthesis, we learn an explicit point-based scene representation with audio-guidance parameters on locally initialized Gaussian points, taking into account the space relation from the listener and sound source. To make the visual scene model audio adaptive, we propose a point densification and pruning strategy to optimally distribute the Gaussian points, with the per-point contribution in sound propagation (e.g., more points needed for texture-less wall surfaces as they affect sound path diversion). Extensive experiments validate the superiority of our AV-GS over existing alternatives on the real-world RWAS and simulation-based SoundSpaces datasets. Project page: \url{https://surrey-uplab.github.io/research/avgs/}

paragraphs: Novel view acoustic synthesis aims to produce the two-ear audio a listener would hear at a chosen location, starting from a mono sound source in a three-dimensional scene. Visual information helps describe the environment, but the paper identifies shortcomings in existing NeRF-based approaches: expensive rendering and limited representation of geometry, materials, and listener–source relationships.

AV-GS represents the scene explicitly using Gaussian points equipped with learned audio-guidance parameters. This representation supplies information about material and geometric properties while accounting for the positions of the listener and source. The scene model is therefore organized to support sound synthesis as well as represent visual surroundings.

The method also adds and removes points according to their contribution to sound propagation. A visually plain wall, for example, may deserve more points because it changes sound paths. Experiments on real-world RWAS and simulated SoundSpaces data report better performance than existing alternatives. The results support adapting the allocation of scene detail to acoustic importance.
summary.tldr: AV-GS learns Gaussian scene representations tailored to geometry, materials, and sound propagation to improve audio synthesis at new viewpoints.

title: AV-GS: Learning Material and Geometry Aware Priors for Novel View Acoustic Synthesis

abstract: Surface electromyography (sEMG) based gesture recognition offers a natural and intuitive interaction modality for wearable devices. Despite significant advancements in sEMG-based gesture recognition models, existing methods often suffer from high computational latency and increased energy consumption. Additionally, the inherent instability of sEMG signals, combined with their sensitivity to distribution shifts in real-world settings, compromises model robustness. To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel SpGesture framework based on Spiking Neural Networks, which possesses several unique merits compared with existing methods: (1) Robustness: By utilizing membrane potential as a memory list, we pioneer the introduction of Source-Free Domain Adaptation into SNN for the first time. This enables SpGesture to mitigate the accuracy degradation caused by distribution shifts. (2) High Accuracy: With a novel Spiking Jaccard Attention, SpGesture enhances the SNNs' ability to represent sEMG features, leading to a notable rise in system accuracy. To validate SpGesture's performance, we collected a new sEMG gesture dataset which has different forearm postures, where SpGesture achieved the highest accuracy among the baselines ($89.26\%$). Moreover, the actual deployment on the CPU demonstrated a latency below 100ms, well within real-time requirements. This impressive performance showcases SpGesture's potential to enhance the applicability of sEMG in real-world scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/guoweiyu/SpGesture/.

However, the signals can be unstable and change across real-world conditions. Existing recognition methods also face latency and energy-consumption challenges. These results support its potential for practical gesture interfaces by jointly demonstrating recognition performance under posture variation and sufficiently fast execution.
summary.tldr: SpGesture combines adaptive spiking networks and Jaccard attention, achieving 89.26% gesture accuracy and CPU latency below 100 milliseconds in its evaluation.

title: SpGesture: Source-Free Domain-adaptive sEMG-based Gesture Recognition with Jaccard Attentive Spiking Neural Network

abstract: Gradient descent and its variants are de facto standard algorithms for training machine learning models. As gradient descent is sensitive to its hyperparameters, we need to tune the hyperparameters carefully using a grid search. However, the method is time-consuming, particularly when multiple hyperparameters exist. Therefore, recent studies have analyzed parameter-free methods that adjust the hyperparameters on the fly. However, the existing work is limited to investigations of parameter-free methods for the stepsize, and parameter-free methods for other hyperparameters have not been explored. For instance, although the gradient clipping threshold is a crucial hyperparameter in addition to the stepsize for preventing gradient explosion issues, none of the existing studies have investigated parameter-free methods for clipped gradient descent. Therefore, in this study, we investigate the parameter-free methods for clipped gradient descent. Specifically, we propose Inexact Polyak Stepsize, which converges to the optimal solution without any hyperparameters tuning, and its convergence rate is asymptotically independent of $L$ under $L$-smooth and $(L_0, L_1)$-smooth assumptions of the loss function, similar to that of clipped gradient descent with well-tuned hyperparameters. We numerically validated our convergence results using a synthetic function and demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed methods using LSTM, Nano-GPT, and T5.

paragraphs: Gradient-based training often requires careful selection of update sizes and other hyperparameters. Clipped gradient descent adds a clipping threshold to control excessively large gradients, increasing the tuning burden. This paper examines how to remove that burden for clipped optimization, extending attention beyond earlier parameter-free work focused on step sizes alone.

The authors propose Inexact Polyak Stepsize, a method with convergence to the optimum without hyperparameter tuning under the stated assumptions. They analyze both L-smooth losses and losses satisfying the specified (L₀, L₁)-smoothness condition. Its convergence rate is asymptotically independent of L, matching that particular property of clipped gradient descent with well-tuned hyperparameters.

The theoretical convergence results are checked numerically using a synthetic function, and practical effectiveness is demonstrated with LSTM, Nano-GPT, and T5. The contribution connects automatic adjustment with guarantees usually associated with carefully configured optimization. The smoothness assumptions remain part of the theoretical claim, while the model experiments provide separate empirical evidence that the proposed methods can be useful in training.
summary.tldr: Inexact Polyak Stepsize removes hyperparameter tuning from clipped gradient optimization, with conditional convergence guarantees and neural-model experiments.

title: Parameter-free Clipped Gradient Descent Meets Polyak

abstract: Data heterogeneity among Federated Learning (FL) users poses a significant challenge, resulting in reduced global model performance. The community has designed various techniques to tackle this issue, among which Knowledge Distillation (KD)-based techniques are common. While these techniques effectively improve performance under high heterogeneity, they inadvertently cause higher accuracy degradation under model poisoning attacks (known as \emph{attack amplification}). This paper presents a case study to reveal this critical vulnerability in KD-based FL systems. We show why KD causes this issue through empirical evidence and use it as motivation to design a hybrid distillation technique. We introduce a novel algorithm, Hybrid Knowledge Distillation for Robust and Accurate FL (HYDRA-FL), which reduces the impact of attacks in attack scenarios by offloading some of the KD loss to a shallow layer via an auxiliary classifier. We model HYDRA-FL as a generic framework and adapt it to two KD-based FL algorithms, FedNTD and MOON. Using these two as case studies, we demonstrate that our technique outperforms baselines in attack settings while maintaining comparable performance in benign settings.

This changes where the distillation objective acts within the model, with the aim of reducing the impact of attacks while preserving the performance benefits that motivated distillation.

summary.tldr: HYDRA-FL redirects part of knowledge distillation to a shallow classifier, reducing poisoning-related performance losses in two federated-learning case studies.

title: HYDRA-FL: Hybrid Knowledge Distillation for Robust and Accurate Federated Learning

abstract: Recently, many methods have been developed to extend the context length of pre-trained large language models (LLMs), but they often require fine-tuning at the target length ($\gg4K$) and struggle to effectively utilize information from the middle part of the context. To address these issues, we propose $\textbf{C}$ontinuity-$\textbf{R}$elativity ind$\textbf{E}$xing with g$\textbf{A}$ussian $\textbf{M}$iddle ($\texttt{CREAM}$), which interpolates positional encodings by manipulating position indices. Apart from being simple, $\texttt{CREAM}$ is training-efficient: it only requires fine-tuning at the pre-trained context window (e.g., Llama 2-4K) and can extend LLMs to a much longer target context length (e.g., 256K). To ensure that the model focuses more on the information in the middle, we introduce a truncated Gaussian to encourage sampling from the middle part of the context during fine-tuning, thus alleviating the ''Lost-in-the-Middle'' problem faced by long-context LLMs. Experimental results show that $\texttt{CREAM}$ successfully extends LLMs to the target length for both Base and Chat versions of $\texttt{Llama2-7B}$ with ``Never Miss A Beat''. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/bigai-nlco/cream.

paragraphs: Extending a language model’s context involves more than allowing a longer input. The model also needs to use information throughout that input, including passages in the middle. Existing extension methods often require training at the desired long context length, while still struggling to use those middle passages effectively.

CREAM addresses both issues by manipulating the position indices used in positional encoding. This interpolates the model’s position representations while requiring fine-tuning only at its original context length. The abstract gives the example of extending a model with a 4K training window to a 256K target window. During fine-tuning, a truncated Gaussian sampling scheme gives additional emphasis to positions in the middle of the context.

Experiments on both the Base and Chat versions of Llama2-7B report successful context extension. The approach matters because it connects training efficiency with where the model learns to attend: longer supported inputs and better use of their middle are addressed together. The stated benefit is alleviating the lost-in-the-middle problem, alongside avoiding fine-tuning at the full target length.
summary.tldr: CREAM extends language-model context using short-window fine-tuning and position sampling that emphasizes the middle of long inputs.

title: An Efficient Recipe for Long Context Extension via Middle-Focused Positional Encoding

abstract: Recent research has made significant strides in aligning large language models (LLMs) with helpfulness and harmlessness. In this paper, we argue for the importance of alignment for \emph{honesty}, ensuring that LLMs proactively refuse to answer questions when they lack knowledge, while still not being overly conservative. However, a pivotal aspect of alignment for honesty involves discerning an LLM's knowledge boundaries, which demands comprehensive solutions in terms of metric development, benchmark creation, and training methodologies. We address these challenges by first establishing a precise problem definition and defining ``honesty'' inspired by the Analects of Confucius. This serves as a cornerstone for developing metrics that effectively measure an LLM's honesty by quantifying its progress post-alignment. Furthermore, we introduce a flexible training framework which is further instantiated by several efficient fine-tuning techniques that emphasize honesty without sacrificing performance on other tasks. Our extensive experiments reveal that these aligned models show a marked increase in honesty, as indicated by our proposed metrics. We open-source all relevant resources to facilitate future research at \url{https://github.com/GAIR-NLP/alignment-for-honesty}.

It should also remain willing to answer questions it can handle. This paper treats that balance as an alignment objective alongside helpfulness and harmlessness, making the model's knowledge boundaries central to the problem.

The authors establish a precise problem definition and formulate honesty using an idea inspired by the Analects of Confucius. They build metrics around that definition to quantify how a model's honesty changes after alignment. The paper then introduces a flexible training framework and implements several efficient fine-tuning techniques. The reported experiments show substantial improvements on the proposed honesty metrics while preserving performance on other tasks. These findings support training models to manage their knowledge boundaries more effectively, with the measured gains specifically grounded in the paper's definition and evaluation of honesty.
summary.tldr: The paper defines, measures, and trains language-model honesty as knowing when to answer and when to decline.

title: Alignment for Honesty

abstract: Availability attacks provide a tool to prevent the unauthorized use of private data and commercial datasets by generating imperceptible noise and crafting unlearnable examples before release. Ideally, the obtained unlearnability can prevent algorithms from training usable models. When supervised learning (SL) algorithms have failed, a malicious data collector possibly resorts to contrastive learning (CL) algorithms to bypass the protection.Through evaluation, we have found that most existing methods are unable to achieve both supervised and contrastive unlearnability, which poses risks to data protection by availability attacks.Different from recent methods based on contrastive learning, we employ contrastive-like data augmentations in supervised learning frameworks to obtain attacks effective for both SL and CL.Our proposed AUE and AAP attacks achieve state-of-the-art worst-case unlearnability across SL and CL algorithms with less computation consumption, showcasing prospects in real-world applications. The code is available at https://github.com/EhanW/AUE-AAP.

paragraphs: Availability attacks aim to make released data difficult to learn from by adding imperceptible noise. The intended protection is that an unauthorized collector cannot train a useful model on the altered examples. This paper examines a weakness in that protection: data that frustrates supervised learning may still be usable through contrastive learning.

The authors evaluate existing approaches and find that most do not prevent learning effectively under both training paradigms. Their proposed attacks, AUE and AAP, incorporate contrastive-like data augmentations into supervised learning frameworks. This brings elements relevant to contrastive training into attack construction without basing the entire construction on a contrastive-learning framework.

The reported results show state-of-the-art worst-case unlearnability across the supervised and contrastive algorithms considered, with lower computational consumption. Focusing on the worse result across both paradigms matters because a collector can switch training methods when one fails. The findings support broader protection in the evaluated settings and suggest practical potential; they do not establish protection against every possible learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: AUE and AAP use contrastive-like augmentations within supervised frameworks to efficiently disrupt both supervised and contrastive learning.

title: Efficient Availability Attacks against Supervised and Contrastive Learning Simultaneously

abstract: The combination of the Bayesian game and learning has a rich history, with the idea of controlling a single agent in a system composed of multiple agents with unknown behaviors given a set of types, each specifying a possible behavior for the other agents. The idea is to plan an agent's own actions with respect to those types which it believes are most likely to maximize the payoff. However, the type beliefs are often learned from past actions and likely to be incorrect. With this perspective in mind, we consider an agent in a game with type predictions of other components, and investigate the impact of incorrect beliefs to the agent’s payoff. In particular, we formally define a tradeoff between risk and opportunity by comparing the payoff obtained against the optimal payoff, which is represented by a gap caused by trusting or distrusting the learned beliefs.Our main results characterize the tradeoff by establishing upper and lower bounds on the Pareto front for both normal-form and stochastic Bayesian games, with numerical results provided.

paragraphs: An agent interacting with others can choose better actions if it predicts their behavior accurately. In a Bayesian game, these predictions can be expressed as beliefs over types, with each type describing a possible behavior. This paper studies what happens when those beliefs, often learned from past actions, are incorrect.

The authors formalize a tradeoff between risk and opportunity through payoff gaps relative to optimal play. Trusting a learned belief can create losses when the belief is wrong, while distrusting it can forgo opportunities when it is useful. This turns the question of how much to rely on predictions into a comparison between two competing consequences.

The main results establish upper and lower bounds on the Pareto front for both normal-form and stochastic Bayesian games. That front describes the achievable tradeoffs where improving one objective requires sacrificing the other. Numerical results accompany the analysis. The work clarifies what kinds of protection and exploitation can coexist when an agent has behavioral predictions it cannot fully trust.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the tradeoff between exploiting predicted behavior and limiting payoff losses when those predictions are wrong.

title: Safe Exploitative Play with Untrusted Type Beliefs

abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) on Large Language Models (LLMs) has been widely used to expand the model’s fundamental understanding of specific downstream domains (e.g., math and code). For the CPT on domain-specific LLMs, one important question is how to choose the optimal mixture ratio between the general-corpus (e.g., Dolma, Slim-pajama) and the downstream domain-corpus. Existing methods usually adopt laborious human efforts by grid-searching on a set of mixture ratios, which require high GPU training consumption costs. Besides, we cannot guarantee the selected ratio is optimal for the specific domain. To address the limitations of existing methods, inspired by the Scaling Law for performance prediction, we propose to investigate the Scaling Law of the Domain-specific Continual Pre-Training (D-CPT Law) to decide the optimal mixture ratio with acceptable training costs for LLMs of different sizes. Specifically, by fitting the D-CPT Law, we can easily predict the general and downstream performance of arbitrary mixture ratios, model sizes, and dataset sizes using small-scale training costs on limited experiments. Moreover, we also extend our standard D-CPT Law on cross-domain settings and propose the Cross-Domain D-CPT Law to predict the D-CPT law of target domains, where very small training costs (about 1\% of the normal training costs) are needed for the target domains. Comprehensive experimental results on six downstream domains demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our proposed D-CPT Law and Cross-Domain D-CPT Law.

paragraphs: Continual pre-training can deepen a language model’s knowledge of a domain such as mathematics or code. A practical challenge is choosing how much domain material to mix with general text. Testing many mixture ratios consumes substantial training resources, and the best ratio among those tested may still miss a better choice.

The paper proposes D-CPT Law, a scaling-law approach that fits relationships between training choices and performance using a limited set of small-scale experiments. The fitted law predicts both general and domain performance for different mixture ratios, model sizes, and dataset sizes. These predictions are intended to guide mixture selection without separately training every candidate configuration.

The authors also introduce a cross-domain extension that predicts the law for a target domain with about 1% of normal training costs spent on that domain. Experiments across six downstream domains support the effectiveness and generalizability of both versions. The findings position performance prediction as a practical tool for allocating continual pre-training effort and choosing data mixtures.
summary.tldr: D-CPT Law predicts continual pre-training performance to guide general-versus-domain data mixtures using limited small-scale experiments.

title: D-CPT Law: Domain-specific Continual Pre-Training Scaling Law for Large Language Models

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated profound capabilities due to their extensive pre-training on diverse corpora. However, LLMs often struggle with catastrophic forgetting when engaged in sequential task learning. In this paper, we propose a novel parameter-efficient approach for continual learning in LLMs, which empirically investigates knowledge transfer from previously learned tasks to new tasks through low-rank matrix parameters, enhancing the learning of new tasks without significant interference. Our method employs sensitivity-based analysis of low-rank matrix parameters to identify knowledge-specific parameters between sequential tasks, which are used to initialize the low-rank matrix parameters in new tasks. To maintain orthogonality and minimize forgetting, we further involve the gradient projection technique that keeps the low-rank subspaces of each new task orthogonal to those of previous tasks. Our experimental results on continual learning benchmarks validate the efficacy of our proposed method, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in reducing forgetting, enhancing task performance, and preserving the model's ability to generalize to unseen tasks.

paragraphs: When a language model learns tasks one after another, adapting to a new task can damage what it learned earlier. This paper proposes a parameter-efficient continual-learning method that tries to transfer useful prior knowledge while reducing that interference. Its adaptation mechanism works through low-rank matrix parameters.

The method uses sensitivity analysis to identify knowledge-specific parameters across sequential tasks. Those parameters help initialize the low-rank matrices for a new task, giving new learning a starting point informed by earlier learning. It then applies gradient projection to keep the new task’s low-rank subspaces orthogonal to those of previous tasks, limiting overlap in the directions used for adaptation.

These two parts serve complementary purposes: initialization encourages knowledge transfer, while projected updates aim to minimize forgetting. On continual-learning benchmarks, the authors report improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods in forgetting, task performance, and generalization to unseen tasks. The evidence supports combining selective reuse with constrained updates, rather than treating transfer and preservation as separate objectives.
summary.tldr: The method combines sensitivity-guided low-rank initialization with orthogonal updates to improve continual learning and reduce forgetting.

title: Learn more, but bother less: parameter efficient continual learning

abstract: Deep neural networks face persistent challenges in defending against backdoor attacks, leading to an ongoing battle between attacks and defenses. While existing backdoor defense strategies have shown promising performance on reducing attack success rates, can we confidently claim that the backdoor threat has truly been eliminated from the model? To address it, we re-investigate the characteristics of the backdoored models after defense (denoted as defense models). Surprisingly, we find that the original backdoors still exist in defense models derived from existing post-training defense strategies, and the backdoor existence is measured by a novel metric called backdoor existence coefficient. It implies that the backdoors just lie dormant rather than being eliminated. To further verify this finding, we empirically show that these dormant backdoors can be easily re-activated during inference stage, by manipulating the original trigger with well-designed tiny perturbation using universal adversarial attack. More practically, we extend our backdoor re-activation to black-box scenario, where the defense model can only be queried by the adversary during inference stage, and develop two effective methods, i.e., query-based and transfer-based backdoor re-activation attacks. The effectiveness of the proposed methods are verified on both image classification and multimodal contrastive learning (i.e., CLIP) tasks. In conclusion, this work uncovers a critical vulnerability that has never been explored in existing defense strategies, emphasizing the urgency of designing more robust and advanced backdoor defense mechanisms in the future.

paragraphs: A defense can reduce a backdoor attack’s success rate without necessarily removing the underlying backdoor. This paper investigates that distinction by examining models after existing post-training defenses have been applied. The authors introduce a backdoor existence coefficient and find evidence that original backdoors remain dormant in the defended models they study.

They then test whether those dormant behaviors can become active again during inference. Their experiments show that small, carefully designed changes to the original trigger can restore the backdoor effect through a universal adversarial attack. This provides behavioral support for the claim that reduced attack success can reflect suppression rather than elimination.

The study also considers black-box access, where an adversary can query the defended model during inference. It develops query-based and transfer-based reactivation methods and evaluates them on image classification and CLIP tasks. The results expose a vulnerability in the tested defenses and motivate evaluating whether backdoors persist after treatment. The relevant security question extends beyond how well a defense handles the original, unchanged trigger.
summary.tldr: The study finds that tested post-training defenses can leave dormant backdoors that modified triggers reactivate during inference.

title: Breaking the False Sense of Security in Backdoor Defense through Re-Activation Attack

abstract: We introduce Image2Struct, a benchmark to evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) on extracting structure from images.Our benchmark 1) captures real-world use cases, 2) is fully automatic and does not require human judgment, and 3) is based on a renewable stream of fresh data.In Image2Struct, VLMs are prompted to generate the underlying structure (e.g., LaTeX code or HTML) from an input image (e.g., webpage screenshot).The structure is then rendered to produce an output image (e.g., rendered webpage), which is compared against the input image to produce a similarity score.This round-trip evaluation allows us to quantitatively evaluate VLMs on tasks with multiple valid structures.We create a pipeline that downloads fresh data from active online communities upon execution and evaluates the VLMs without human intervention.We introduce three domains (Webpages, LaTeX, and Musical Scores) and use five image metrics (pixel similarity, cosine similarity between the Inception vectors, learned perceptual image patch similarity, structural similarity index measure, and earth mover similarity) that allow efficient and automatic comparison between pairs of images. We evaluate Image2Struct on 14 prominent VLMs and find that scores vary widely, indicating that Image2Struct can differentiate between the performances of different VLMs.Additionally, the best score varies considerably across domains (e.g., 0.402 on sheet music vs. 0.830 on LaTeX equations), indicating that Image2Struct contains tasks of varying difficulty.For transparency, we release the full results at https://crfm.stanford.edu/helm/image2struct/v1.0.1/.

paragraphs: Image2Struct evaluates whether a vision-language model can recover a usable structured representation from an image. Examples include generating HTML from a webpage screenshot or LaTeX from a rendered equation. This is challenging to assess through exact output matching because different underlying structures can produce valid versions of the same visible result.

The benchmark uses a round trip: the model generates structure, that structure is rendered into an image, and the rendered image is compared with the original. Five image metrics measure different aspects of similarity. This makes evaluation automatic while accommodating multiple possible structures. A pipeline downloads fresh material from active online communities whenever it runs, providing renewable evaluation data.

The benchmark covers webpages, LaTeX, and musical scores. Testing 14 prominent models produced widely varying scores, indicating that the benchmark distinguishes model performance. Best scores also differed substantially between domains, including 0.402 for sheet music and 0.830 for LaTeX equations. These findings show that the evaluated structure-extraction tasks differ considerably in difficulty.
summary.tldr: Image2Struct evaluates image-to-structure generation by rendering model outputs and automatically comparing them with the source images.

title: Image2Struct: Benchmarking Structure Extraction for Vision-Language Models

abstract: We consider stochastic optimization problems where the objective depends on some parameter, as commonly found in hyperparameter optimization for instance. We investigate the behavior of the derivatives of the iterates of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with respect to that parameter and show that they are driven by an inexact SGD recursion on a different objective function, perturbed by the convergence of the original SGD. This enables us to establish that the derivatives of SGD converge to the derivative of the solution mapping in terms of mean squared error whenever the objective is strongly convex. Specifically, we demonstrate that with constant step-sizes, these derivatives stabilize within a noise ball centered at the solution derivative, and that with vanishing step-sizes they exhibit $O(\log(k)^2 / k)$ convergence rates. Additionally, we prove exponential convergence in the interpolation regime. Our theoretical findings are illustrated by numerical experiments on synthetic tasks.

paragraphs: When an optimization objective depends on a parameter, it can be useful to know how its solution changes as that parameter changes. Hyperparameter optimization is one example. This paper studies whether differentiating the successive updates of stochastic gradient descent, or SGD, yields an accurate estimate of that sensitivity.

The authors show that these derivatives follow another optimization process: an inexact SGD recursion on a different objective. The original SGD process introduces a perturbation into this second process as it approaches its solution. This connection makes it possible to analyze derivative accuracy through the behavior of a related stochastic optimization problem.

For strongly convex objectives, the authors establish mean-squared-error results for approaching the derivative of the solution mapping. With constant step sizes, derivative estimates settle within a noise region around the target. With shrinking step sizes, the stated convergence rate is O(log(k)^2/k). They additionally prove exponential convergence in the interpolation regime. Numerical experiments on synthetic tasks illustrate these theoretical findings, whose conclusions depend on the specified optimization setting.
summary.tldr: Under strong convexity, derivatives through SGD approach solution sensitivities with behavior determined by the step-size schedule and optimization regime.

title: Derivatives of Stochastic Gradient Descent in parametric optimization

abstract: In our study, we explore methods for detecting unwanted content lurking in visual datasets. We provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that a model capable of successfully partitioning visual data can be obtained using only textual data. Based on the analysis, we propose Hassle-Free Textual Training (HFTT), a streamlined method capable of acquiring detectors for unwanted visual content, using only textual data in conjunction with pre-trained vision-language models. HFTT features an innovative objective function that significantly reduces the necessity for human involvement in data annotation. Furthermore, HFTT employs a clever textual data synthesis method, effectively emulating the integration of unknown visual data distribution into the training process at no extra cost. The unique characteristics of HFTT extend its utility beyond traditional out-of-distribution detection, making it applicable to tasks that address more abstract concepts. We complement our analyses with experiments in hateful image detection and out-of-distribution detection. Our codes are available at https://github.com/HFTT-anonymous/HFTT.

paragraphs: Detecting unwanted images usually raises the question of how to obtain suitable training examples and annotations. This paper explores whether a detector for visual content can instead be trained using text. Its theoretical analysis shows that textual data can be sufficient to obtain a model capable of successfully partitioning visual data.

Hassle-Free Textual Training, or HFTT, turns that analysis into a method using textual data together with pretrained vision-language models. Its objective function substantially reduces the need for human annotation. A text-synthesis procedure also emulates incorporating information from an unknown visual-data distribution into training, which the authors describe as adding no extra cost.

The approach is intended to reach beyond conventional out-of-distribution detection to unwanted content defined by more abstract concepts. Experiments investigate both out-of-distribution detection and hateful-image detection. These case studies accompany the theoretical argument and show the method’s application to distinct detection problems. The contribution is a text-driven route to acquiring visual detectors that draws on an existing vision-language model.
summary.tldr: HFTT uses textual training data and pretrained vision-language models to build detectors for unwanted visual content.

title: Textual Training for the Hassle-Free Removal of Unwanted Visual Data: Case Studies on OOD and Hateful Image Detection

abstract: Solving large-scale sparse linear systems is essential in fields like mathematics, science, and engineering. Traditional numerical solvers, mainly based on the Krylov subspace iteration algorithm, suffer from the low-efficiency problem, which primarily arises from the less-than-ideal iteration. To tackle this problem, we propose a novel method, namely **Neur**al **K**rylov **It**era**t**ion (**NeurKItt**), for accelerating linear system solving.Specifically, NeurKItt employs a neural operator to predict the invariant subspace of the linear system and then leverages the predicted subspace to accelerate linear system solving. To enhance the subspace prediction accuracy, we utilize QR decomposition for the neural operator outputs and introduce a novel projection loss function for training. NeurKItt benefits the solving by using the predicted subspace to guide the iteration process, significantly reducing the number of iterations.We provide extensive experiments and comprehensive theoretical analyses to demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of NeurKItt. In our main experiments, NeurKItt accelerates the solving of linear systems across various settings and datasets, achieving up to a 5.5× speedup in computation time and a 16.1× speedup in the number of iterations.

paragraphs: Large sparse linear systems appear throughout mathematics, science, and engineering. Traditional Krylov methods solve them through repeated iterations, and ineffective iteration can make the computation expensive. NeurKItt introduces a learned component that guides this process, aiming to reduce the work required by the numerical solver.

A neural operator predicts an invariant subspace associated with the linear system. The method then uses that predicted subspace to guide subsequent iterations. To improve the prediction, the authors apply QR decomposition to the neural operator's outputs and train with a projection-based loss. The learned output thus supplies structural information for solving the system, with the training design focused on making that information more accurate.

The paper presents theoretical analysis and experiments supporting feasibility and efficiency across multiple settings and datasets. Its main experiments report up to 5.5 times faster computation and a 16.1-fold improvement in iteration count. The different gains distinguish reducing iteration work from reducing total runtime, while both support the value of using learned subspaces to accelerate the solver.
summary.tldr: NeurKItt predicts useful invariant subspaces to guide Krylov solvers, reporting up to 5.5 times faster computation.

title: Neural Krylov Iteration for Accelerating Linear System Solving

abstract: We propose a new algorithm for model-based distributional reinforcement learning (RL), and prove that it is minimax-optimal for approximating return distributions in the generative model regime (up to logarithmic factors), the first result of this kind for any distributional RL algorithm. Our analysis also provides new theoretical perspectives on categorical approaches to distributional RL, as well as introducing a new distributional Bellman equation, the stochastic categorical CDF Bellman equation, which we expect to be of independent interest. Finally, we provide an experimental study comparing a variety of model-based distributional RL algorithms, with several key takeaways for practitioners.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning approximates the distribution of returns, describing the range of possible outcomes rather than only their average. This paper introduces a model-based algorithm for that problem and analyzes it in the generative model regime. Its central contribution is a guarantee about how efficiently return distributions can be approximated in that setting.

The authors prove minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors. This means the algorithm's requirement is close to the best achievable worst-case requirement under the analyzed regime. They identify this as the first guarantee of its kind for a distributional reinforcement learning algorithm. The scope of the result is the generative model setting specified in the paper.

The analysis also offers theoretical perspectives on categorical distributional methods and introduces a stochastic categorical cumulative-distribution-function Bellman equation. The authors expect this equation to be useful independently of the algorithm. An experimental comparison of several model-based distributional approaches complements the theory and provides practical takeaways, connecting a worst-case guarantee with an empirical study of algorithm choices.
summary.tldr: A new model-based distributional RL algorithm achieves minimax-optimal return-distribution approximation up to logarithmic factors in the generative model regime.

title: Near-Minimax-Optimal Distributional Reinforcement Learning with a Generative Model

abstract: Generative AI has revolutionised visual content editing, empowering users to effortlessly modify images and videos. However, not all edits are equal. To perform realistic edits in domains such as natural image or medical imaging, modifications must respect causal relationships inherent to the data generation process. Such image editing falls into the counterfactual image generation regime. Evaluating counterfactual image generation is substantially complex: not only it lacks observable ground truths, but also requires adherence to causal constraints. Although several counterfactual image generation methods and evaluation metrics exist a comprehensive comparison within a unified setting is lacking. We present a comparison framework to thoroughly benchmark counterfactual image generation methods. We evaluate the performance of three conditional image generation model families developed within the Structural Causal Model (SCM) framework. We incorporate several metrics that assess diverse aspects of counterfactuals, such as composition, effectiveness, minimality of interventions, and image realism. We integrate all models that have been used for the task at hand and expand them to novel datasets and causal graphs, demonstrating the superiority of Hierarchical VAEs across most datasets and metrics. Our framework is implemented in a user-friendly Python package that can be extended to incorporate additional SCMs, causal methods, generative models, and datasets for the community to build on. Code: https://github.com/gulnazaki/counterfactual-benchmark.
