paragraphs: Counterfactual image editing asks how an image would change under an intervention while respecting the causal relationships behind its creation. A visually plausible edit alone is therefore insufficient. Evaluation is especially difficult because the corresponding counterfactual ground truth is generally unobservable, and successful editing must satisfy causal constraints as well as produce realistic images.

This paper provides a shared comparison framework for three families of conditional image generators developed within structural causal models. It brings together models previously used for this task and extends their evaluation to additional datasets and causal graphs. The evaluation examines several properties, including composition, whether interventions take effect, how limited the changes are, and visual realism.

Hierarchical variational autoencoders perform best across most of the evaluated datasets and metrics. That qualified result identifies a strong model family within the comparison while preserving differences across evaluation settings. The framework is also packaged as extensible Python software, allowing researchers to add causal models, generation methods, and datasets to the same benchmarking structure.
summary.tldr: A unified counterfactual image-generation benchmark finds hierarchical VAEs strongest across most evaluated datasets and metrics.

title: Benchmarking Counterfactual Image Generation

abstract: The comic domain is rapidly advancing with the development of single-page analysis and synthesis models. However, evaluation metrics and datasets lag behind, often limited to small-scale or single-style test sets. We introduce a novel benchmark, CoMix, designed to evaluate the multi-task capabilities of models in comic analysis. Unlike existing benchmarks that focus on isolated tasks such as object detection or text recognition, CoMix addresses a broader range of tasks including object detection, speaker identification, character re-identification, reading order, and multi-modal reasoning tasks like character naming and dialogue generation. Our benchmark comprises three existing datasets with expanded annotations to support multi-task evaluation. To mitigate the over-representation of manga-style data, we have incorporated a new dataset of carefully selected American comic-style books, thereby enriching the diversity of comic styles. CoMix is designed to assess pre-trained models in zero-shot and limited fine-tuning settings, probing their transfer capabilities across different comic styles and tasks. The validation split of the benchmark is publicly available for research purposes, and an evaluation server for the held-out test split is also provided. Comparative results between human performance and state-of-the-art models reveal a significant performance gap, highlighting substantial opportunities for advancements in comic understanding. The dataset, baseline models, and code are accessible at https://github.com/emanuelevivoli/CoMix-dataset. This initiative sets a new standard for comprehensive comic analysis, providing the community with a common benchmark for evaluation on a large and varied set.

paragraphs: Understanding a comic page involves more than finding objects or reading text. A model may need to identify who is speaking, recognize a recurring character, determine reading order, and connect dialogue with visual content. CoMix brings these capabilities into a shared benchmark, addressing the limited size, stylistic range, and task coverage of earlier evaluations.

The benchmark expands annotations in three existing datasets and adds a collection of American-style comic books to reduce the dominance of manga. Its tasks include object detection, speaker identification, character re-identification, reading order, character naming, and dialogue generation. Models are evaluated without task-specific training or with limited fine-tuning, allowing researchers to examine transfer across both tasks and comic styles.

Comparisons between people and leading models reveal a substantial performance gap. This indicates that the tested systems still struggle with the combined visual, textual, and narrative demands captured by the benchmark. A public validation split and an evaluation server for held-out test data provide a common basis for measuring future progress on this broader set of comic-understanding abilities.
summary.tldr: CoMix evaluates diverse comic-understanding tasks and styles, revealing a substantial gap between humans and leading models.

title: CoMix: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multi-Task Comic Understanding

abstract: World models are critical for autonomous driving to simulate environmental dynamics and generate synthetic data. Existing methods struggle to disentangle ego-vehicle motion (perspective shifts) from scene evolvement (agent interactions), leading to suboptimal predictions. Instead, we propose to separate environmental changes from ego-motion by leveraging the scene-centric coordinate systems. In this paper, we introduce COME: a framework that integrates scene-centric forecasting Control into the Occupancy world ModEl. Specifically, COME first generates ego-irrelevant, spatially consistent future features through a scene-centric prediction branch, which are then converted into scene condition using a tailored ControlNet. These condition features are subsequently injected into the occupancy world model, enabling more accurate and controllable future occupancy predictions. Experimental results on the nuScenes-Occ3D dataset show that COME achieves consistent and significant improvements over state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods across diverse configurations, including different input sources (ground-truth, camera-based, fusion-based occupancy) and prediction horizons (3s and 8s). For example, under the same settings, COME achieves 26.3% better mIoU metric than DOME and 23.7% better mIoU metric than UniScene. These results highlight the efficacy of disentangled representation learning in enhancing spatio-temporal prediction fidelity for world models. Code is available at https://github.com/synsin0/COME.

paragraphs: A driving world model must predict how the surrounding scene changes, but its observations also change when the vehicle itself moves. Mixing these effects makes it harder to distinguish actual interactions from shifts in viewpoint. COME addresses this by making predictions in coordinates centered on the scene, separating environmental evolution from ego-vehicle motion.

A dedicated prediction branch first generates future features that remain spatially consistent and independent of ego motion. A tailored ControlNet converts those features into conditioning information, which is injected into an occupancy world model. This gives the model scene-level guidance for predicting what space will be occupied in the future.

On nuScenes-Occ3D, COME reports consistent, significant improvements across ground-truth, camera-based, and fusion-based occupancy inputs, with prediction horizons of three and eight seconds. Under matched settings, reported mIoU improvements are 26.3% over DOME and 23.7% over UniScene. These findings support separating viewpoint changes from scene dynamics as a useful way to improve the accuracy and controllability of future occupancy predictions.
summary.tldr: COME separates scene changes from vehicle motion and uses scene-centered guidance to improve future occupancy predictions.

title: COME: Adding Scene-Centric Forecasting Control to Occupancy World Model

abstract: We present new fast-rate PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds for multi-task and meta-learning in the unbalanced setting, i.e. when the tasks have training sets of different sizes, as is typically the case in real-world scenarios. Previously, only standard-rate bounds were known for this situation, while fast-rate bounds were limited to the setting where all training sets are of equal size. Our new bounds are numerically computable as well as interpretable, and we demonstrate their flexibility in handling a number of cases where they give stronger guarantees than previous bounds. Besides the bounds themselves, we also make conceptual contributions: we demonstrate that the unbalanced multi-task setting has different statistical properties than the balanced situation, specifically that proofs from the balanced situation do not carry over to the unbalanced setting. Additionally, we shed light on the fact that the unbalanced situation allows two meaningful definitions of multi-task risk, depending on whether all tasks should be considered equally important or if sample-rich tasks should receive more weight than sample-poor ones.

paragraphs: This paper develops generalization guarantees for learning across tasks whose training datasets have different sizes. That imbalance matters because earlier fast-rate bounds covered equally sized task datasets, while the unequal-size setting had only standard-rate results. The new analysis addresses multi-task learning and meta-learning using PAC-Bayesian bounds.

The bounds are numerically computable and interpretable, and the authors demonstrate cases where they provide stronger guarantees than previous results. Here, a faster rate concerns how the statistical guarantee improves with available data; the contribution is about generalization analysis rather than a claim that model training executes faster.

The paper also shows why unequal dataset sizes require distinct reasoning: proofs from the balanced setting do not simply transfer. It identifies two meaningful definitions of multi-task risk, one giving every task equal importance and another assigning more weight to tasks with more samples. This distinction makes the evaluation objective explicit. A guarantee can mean different things depending on whether the goal is balanced performance across tasks or performance weighted by data availability.
summary.tldr: New PAC-Bayesian bounds provide fast-rate guarantees for tasks with unequal dataset sizes and clarify alternative ways to weight task risk.

title: Fast Rate Bounds for Multi-Task and Meta-Learning with Different Sample Sizes

abstract: Recovering the dynamics from a few snapshots of a high-dimensional system is a challenging task in statistical physics and machine learning, with important applications in computational biology. Many algorithms have been developed to tackle this problem, based on frameworks such as optimal transport and the Schrödinger bridge. A notable recent framework is Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport (RUOT), which integrates both stochastic dynamics and unnormalized distributions. However, since many existing methods do not explicitly enforce optimality conditions, their solutions often struggle to satisfy the principle of least action and meet challenges to converge in a stable and reliable way. To address these issues, we propose Variational RUOT (Var-RUOT), a new framework to solve the RUOT problem. By incorporating the optimal necessary conditions for the RUOT problem into both the parameterization of the search space and the loss function design, Var-RUOT only needs to learn a scalar field to solve the RUOT problem and can search for solutions with lower action. We also examined the challenge of selecting a growth penalty function in the widely used Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric and proposed a solution that better aligns with biological priors in Var-RUOT. We validated the effectiveness of Var-RUOT on both simulated data and real single-cell datasets. Compared with existing algorithms, Var-RUOT can find solutions with lower action while exhibiting faster convergence and improved training stability. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZerooVector/VarRUOT.

paragraphs: Recovering system dynamics from a few high-dimensional snapshots requires choosing plausible changes between observations. Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport accommodates stochastic dynamics and distributions whose total mass can vary. However, the paper argues that methods which do not explicitly enforce optimality conditions can struggle to find low-action solutions and train reliably.

Var-RUOT incorporates necessary optimality conditions into both its search-space parameterization and its training objective. This reduces the learned description to a single scalar field and helps the method search for solutions with lower action, the quantity minimized by the least-action formulation. The design directly connects the optimization procedure to conditions the desired solution must satisfy.

The authors also address the choice of growth penalty in the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric, proposing an option better aligned with biological priors. Evaluations use simulated data and real single-cell datasets. Compared with existing algorithms, Var-RUOT finds lower-action solutions with faster convergence and improved training stability. These results support the benefit of embedding optimality conditions into the learning problem; they do not establish that every learned solution is a global optimum.
summary.tldr: Var-RUOT embeds necessary optimality conditions into a single-field model, finding lower-action dynamics with faster and more stable reported training.

title: Variational Regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport: Single Network, Least Action

abstract: Neural radiance fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) are popular techniques to reconstruct and render photorealistic images. However, the prerequisite of running Structure-from-Motion (SfM) to get camera poses limits their completeness. Although previous methods can reconstruct a few unposed images, they are not applicable when images are unordered or densely captured. In this work, we propose a method to train 3DGS from unposed images. Our method leverages a pre-trained 3D geometric foundation model as the neural scene representation. Since the accuracy of the predicted pointmaps does not suffice for accurate image registration and high-fidelity image rendering, we propose to mitigate the issue by initializing and fine-tuning the pre-trained model from a seed image. The images are then progressively registered and added to the training buffer, which is used to train the model further. We also propose to refine the camera poses and pointmaps by minimizing a point-to-camera ray consistency loss across multiple views. When evaluated on diverse challenging datasets, our method outperforms state-of-the-art pose-free NeRF/3DGS methods in terms of both camera pose accuracy and novel view synthesis, and even renders higher fidelity images than 3DGS trained with COLMAP poses.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to train 3D Gaussian Splatting from images whose camera poses are unknown. Standard reconstruction pipelines depend on a separate Structure-from-Motion stage to estimate those poses. Existing approaches using a few unposed images also struggle with unordered or densely captured collections, motivating a more integrated reconstruction process.

The method uses a pretrained 3D geometric foundation model as its scene representation. Its initial pointmap predictions are not accurate enough for reliable image registration and rendering, so the process starts from a seed image and fine-tunes the model. Additional images are progressively registered and placed in a training buffer, allowing the scene model to improve as more views become available.

A further consistency loss refines camera poses and pointmaps by checking agreement between 3D points and camera rays across views. On challenging datasets, the method improves both camera-pose accuracy and novel-view rendering over evaluated pose-free alternatives. It also produces higher-fidelity images than Gaussian Splatting trained with COLMAP poses in the reported evaluation, supporting the value of jointly improving geometry and registration.
summary.tldr: Progressively refining a pretrained geometric model enables Gaussian Splatting from unposed images and improves pose estimation and rendering in evaluations.

title: Deep Gaussian from Motion: Exploring 3D Geometric Foundation Models for Gaussian Splatting

abstract: Few-shot knowledge graph relational learning seeks to perform reasoning over relations given only a limited number of training examples. While existing approaches largely adopt a meta-learning framework for enabling fast adaptation to new relations, they suffer from two key pitfalls. First, they learn relation meta-knowledge in isolation, failing to capture common relational patterns shared across tasks. Second, they struggle to effectively incorporate local, task-specific contexts crucial for rapid adaptation. To address these limitations, we propose MoEMeta, a novel meta-learning framework that disentangles globally shared knowledge from task-specific contexts to enable both effective generalization and rapid adaptation. MoEMeta introduces two key innovations: (i) a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model that learns globally shared relational prototypes to enhance generalization, and (ii) a task-tailored adaptation mechanism that captures local contexts for fast task-specific adaptation. By balancing global generalization with local adaptability, MoEMeta significantly advances few-shot relational learning. Extensive experiments and analyses on three KG benchmarks demonstrate that MoEMeta consistently outperforms existing baselines, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Few-shot relational learning asks a model to reason about knowledge-graph relations from only a small number of examples. Meta-learning methods aim to make adaptation to a new relation fast, but the paper identifies two weaknesses: learning relation knowledge in isolation and failing to use the local context specific to each task.

MoEMeta separates shared relational knowledge from task-specific information. A mixture-of-experts component learns global relational prototypes, allowing recurring patterns to be represented across tasks. A separate adaptation mechanism captures local context for the current task. These two components address different needs: generalizing from what relations have in common and adjusting quickly to what makes a new relation distinctive.

The combined framework is designed to balance transfer across tasks with rapid local adaptation when examples are scarce. Experiments and analyses on three knowledge-graph benchmarks show consistent improvements over existing baselines and report state-of-the-art performance. The findings support explicitly modeling both shared patterns and local context, rather than expecting a single undifferentiated adaptation process to capture both effectively.
summary.tldr: MoEMeta combines shared relational prototypes with task-specific adaptation to improve knowledge-graph learning from few examples.

title: MoEMeta: Mixture-of-Experts Meta Learning for Few-Shot Relational Learning

abstract: Transformers have revolutionized the field of machine learning. In particular, they can be used to solve complex algorithmic problems, including graph-based tasks. In such algorithmic tasks a key question is what is the minimal size of a transformer that can implement the task. Recent work has begun to explore this problem for graph-based tasks, showing that for sub-linear embedding dimension (i.e., model width) logarithmic depth suffices. However, an open question, which we address here, is what happens if width is allowed to grow linearly, while depth is kept fixed. Here we analyze this setting, and provide the surprising result that with linear width, constant depth suffices for solving a host of graph-based problems. This suggests that a moderate increase in width can allow much shallower models, which are advantageous in terms of inference and train time. For other problems, we show that quadratic width is required. Our results demonstrate the complex and intriguing landscape of transformer implementations of graph-based algorithms. We empirically investigate these trade-offs between the relative powers of depth and width and find tasks where wider models have the same accuracy as deep models, while having much faster train and inference time due to parallelizable hardware.

paragraphs: When a transformer implements a graph algorithm, model size involves both depth and embedding width. Previous work showed that logarithmic depth can suffice when width grows sublinearly. This paper studies a different allocation of resources: allowing width to grow linearly while keeping the number of layers fixed as the problem grows.

The theoretical results show that linear width and constant depth suffice for a range of graph problems. Other problems require quadratic width. This distinction matters because it shows that replacing depth with width depends on the task; one architectural tradeoff does not describe every graph computation. The results map out several different possibilities for implementing these algorithms.

The authors also investigate the tradeoffs empirically. They identify tasks where wider models match deeper models’ accuracy while training and running much faster on parallelizable hardware. These experiments connect representational results to practical computation: a shallower architecture can be advantageous when its extra width is sufficient for the task and the hardware can exploit that width.
summary.tldr: For several graph tasks, linear transformer width permits constant depth, while other tasks require quadratic width.

title: Depth-Width Tradeoffs for Transformers on Graph Tasks

abstract: Recent advancements in Long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning models have improved performance on complex tasks, but they suffer from overthinking, which generates redundant reasoning steps, especially for simple questions. This paper revisits the reasoning patterns of Long and Short CoT models, observing that the Short CoT patterns offer concise reasoning efficiently, while the Long CoT patterns excel in challenging scenarios where the Short CoT patterns struggle. To enable models to leverage both patterns, we propose Question-Free Fine-Tuning (QFFT), a fine-tuning approach that removes the input question during training and learns exclusively from Long CoT responses. This approach enables the model to adaptively employ both reasoning patterns: it prioritizes the Short CoT patterns and activates the Long CoT patterns only when necessary. Experiments on various mathematical datasets demonstrate that QFFT reduces average response length by more than 50\%, while achieving performance comparable to Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). Additionally, QFFT exhibits superior performance compared to SFT in noisy, out-of-domain, and low-resource scenarios.

paragraphs: Long chains of reasoning can help with difficult problems, but they can also produce redundant steps on easy ones. This paper compares long and short chain-of-thought patterns, observing that shorter reasoning is efficient while longer reasoning helps in challenging cases where short reasoning struggles. The goal is to let one model use both patterns adaptively.

Question-Free Fine-Tuning changes the training input in a simple but consequential way: it removes the question and learns exclusively from long chain-of-thought responses. The reported effect is a model that prioritizes short reasoning and activates longer reasoning when needed. Removing questions is a training choice; the method is presented as a way to adapt reasoning behavior when answering questions.

Across mathematical datasets, QFFT reduces average response length by more than 50% while achieving performance comparable to supervised fine-tuning. It also outperforms that comparison in noisy, out-of-domain, and low-resource settings. The findings suggest that learning from long responses without their associated questions can support selective use of extended reasoning, yielding shorter answers without the reported loss of overall mathematical performance.
summary.tldr: QFFT trains on long reasoning responses without questions, cutting average response length by over 50% while matching supervised fine-tuning performance on mathematical datasets.

title: QFFT, Question-Free Fine-Tuning for Adaptive Reasoning

abstract: Token embeddings play a crucial role in language modeling but, despite this practical relevance, their theoretical understanding is limited. Our paper addresses the gap by characterizing the structure of embeddings obtained via gradient descent. Specifically, we consider a one-layer softmax attention model with a linear head for binary classification, i.e., $\mathrm{Softmax}( p^\top E_X^\top ) E_X v = \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^T \exp(p^\top E_{x_i}) E_{x_i}^\top v}{\sum_{j=1}^T \exp(p^\top E_{x_{j}}) }$, where $E_X = [ E_{x_1} , \dots, E_{x_T} ]^\top$ contains the embeddings of the input sequence, $p$ is the embedding of the $\mathrm{\langle cls \rangle}$ token and $v$ the output vector. First, we show that, already after a single step of gradient training with the standard logistic loss, the embeddings $E_X$ capture the importance of tokens in the dataset by aligning with the output vector $v$ proportionally to the corresponding average signed frequency that captures the relevance of tokens to the labels. Then, after training $p$ via gradient flow until convergence, the softmax selects the important tokens in the sentence (i.e., those that are predictive of the label), and the resulting $\mathrm{\langle cls \rangle}$ embedding maximizes the margin for such a selection. Experiments on real-world datasets (IMDB, Yelp) exhibit a phenomenology close to that unveiled by our theory.

title: Attention with Trained Embeddings Provably Selects Important Tokens

abstract: Predicting accurate future trajectories of pedestrians is essential for autonomous systems but remains a challenging task due to the need for adaptability in different environments and domains. A common approach involves collecting scenario-specific data and performing fine-tuning via backpropagation. However, the need to fine-tune for each new scenario is often impractical for deployment on edge devices. To address this challenge, we introduce TrajICL, an In-Context Learning (ICL) framework for pedestrian trajectory prediction that enables adaptation without fine-tuning on the scenario-specific data at inference time without requiring weight updates. We propose a spatio-temporal similarity-based example selection (STES) method that selects relevant examples from previously observed trajectories within the same scene by identifying similar motion patterns at corresponding locations. To further refine this selection, we introduce prediction-guided example selection (PG-ES), which selects examples based on both the past trajectory and the predicted future trajectory, rather than relying solely on the past trajectory. This approach allows the model to account for long-term dynamics when selecting examples. Finally, instead of relying on small real-world datasets with limited scenario diversity, we train our model on a large-scale synthetic dataset to enhance its prediction ability by leveraging in-context examples. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TrajICL achieves remarkable adaptation across both in-domain and cross-domain scenarios, outperforming even fine-tuned approaches across multiple public benchmarks.

Experiments show strong adaptation in both in-domain and cross-domain settings, outperforming even fine-tuned approaches on multiple public benchmarks. The results support example selection as a practical mechanism for adapting trajectory prediction, with relevant scene history supplying information that would otherwise require scenario-specific training.
summary.tldr: TrajICL adapts pedestrian trajectory prediction without weight updates by selecting scene-specific examples using spatial, temporal, and predicted-motion similarity.

title: Towards Predicting Any Human Trajectory In Context

abstract: The Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) is one of the simplest generative neural networks capable of learning input distributions. Despite its simplicity, the analysis of its performance in learning from the training data is only well understood in cases that essentially reduce to singular value decomposition of the data. Here, we consider the limit of a large dimension of the input space and a constant number of hidden units. In this limit, we simplify the standard RBM training objective into a form that is equivalent to the multi-index model with non-separable regularization. This opens a path to analyze training of the RBM using methods that are established for multi-index models, such as Approximate Message Passing (AMP) and its state evolution, and the analysis of Gradient Descent (GD) via the dynamical mean-field theory. We then give rigorous asymptotics of the training dynamics of RBMs on data generated by the spiked covariance model as a prototype of a structure suitable for unsupervised learning. We show in particular that RBMs reach the optimal computational weak recovery threshold, aligning with the Baik-Ben Arous-Péché (BBP) transition, in the spiked covariance model.

title: Learning with Restricted Boltzmann Machines: Asymptotics of AMP and GD in High Dimensions

abstract: Agents that understand objects and their interactions can learn policies that are more robust and transferable. However, most object-centric RL methods factor state by individual objects while leaving interactions implicit. We introduce the Factored Interactive Object-Centric World Model (FIOC-WM), a unified framework that learns structured representations of both objects and their interactions within a world model. FIOC-WM captures environment dynamics with disentangled and modular representations of object interactions, improving sample efficiency and generalization for policy learning. Concretely, FIOC-WM first learns object-centric latents and an interaction structure directly from pixels, leveraging pre-trained vision encoders. The learned world model then decomposes tasks into composable interaction primitives, and a hierarchical policy is trained on top: a high level selects the type and order of interactions, while a low level executes them. On simulated robotic and embodied-AI benchmarks, FIOC-WM improves policy-learning sample efficiency and generalization over world-model baselines, indicating that explicit, modular interaction learning is crucial for robust control.

paragraphs: Representing an environment as separate objects can help a reinforcement-learning agent organize what it observes. However, the paper argues that many object-centric methods leave interactions between objects implicit. FIOC-WM makes those interactions an explicit, structured part of a learned world model.

Using pretrained vision encoders, the framework learns object representations and an interaction structure directly from pixels. It models dynamics through modular, disentangled interaction representations and decomposes tasks into composable interaction primitives. A hierarchical policy then uses this structure: its high level selects which interactions to perform and in what order, while its low level carries them out.

On simulated robotics and embodied-AI benchmarks, the framework improves policy-learning sample efficiency and generalization relative to world-model baselines. These results support the value of explicitly learning reusable interactions alongside object representations. The proposed structure links perception, prediction, and action selection: objects organize the scene, interaction primitives organize possible changes, and the policy organizes how those changes should be executed to accomplish a task.
summary.tldr: FIOC-WM explicitly models objects and modular interactions, enabling hierarchical policies with improved sample efficiency and generalization in simulation.

title: Learning Interactive World Model for Object-Centric Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) excel at multimodal understanding but suffer from high computational costs due to redundant vision tokens. Existing pruning methods typically rely on single-layer attention scores to rank and prune redundant visual tokens to solve this inefficiency. However, as the interaction between tokens and layers is complicated, this raises a basic question: Is such a simple single-layer criterion sufficient to identify redundancy? To answer this question, we rethink the emergence of redundant visual tokens from a fundamental perspective: information flow, which models the interaction between tokens and layers by capturing how information moves between tokens across layers. We find (1) the CLS token acts as an information relay, which can simplify the complicated flow analysis; (2) the redundancy emerges progressively and dynamically via layer-wise attention concentration; and (3) relying solely on attention scores from single layers can lead to contradictory redundancy identification. Based on this, we propose FlowCut, an information-flow-aware pruning framework, mitigating the insufficiency of the current criterion for identifying redundant tokens and better aligning with the model's inherent behaviors. Extensive experiments show FlowCut achieves superior results, outperforming SoTA by 1.6% on LLaVA-1.5-7B with 88.9% token reduction, and by 4.3% on LLaVA-NeXT-7B with 94.4% reduction, delivering 3.2$\times$ speed-up in the prefilling stage. Our code is available at https://github.com/TungChintao/FlowCut.

paragraphs: Vision-language models spend substantial computation processing visual tokens, some of which become redundant. Many pruning methods identify expendable tokens using attention scores from a single layer. FlowCut examines whether that snapshot is enough when information moves between tokens and changes across multiple layers.

The authors analyze information flow and identify three relevant behaviors. The CLS token serves as a relay that simplifies the analysis; redundancy develops progressively as attention becomes concentrated; and different single-layer attention views can disagree about which tokens are redundant. summary.tldr: FlowCut tracks information flow across layers to prune visual tokens while improving the reported performance-efficiency trade-off.

title: FlowCut: Rethinking Redundancy via Information Flow for Efficient Vision-Language Models

abstract: Text-3D Scene Retrieval (T3SR) aims to retrieve relevant scenes using linguistic queries. Although traditional T3SR methods have made significant progress in capturing fine-grained associations, they implicitly assume that query descriptions are information-complete. In practical deployments, however, limited by the capabilities of users and models, it is difficult or even impossible to directly obtain a perfect textual query suiting the entire scene and model, thereby leading to performance degradation. To address this issue, we propose a novel Interactive Text-3D Scene Retrieval Method (IDeal), which promotes the enhancement of the alignment between texts and 3D scenes through continuous interaction. To achieve this, we present an Interactive Retrieval Refinement framework (IRR), which employs a questioner to pose contextually relevant questions to an answerer in successive rounds that either promote detailed probing or encourage exploratory divergence within scenes. Upon the iterative responses received from the answerer, IRR adopts a retriever to perform both feature-level and semantic-level information fusion, facilitating scene-level interaction and understanding for more precise re-rankings. To bridge the domain gap between queries and interactive texts, we propose an Interaction Adaptation Tuning strategy (IAT). IAT mitigates the discriminability and diversity risks among augmented text features that approximate the interaction text domain, achieving contrastive domain adaptation for our retriever. Extensive experimental results on three datasets demonstrate the superiority of IDeal.

paragraphs: Searching for a 3D scene through text is difficult when the initial description leaves out relevant information. Existing retrieval approaches often implicitly assume a complete query. IDeal instead makes retrieval interactive, using successive questions and answers to improve the correspondence between the description and candidate scenes.

Its Interactive Retrieval Refinement framework includes a questioner, an answerer, and a retriever. Questions can probe scene details or encourage broader exploration. As answers accumulate, the retriever combines information at both the feature and semantic levels to refine scene rankings. This turns the query into an evolving source of evidence rather than a fixed description used only once.

Experiments on three datasets show that IDeal outperforms the compared approaches. The results support jointly designing the interaction process and retriever adaptation, so additional dialogue can translate into more precise scene retrieval.
summary.tldr: IDeal improves text-to-3D-scene retrieval through iterative questioning, information fusion, and adaptation to conversational descriptions.

title: Interactive Cross-modal Learning for Text-3D Scene Retrieval

abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has emerged as an effective approach for mitigating hallucination in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Although existing methods have achieved significant progress by utilizing vision-oriented contrastive objectives for enhancing MLLMs' attention to visual inputs and hence reducing hallucination, they suffer from non-rigorous optimization objective function and indirect preference supervision. To address these limitations, we propose a Symmetric Multimodal Preference Optimization (SymMPO), which conducts symmetric preference learning with direct preference supervision (i.e., response pairs) for visual understanding enhancement, while maintaining rigorous theoretical alignment with standard DPO. In addition to conventional ordinal preference learning, SymMPO introduces a preference margin consistency loss to quantitatively regulate the preference gap between symmetric preference pairs. Comprehensive evaluation across five benchmarks demonstrate SymMPO's superior performance, validating its effectiveness in hallucination mitigation of MLLMs.

paragraphs: Preference optimization can help multimodal language models reduce hallucination by learning which responses should be favored. Existing approaches use visual contrastive objectives to increase attention to image inputs. This paper identifies two weaknesses in those approaches: insufficiently rigorous optimization objectives and preference supervision that reaches the model indirectly.

The proposed Symmetric Multimodal Preference Optimization method uses response pairs to provide direct preference supervision for improving visual understanding. It organizes learning symmetrically while preserving theoretical consistency with standard Direct Preference Optimization. This alignment is central to the contribution: the method changes how multimodal preferences are used while retaining a rigorous connection to the underlying preference-optimization framework.

SymMPO also introduces a preference margin consistency loss. Ordinary ordinal preference learning indicates which response should rank higher; the added loss regulates the size of the preference gap between symmetric pairs. Evaluations across five benchmarks report superior performance and support the method's effectiveness in reducing multimodal hallucination. The findings suggest that both direct supervision and control over preference margins can contribute to better visual grounding.
summary.tldr: SymMPO combines theoretically aligned symmetric preference learning with preference-gap consistency to reduce multimodal hallucination across five benchmarks.

title: Mitigating Hallucination Through Theory-Consistent Symmetric Multimodal Preference Optimization

abstract: Coordinating multiple embodied agents in dynamic environments remains a core challenge in artificial intelligence, requiring both perception-driven reasoning and scalable cooperation strategies. While recent works have leveraged large language models (LLMs) for multi-agent planning, a few have begun to explore vision-language models (VLMs) for visual reasoning. However, these VLM-based approaches remain limited in their support for diverse embodiment types. In this work, we introduce VIKI-Bench, the first hierarchical benchmark tailored for embodied multi-agent cooperation, featuring three structured levels: agent activation, task planning, and trajectory perception. VIKI-Bench includes diverse robot embodiments, multi-view visual observations, and structured supervision signals to evaluate reasoning grounded in visual inputs. To demonstrate the utility of VIKI-Bench, we propose VIKI-R, a two-stage framework that fine-tunes a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) using Chain-of-Thought annotated demonstrations, followed by reinforcement learning under multi-level reward signals. Our extensive experiments show that VIKI-R significantly outperforms baselines method across all task levels. Furthermore, we show that reinforcement learning enables the emergence of compositional cooperation patterns among heterogeneous agents. Together, VIKI-Bench and VIKI-R offer a unified testbed and method for advancing multi-agent, visual-driven cooperation in embodied AI systems.

This paper introduces VIKI-Bench to evaluate that combination. The contribution combines a structured evaluation environment with a training method that uses both demonstrations and rewards. This pairing makes it possible to assess visually grounded cooperation while investigating how learning can improve coordination across heterogeneous agents.
summary.tldr: VIKI-Bench evaluates visually grounded robot cooperation, while VIKI-R improves it through reasoning demonstrations and multi-level reinforcement learning.

title: VIKI‑R: Coordinating Embodied Multi-Agent Cooperation via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper is concerned with online time series forecasting, where unknown distribution shifts occur over time, i.e., latent variables influence the mapping from historical to future observations. To develop an automated way of online time series forecasting, we propose a Theoretical framework for Online Time-series forecasting (TOT in short) with theoretical guarantees. Specifically, we prove that supplying a forecaster with latent variables tightens the Bayes risk—the benefit endures under estimation uncertainty of latent variables and grows as the latent variables achieve a more precise identifiability. To better introduce latent variables into online forecasting algorithms, we further propose to identify latent variables with minimal adjacent observations. Based on these results, we devise a model-agnostic blueprint by employing a temporal decoder to match the distribution of observed variables and two independent noise estimators to model the causal inference of latent variables and mixing procedures of observed variables, respectively. Experiment results on synthetic data support our theoretical claims. Moreover, plug-in implementations built on several baselines yield general improvement across multiple benchmarks, highlighting the effectiveness in real-world applications.

paragraphs: TOT studies online forecasting when hidden variables change the relationship between past and future observations. These latent influences can produce unknown distribution shifts over time. The framework aims to make them useful to a forecaster, combining a theoretical account of their value with a model-agnostic approach to incorporating them.

The authors prove that providing latent variables tightens the Bayes risk. The benefit persists when those variables are estimated with uncertainty and increases when they are more precisely identifiable. They further propose identifying latent variables from minimal adjacent observations. These results connect forecasting performance to how well the hidden factors can be recovered.

Synthetic experiments support the theoretical claims. Plug-in implementations across several forecasting baselines also produce general improvements on multiple benchmarks, providing empirical support for adding latent-variable modeling to existing online forecasters.
summary.tldr: TOT combines theory and a model-agnostic design to improve online forecasting by identifying latent factors behind changing data distributions.

title: Online Time Series Forecasting with Theoretical Guarantees

abstract: Progress in a research field can be hard to assess, in particular when many concurrent methods are proposed in a short period of time. This is the case in digital pathology, where many foundation models have been released recently to serve as feature extractors for tile-level images, being used in a variety of downstream tasks, both for tile- and slide-level problems. Benchmarking available methods then becomes paramount to get a clearer view of the research landscape. In particular, in critical domains such as healthcare, a benchmark should not only focus on evaluating downstream performance, but also provide insights about the main differences between methods, and importantly, further consider uncertainty and robustness to ensure a reliable usage of proposed models. For these reasons, we introduce THUNDER, a tile-level benchmark for digital pathology foundation models, allowing for efficient comparison of many models on diverse datasets with a series of downstream tasks, studying their feature spaces and assessing the robustness and uncertainty of predictions informed by their embeddings. THUNDER is a fast, easy-to-use, dynamic benchmark that can already support a large variety of state-of-the-art foundation, as well as local user-defined models for direct tile-based comparison. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive comparison of 23 foundation models on 16 different datasets covering diverse tasks, feature analysis, and robustness. The code for THUNDER is publicly available at https://github.com/MICS-Lab/thunder.

For these reasons, we introduce THUNDER, a tile-level benchmark for digital pathology foundation models, allowing for efficient comparison of many models on diverse datasets with a series of downstream tasks, studying their feature spaces and assessing the robustness and uncertainty of predictions informed by their embeddings. THUNDER is a fast, easy-to-use, dynamic benchmark that can already support a large variety of state-of-the-art foundation, as well as local user-defined models for direct tile-based comparison. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive comparison of 23 foundation models on 16 different datasets covering diverse tasks, feature analysis, and robustness. The code for THUNDER is publicly available at https://github.com/MICS-Lab/thunder.

paragraphs: Digital pathology has gained many foundation models that convert small image tiles into feature representations for later prediction tasks. With many models appearing in a short period, comparing their usefulness becomes difficult. THUNDER provides a common benchmark for examining these tile-level representations across datasets and tasks.

The benchmark evaluates more than downstream predictive performance. It also studies the models' feature spaces and assesses robustness and uncertainty in predictions based on their embeddings. This broader comparison matters in healthcare, where an accuracy score alone does not describe how reliably a representation supports predictions. THUNDER supports both existing foundation models and locally supplied models for direct comparison.

The paper presents a comparison of 23 foundation models across 16 datasets, covering diverse tasks, representation analysis, and robustness. The benchmark is designed to be fast, easy to use, and adaptable as the model landscape changes. Its contribution is an evaluation framework and a broad comparative study that help characterize differences among pathology representations, rather than a newly proposed feature extractor.
summary.tldr: THUNDER compares pathology foundation models across predictive performance, feature structure, robustness, and uncertainty.

title: THUNDER: Tile-level Histopathology image UNDERstanding benchmark

abstract: Deep learning models are vulnerable to privacy attacks due to their tendency to memorize individual training examples. Theoretically-sound defenses such as differential privacy can defend against this threat, but model performance often suffers. Empirical defenses may thwart existing attacks while maintaining model performance but do not offer any robust theoretical guarantees. In this paper, we explore a new strategy based on the concept of plausible deniability. We introduce a training algorithm called **P**lausibly **D**eniable **S**tochastic **G**radient **D**escent (PD-SGD). The core of this approach is a rejection sampling technique, which probabilistically prevents updating model parameters whenever a mini-batch cannot be plausibly denied. We provide theoretical results showing that PD-SGD effectively mitigates privacy leakage from individual data points. Experiments demonstrate the scalability of PD-SGD and the favorable privacy-utility trade-off it offers compared to existing defense methods.

paragraphs: Neural networks can memorize individual training examples, creating opportunities for privacy attacks. Established defenses present a difficult trade-off: theoretically grounded protection can reduce model performance, while defenses tested against particular attacks may lack robust guarantees. This paper explores plausible deniability as a different foundation for protecting individual training data during learning.

The proposed algorithm, Plausibly Deniable Stochastic Gradient Descent, modifies the process of accepting parameter updates. It uses rejection sampling to probabilistically prevent an update when the associated mini-batch cannot be plausibly denied. Privacy protection therefore enters the training procedure through decisions about which proposed changes to the model are allowed to proceed.

The authors provide theoretical results showing that the algorithm mitigates information leakage from individual examples. Their experiments also demonstrate scalability and a favorable privacy–utility trade-off compared with existing defense methods. The contribution combines an explicit training mechanism with theoretical and empirical support: plausible deniability guides update selection, and the reported results indicate that this can protect privacy while preserving useful model performance.
summary.tldr: PD-SGD probabilistically rejects training updates that fail plausible deniability, offering theoretical privacy protection and a favorable empirical privacy–utility trade-off.

title: Deep Learning with Plausible Deniability

abstract: Post-training plays a crucial role in refining and aligning large language models to meet specific tasks and human preferences. While recent advancements in post-training techniques, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), leverage increased sampling with relative reward scoring to achieve superior performance, these methods often suffer from training instability that limits their practical adoption. As a next step, we present Group Variance Policy Optimization (GVPO). GVPO incorporates the analytical solution to KL-constrained reward maximization directly into its gradient weights, ensuring alignment with the optimal policy. The method provides intuitive physical interpretations: its gradient mirrors the mean squared error between the central distance of implicit rewards and that of actual rewards. GVPO offers two key advantages: (1) it guarantees a unique optimal solution, exactly the KL-constrained reward maximization objective, (2) it supports flexible sampling distributions that avoids on-policy and importance sampling limitations. By unifying theoretical guarantees with practical adaptability, GVPO establishes a new paradigm for reliable and versatile LLM post-training.

paragraphs: Language-model post-training uses feedback to improve task performance and alignment with preferences. Methods that compare rewards across groups of sampled responses can be effective, but training instability complicates their use. This paper proposes Group Variance Policy Optimization, or GVPO, to connect the update rule more directly to a defined reward-maximization objective.

The objective maximizes reward subject to a KL constraint, which limits how far the policy moves. GVPO incorporates the analytical solution of that problem into the weights of its gradient updates. The authors interpret the gradient through a mean-squared-error comparison between centered implicit rewards and centered actual rewards, linking the policy's implied preferences to the feedback it receives.

The paper establishes a unique optimum corresponding exactly to the stated KL-constrained reward-maximization problem. It also supports flexible sampling distributions, avoiding the stated restrictions of on-policy and importance-sampling approaches. These contributions provide a theoretical foundation for the update rule and more freedom in how training responses are sampled, rather than a benchmark-specific performance claim.
summary.tldr: GVPO derives language-model post-training updates from KL-constrained reward maximization, with a unique optimum and flexible sampling distributions.

title: GVPO: Group Variance Policy Optimization for Large Language Model Post-Training

abstract: Metric learning algorithms produce a linear transformation of data which is optimized for a prediction task, such as nearest-neighbor classification or ranking. However, when the input data contains a large portion of non-informative features, existing methods fail to identify the relevant features, and performance degrades accordingly. In this paper, we present an efficient and robust structural metric learning algorithm which enforces group sparsity on the learned transformation, while optimizing for structured ranking output prediction. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms previous methods in both high- and low-noise settings.
originalAbstract: Metric learning algorithms produce a linear transformation of data which is optimized for a prediction task, such as nearest-neighbor classification or ranking. However, when the input data contains a large portion of non-informative features, existing methods fail to identify the relevant features, and performance degrades accordingly. In this paper, we present an efficient and robust structural metric learning algorithm which enforces group sparsity on the learned transformation, while optimizing for structured ranking output prediction. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms previous methods in both high- and low-noise settings.

paragraphs: Metric learning transforms data so that distances better serve a prediction task, such as ranking or nearest-neighbor classification. The paper focuses on a difficulty that arises when many input features carry little useful information. In that setting, existing methods can fail to identify the relevant features, and prediction quality deteriorates.

The proposed method learns a linear transformation while imposing group sparsity on it. This structural constraint encourages selective use of groups within the transformation. At the same time, training optimizes structured ranking output prediction, tying the learned representation to the ranking task it is intended to support.

The authors present the algorithm as efficient and robust, and evaluate it on synthetic and real datasets. It outperforms previous methods in both high-noise and low-noise settings in those experiments. The contribution is the combination of structural feature selection and task-oriented metric learning, with evidence that the combination helps across the evaluated noise conditions.
summary.tldr: Group sparsity helps a ranking-oriented metric learner handle uninformative features, outperforming previous methods in the reported noise settings.

title: Robust Structural Metric Learning

abstract: In recent applications with massive but less reliable data (e.g., labels obtained by a semi-supervised learning method or crowdsourcing), non-robustness of the support vector machine (SVM) often causes considerable performance deterioration. Although improving the robustness of SVM has been investigated for long time, robust SVM (RSVM) learning still poses two major challenges: obtaining a good (local) solution from a non-convex optimization problem and optimally controlling the robustness-efficiency trade-off. In this paper, we address these two issues simultaneously in an integrated way by introducing a novel homotopy approach to RSVM learning. Based on theoretical investigation of the geometry of RSVM solutions, we show that a path of local RSVM solutions can be computed efficiently when the influence of outliers is gradually suppressed as simulated annealing. We experimentally demonstrate that our algorithm tends to produce better local solutions than the alternative approach based on the concave-convex procedure, with the ability of stable and efficient model selection for controlling the influence of outliers.

paragraphs: Support vector machines can lose substantial performance when training data are unreliable, including when labels come from crowdsourcing or semi-supervised methods. Robust SVMs address this concern but introduce two linked difficulties: their non-convex objectives make good local solutions hard to obtain, and the influence assigned to outliers must be controlled.

The paper handles these difficulties together through a homotopy approach. It gradually suppresses the influence of outliers and follows a path of local robust SVM solutions, in a process compared with simulated annealing. A theoretical study of solution geometry establishes that this path can be computed efficiently.

Following the path also supports model selection over different degrees of outlier influence. Experiments show that the algorithm tends to find better local solutions than an alternative based on the concave-convex procedure, while allowing stable and efficient model selection. These are qualified empirical advantages among local solutions. The method connects optimization and robustness tuning through a single changing sequence of robust SVM problems.
summary.tldr: Outlier Path gradually reduces outlier influence while tracking robust SVM solutions, supporting efficient tuning and empirically better local solutions.

title: Outlier Path: A Homotopy Algorithm for Robust SVM

abstract: We consider sequential decision problems under uncertainty, where we seek to optimize an unknown function from noisy samples. This requires balancing exploration (learning about the objective) and exploitation (localizing the maximum), a problem well-studied in the multi-armed bandit literature. In many applications, however, we require that the sampled function values exceed some prespecified "safety" threshold, a requirement that existing algorithms fail to meet. Examples include medical applications where patient comfort must be guaranteed, recommender systems aiming to avoid user dissatisfaction, and robotic control, where one seeks to avoid controls causing physical harm to the platform. We tackle this novel, yet rich, set of problems under the assumption that the unknown function satisfies regularity conditions expressed via a Gaussian process prior. We develop an efficient algorithm called SafeOpt, and theoretically guarantee its convergence to a natural notion of optimum reachable under safety constraints. We evaluate SafeOpt on synthetic data, as well as two real applications: movie recommendation, and therapeutic spinal cord stimulation.

paragraphs: Optimizing an unknown function from noisy observations requires choosing where to gather information and where to pursue promising outcomes. Some applications add a stricter requirement: every sampled function value must stay above a specified safety threshold. This paper studies that requirement as part of sequential optimization, rather than judging a method only by the final value it finds.

The authors introduce SafeOpt under regularity assumptions expressed through a Gaussian process prior. The algorithm addresses exploration and optimization together with the safety constraint. Their theoretical result guarantees convergence to a notion of optimum that is reachable under those constraints, making safe reachability part of the objective being analyzed.

This reachable optimum is the relevant target because the safety requirement constrains which evaluations the procedure can make. The paper evaluates SafeOpt on synthetic data and in movie recommendation and therapeutic spinal cord stimulation. These applications illustrate the intended setting: learning useful decisions while respecting a threshold throughout the process, under the assumptions supporting the analysis.
summary.tldr: SafeOpt optimizes from noisy observations under a safety threshold, with conditional convergence to a safely reachable optimum.

title: Safe Exploration for Optimization with Gaussian Processes

abstract: We revisit the task of learning a Euclidean metric from data. We approach this problem from first principles and formulate it as a surprisingly simple optimization problem. Indeed, our formulation even admits a closed form solution. This solution possesses several very attractive properties: (i) an innate geometric appeal through the Riemannian geometry of positive definite matrices; (ii) ease of interpretability; and (iii) computational speed several orders of magnitude faster than the widely used LMNN and ITML methods. Furthermore, on standard benchmark datasets, our closed-form solution consistently attains higher classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Metric learning asks how to choose a distance measure from data. This paper revisits learning a Euclidean metric and derives a simple optimization formulation from first principles. Its central computational feature is a closed-form solution, giving a direct way to obtain the learned metric from the formulation.

The solution also has a geometric interpretation through the Riemannian geometry of positive definite matrices. That connection gives the method mathematical structure alongside its computational simplicity. The authors emphasize interpretability as another attractive property, making the proposal a combination of a clear optimization problem, an interpretable solution, and a geometric account of that solution.

The reported computations are several orders of magnitude faster than the widely used LMNN and ITML methods. On standard benchmark datasets, the closed-form method also consistently achieves higher classification accuracy. These empirical findings suggest that the simpler formulation can improve both speed and predictive usefulness in the evaluated settings. The paper’s contribution is therefore broader than obtaining a convenient formula: it connects that formula to favorable practical metric-learning results.
summary.tldr: A closed-form metric-learning formulation combines geometric interpretability with reported speed and classification-accuracy gains over LMNN and ITML.

title: Geometric Mean Metric Learning

abstract: Observational studies are rising in importance due to the widespread accumulation of data in fields such as healthcare, education, employment and ecology. We consider the task of answering counterfactual questions such as, “Would this patient have lower blood sugar had she received a different medication?". We propose a new algorithmic framework for counterfactual inference which brings together ideas from domain adaptation and representation learning. In addition to a theoretical justification, we perform an empirical comparison with previous approaches to causal inference from observational data. Our deep learning algorithm significantly outperforms the previous state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Counterfactual inference asks what would have happened under a different choice from the one observed. The paper illustrates this with a patient whose blood sugar might have differed under another medication. It studies such questions using observational data, motivated by the growing availability of records in healthcare, education, employment, and ecology.

The authors propose an algorithmic framework that combines representation learning with ideas from domain adaptation. Representation learning concerns how data are encoded for prediction, while domain adaptation addresses differences between prediction settings. Bringing them together makes the representation of observational data part of the approach to estimating outcomes under alternative choices.

The framework has a theoretical justification and is evaluated against earlier approaches to causal inference from observational data. The authors report that their deep learning algorithm significantly outperforms the previous state of the art in that comparison. The result supports the proposed combination as a promising computational approach to counterfactual questions, with the improvement grounded in the paper's empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: A counterfactual inference framework combines representation learning and domain adaptation, with strong reported empirical improvements.

title: Learning Representations for Counterfactual Inference

abstract: We consider Multiclass and Multilabel classification with extremely large number of classes, of which only few are labeled to each instance. In such setting, standard methods that have training, prediction cost linear to the number of classes become intractable. State-of-the-art methods thus aim to reduce the complexity by exploiting correlation between labels under assumption that the similarity between labels can be captured by structures such as low-rank matrix or balanced tree. However, as the diversity of labels increases in the feature space, structural assumption can be easily violated, which leads to degrade in the testing performance. In this work, we show that a margin-maximizing loss with l1 penalty, in case of Extreme Classification, yields extremely sparse solution both in primal and in dual without sacrificing the expressive power of predictor. We thus propose a Fully-Corrective Block-Coordinate Frank-Wolfe (FC-BCFW) algorithm that exploits both primal and dual sparsity to achieve a complexity sublinear to the number of primal and dual variables. A bi-stochastic search method is proposed to further improve the efficiency. In our experiments on both Multiclass and Multilabel problems, the proposed method achieves significant higher accuracy than existing approaches of Extreme Classification with very competitive training and prediction time.

paragraphs: Extreme classification involves a very large set of possible classes, with only a few labels attached to each example. Methods whose training and prediction costs grow linearly with the class count can become impractical. Existing approaches exploit label relationships through structures such as low-rank matrices or balanced trees, but those assumptions can fail as labels become more diverse.

The paper shows that a margin-maximizing loss combined with an l1 penalty produces highly sparse primal and dual solutions in this setting without sacrificing the predictor's expressive power. The proposed Fully-Corrective Block-Coordinate Frank-Wolfe algorithm exploits both forms of sparsity, achieving complexity sublinear in the numbers of primal and dual variables. A bi-stochastic search procedure further improves efficiency.

In experiments covering multiclass and multilabel problems, the method achieves significantly higher accuracy than existing extreme-classification approaches while keeping training and prediction times very competitive. The contribution is a route to scalability based on sparsity in the optimization problem, addressing the practical difficulties associated with imposing restrictive structures on label relationships.
summary.tldr: PD-Sparse exploits primal and dual sparsity to make extreme classification efficient while preserving expressive power.

title: PD-Sparse : A Primal and Dual Sparse Approach to Extreme Multiclass and Multilabel Classification

abstract: This paper presents OptNet, a network architecture that integrates optimization problems (here, specifically in the form of quadratic programs) as individual layers in larger end-to-end trainable deep networks. These layers encode constraints and complex dependencies between the hidden states that traditional convolutional and fully-connected layers often cannot capture. In this paper, we explore the foundations for such an architecture: we show how techniques from sensitivity analysis, bilevel optimization, and implicit differentiation can be used to exactly differentiate through these layers and with respect to layer parameters; we develop a highly efficient solver for these layers that exploits fast GPU-based batch solves within a primal-dual interior point method, and which provides backpropagation gradients with virtually no additional cost on top of the solve; and we highlight the application of these approaches in several problems. In one notable example, we show that the method is capable of learning to play mini-Sudoku (4x4) given just input and output games, with no a priori information about the rules of the game; this highlights the ability of our architecture to learn hard constraints better than other neural architectures.

Specifically, each such layer solves a quadratic program, allowing it to express constraints and dependencies among hidden states that conventional convolutional or fully connected layers often struggle to capture. The surrounding network remains trainable end to end.

The paper explains how sensitivity analysis, bilevel optimization, and implicit differentiation provide exact derivatives through these layers and with respect to their parameters. It also introduces a solver using GPU-based batch computations within a primal-dual interior-point method. The solver supplies backpropagation gradients at virtually no extra cost beyond solving the optimization problem itself.

Applications demonstrate how this architecture can learn constrained behavior. In a highlighted example, it learns to play 4-by-4 mini-Sudoku from input and output games without being given the rules beforehand. The example supports the authors' claim that the architecture can learn hard constraints better than other neural architectures. The contribution joins an expressive layer design with differentiation techniques and an efficient implementation.
summary.tldr: OptNet makes quadratic programs differentiable neural-network layers, enabling end-to-end learning of constraints and structured dependencies.

title: OptNet: Differentiable Optimization as a Layer in Neural Networks

abstract: Infinite Layer Networks (ILN) have been proposed as an architecture that mimics neural networks while enjoying some of the advantages of kernel methods. ILN are networks that integrate over infinitely many nodes within a single hidden layer. It has been demonstrated by several authors that the problem of learning ILN can be reduced to the kernel trick, implying that whenever a certain integral can be computed analytically they are efficiently learnable. In this work we give an online algorithm for ILN, which avoids the kernel trick assumption. More generally and of independent interest, we show that kernel methods in general can be exploited even when the kernel cannot be efficiently computed but can only be estimated via sampling. We provide a regret analysis for our algorithm, showing that it matches the sample complexity of methods which have access to kernel values. Thus, our method is the first to demonstrate that the kernel trick is not necessary, as such, and random features suffice to obtain comparable performance.

paragraphs: Infinite Layer Networks integrate over infinitely many nodes in a single hidden layer. Earlier approaches connect learning these networks to kernel methods, making efficient learning possible when a particular integral can be evaluated analytically. This paper develops an online algorithm that avoids relying on that analytic kernel computation.

The broader idea is to use kernels that can be estimated through sampling even when their values cannot be computed efficiently. Random features supply the approximation needed by the learning procedure. This extends the usable setting from access to efficiently calculated kernel values to access to sampled estimates of those values.

The authors provide a regret analysis showing that their algorithm matches the sample complexity of methods with access to kernel values. That is the precise sense in which the proposed approach achieves comparable performance. The result establishes that explicit use of the kernel trick is not necessary for the analyzed learning guarantees, and it gives a route to learning infinite-layer models through random features.
summary.tldr: An online random-feature algorithm learns infinite-layer networks with sample complexity matching methods that can access kernel values.

title: Learning Infinite Layer Networks Without the Kernel Trick

abstract: We propose a hierarchical approach for making long-term predictions of future frames. To avoid inherent compounding errors in recursive pixel-level prediction, we propose to first estimate high-level structure in the input frames, then predict how that structure evolves in the future, and finally by observing a single frame from the past and the predicted high-level structure, we construct the future frames without having to observe any of the pixel-level predictions. Long-term video prediction is difficult to perform by recurrently observing the predicted frames because the small errors in pixel space exponentially amplify as predictions are made deeper into the future. Our approach prevents pixel-level error propagation from happening by removing the need to observe the predicted frames. Our model is built with a combination of LSTM and analogy based encoder-decoder convolutional neural networks, which independently predict the video structure and generate the future frames, respectively. In experiments, our model is evaluated on the Human3.6M and Penn Action datasets on the task of long-term pixel-level video prediction of humans performing actions and demonstrate significantly better results than the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Predicting a video by repeatedly feeding generated frames back into a model can amplify small pixel errors over time. This paper separates prediction of the scene's high-level structure from generation of its visual appearance. The goal is to remove the feedback path through which errors in generated pixels propagate into later predictions.

The method first estimates structure from the input frames and then predicts how that structure evolves. It generates future frames using the predicted structure and a single observed past frame. An LSTM predicts the structural evolution, while an analogy-based convolutional encoder-decoder produces the images. Future image generation therefore does not require observing earlier pixel-level predictions.

The model is evaluated on long-term prediction of human actions using Human3.6M and Penn Action. The authors report significantly better results than existing leading methods. The architecture specifically prevents propagation through recursively observed generated frames; its contribution is to organize the prediction task around structure and appearance as separate components.
summary.tldr: Predicting high-level structure before rendering future frames avoids recursive pixel-error propagation and improves long-term human-action video prediction.

title: Learning to Generate Long-term Future via Hierarchical Prediction

abstract: Interpretability of representations in both deep generative and discriminative models is highly desirable. Current methods jointly optimize an objective combining accuracy and interpretability. However, this may reduce accuracy, and is not applicable to already trained models. We propose two interpretability frameworks. First, we provide an interpretable lens for an existing model. We use a generative model which takes as input the representation in an existing (generative or discriminative) model, weakly supervised by limited side information. Applying a flexible and invertible transformation to the input leads to an interpretable representation with no loss in accuracy. We extend the approach using an active learning strategy to choose the most useful side information to obtain, allowing a human to guide what "interpretable" means. Our second framework relies on joint optimization for a representation which is both maximally informative about the side information and maximally compressive about the non-interpretable data factors. This leads to a novel perspective on the relationship between compression and regularization. We also propose a new interpretability evaluation metric based on our framework. Empirically, we achieve state-of-the-art results on three datasets using the two proposed algorithms.
