We propose two interpretability frameworks. First, we provide an interpretable lens for an existing model. We use a generative model which takes as input the representation in an existing (generative or discriminative) model, weakly supervised by limited side information. Applying a flexible and invertible transformation to the input leads to an interpretable representation with no loss in accuracy. We extend the approach using an active learning strategy to choose the most useful side information to obtain, allowing a human to guide what "interpretable" means. Our second framework relies on joint optimization for a representation which is both maximally informative about the side information and maximally compressive about the non-interpretable data factors. This leads to a novel perspective on the relationship between compression and regularization. We also propose a new interpretability evaluation metric based on our framework. Empirically, we achieve state-of-the-art results on three datasets using the two proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: Making a learned representation understandable often involves training for both accuracy and interpretability at once. That can reduce accuracy and cannot directly help a model that has already been trained. This paper offers two frameworks that use limited side information to define which aspects of a representation should be interpretable.

The first provides a new view of an existing generative or discriminative model’s representation. A generative model and a flexible, invertible transformation produce an interpretable representation without losing accuracy. An active learning extension chooses useful side information to request, allowing a person to guide the meaning of interpretability rather than leaving it entirely predetermined.

The second framework jointly learns a representation that retains as much information as possible about the side information while compressing factors deemed non-interpretable. This connects interpretability with compression and regularization. The authors also introduce an evaluation metric and report state-of-the-art results across three datasets using their two algorithms, supporting both adapting existing representations and learning new ones.
summary.tldr: Two frameworks use limited side information to make existing or newly learned representations interpretable.

title: Discovering Interpretable Representations for Both Deep Generative and Discriminative Models

abstract: Recurrent neural networks have gained widespread use in modeling sequence data across various domains. While many successful recurrent architectures employ a notion of gating, the exact mechanism that enables such remarkable performance is not well understood. We develop a theory for signal propagation in recurrent networks after random initialization using a combination of mean field theory and random matrix theory. To simplify our discussion, we introduce a new RNN cell with a simple gating mechanism that we call the minimalRNN and compare it with vanilla RNNs. Our theory allows us to define a maximum timescale over which RNNs can remember an input. We show that this theory predicts trainability for both recurrent architectures. We show that gated recurrent networks feature a much broader, more robust, trainable region than vanilla RNNs, which corroborates recent experimental findings. Finally, we develop a closed-form critical initialization scheme that achieves dynamical isometry in both vanilla RNNs and minimalRNNs. We show that this results in significantly improved training dynamics. Finally, we demonstrate that the minimalRNN achieves comparable performance to its more complex counterparts, such as LSTMs or GRUs, on a language modeling task.

summary.tldr: A signal-propagation theory explains gating's broader trainable region and yields improved initialization for vanilla and minimal gated recurrent networks.

title: Dynamical Isometry and a Mean Field Theory of RNNs: Gating Enables Signal Propagation in Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: We study the problem of meta-learning through the lens of online convex optimization, developing a meta-algorithm bridging the gap between popular gradient-based meta-learning and classical regularization-based multi-task transfer methods. Our method is the first to simultaneously satisfy good sample efficiency guarantees in the convex setting, with generalization bounds that improve with task-similarity, while also being computationally scalable to modern deep learning architectures and the many-task setting. Despite its simplicity, the algorithm matches, up to a constant factor, a lower bound on the performance of any such parameter-transfer method under natural task similarity assumptions. We use experiments in both convex and deep learning settings to verify and demonstrate the applicability of our theory.

paragraphs: Meta-learning seeks to use experience across tasks to improve learning on individual tasks. This paper studies that goal through online convex optimization. It develops a meta-algorithm connecting popular gradient-based methods with classical approaches that transfer information across tasks through regularization, giving these related learning strategies a shared theoretical treatment.

In the convex setting, the method has sample efficiency guarantees and generalization bounds that improve as tasks become more similar. Under natural task similarity assumptions, its performance matches a lower bound for such parameter-transfer methods up to a constant factor. This provides a qualified optimality result within the analyzed class and assumptions.

The algorithm is also designed to scale computationally to many tasks and modern deep learning architectures. Experiments in both convex and deep learning settings examine the theory and demonstrate applicability. The distinction matters: the formal sample efficiency guarantees are stated for convex problems, while the experiments establish that the method can also be used in deep learning.
summary.tldr: A scalable meta-learning algorithm links gradient-based transfer to regularization and provides convex guarantees that improve with task similarity.

title: Provable Guarantees for Gradient-Based Meta-Learning

abstract: We introduce a new beam search decoder that is fully differentiable, making it possible to optimize at training time through the inference procedure. Our decoder allows us to combine models which operate at different granularities (e.g. acoustic and language models). It can be used when target sequences are not aligned to input sequences by considering all possible alignments between the two. We demonstrate our approach scales by applying it to speech recognition, jointly training acoustic and word-level language models. The system is end-to-end, with gradients flowing through the whole architecture from the word-level transcriptions. Recent research efforts have shown that deep neural networks with attention-based mechanisms can successfully train an acoustic model from the final transcription, while implicitly learning a language model. Instead, we show that it is possible to discriminatively train an acoustic model jointly with an explicit and possibly pre-trained language model.

paragraphs: Sequence models must turn their predictions into an output sequence, and beam search is one way to perform that decoding. This paper introduces a fully differentiable beam search decoder. Its central contribution is to let training signals pass through the inference procedure, making decoding part of the computation that can be optimized during training.

This allows models operating at different levels of detail to be trained together. In speech recognition, an acoustic model and a word-level language model contribute different kinds of information. The decoder also supports cases where input and output sequences are not aligned, by considering all possible alignments between them.

The authors demonstrate scalability through an end-to-end speech recognition system trained from word-level transcriptions. Gradients flow through the complete architecture, jointly training the acoustic model and an explicit language model, which may already be pretrained. The result establishes a way to integrate that explicit language model into discriminative training, alongside approaches that learn language structure implicitly.
summary.tldr: A differentiable beam search decoder enables joint training of acoustic and explicit language models through the decoding procedure.

title: A fully differentiable beam search decoder

abstract: In a recent study, Friedler et al. pointed out that several fair classification algorithms are not stable with respect to variations in the training set – a crucial consideration in several applications. Motivated by their work, we study the problem of designing classification algorithms that are both fair and stable. We propose an extended framework based on fair classification algorithms that are formulated as optimization problems, by introducing a stability-focused regularization term. Theoretically, we prove an additional stability guarantee, that was lacking in fair classification algorithms, and also provide an accuracy guarantee for our extended framework. Our accuracy guarantee can be used to inform the selection of the regularization parameter in our framework. We assess the benefits of our approach empirically by extending several fair classification algorithms that are shown to achieve the best balance between fairness and accuracy over the \textbf{Adult} dataset. Our empirical results show that our extended framework indeed improves the stability at only a slight sacrifice in accuracy.

paragraphs: A fair classifier can still be unstable if changes in its training data produce substantial changes in the learned model. Motivated by evidence of this problem in existing fair-classification algorithms, the paper studies how to obtain fairness and stability together. The focus is on methods expressed as optimization problems.

The proposed framework adds a regularization term specifically aimed at stability. The authors prove an additional stability guarantee and provide an accuracy guarantee for the extended framework. The accuracy result can guide the choice of regularization strength, connecting the theoretical analysis to the practical decision of how strongly to encourage stability during training.

The empirical study extends several fair-classification methods with strong fairness-accuracy balance on the Adult dataset. The modified versions improve stability with only a slight loss of accuracy in those experiments. This shows that stability can be incorporated into existing optimization-based fair-learning methods and evaluated alongside their predictive performance, rather than assuming that a favorable fairness-accuracy balance already ensures robustness to training-set variation.
summary.tldr: Stability-focused regularization adds guarantees to fair classifiers and improves empirical stability with a slight accuracy cost.

title: Stable and Fair Classification

abstract: We examine popular gradient-based algorithms for nonlinear control in the light of the modern complexity analysis of first-order optimization algorithms. The examination reveals that the complexity bounds can be clearly stated in terms of calls to a computational oracle related to dynamic programming and implementable by gradient back-propagation using machine learning software libraries such as PyTorch or TensorFlow. Finally, we propose a regularized Gauss-Newton algorithm enjoying worst-case complexity bounds and improved convergence behavior in practice. The software library based on PyTorch is publicly available.

Finally, we propose a regularized Gauss-Newton algorithm enjoying worst-case complexity bounds and improved convergence behavior in practice. The software library based on PyTorch is publicly available.

paragraphs: The paper examines gradient-based methods for nonlinear control using the complexity-analysis tools of first-order optimization. Its focus is how to describe the computational work these methods require. This connects control algorithms to a language in which progress can be analyzed through repeated calls to a clearly specified computational operation.

The authors show that complexity bounds can be expressed in terms of an oracle related to dynamic programming. That oracle can be implemented through gradient back-propagation in machine-learning libraries such as PyTorch or TensorFlow. The connection matters because the operation used in the theoretical accounting is also available through familiar computational tools.

Building on this perspective, the paper proposes a regularized Gauss–Newton algorithm with worst-case complexity bounds and improved convergence behavior in practice. It also reports a publicly available PyTorch implementation. The contribution combines an analytical view of existing nonlinear-control methods with a new algorithm: the guarantees characterize worst-case computational requirements, while the practical findings concern its observed convergence behavior.
summary.tldr: An oracle-based analysis of nonlinear control leads to a regularized Gauss–Newton method with worst-case bounds and improved practical convergence.

title: Iterative Linearized Control: Stable Algorithms and Complexity Guarantees

abstract: We propose a novel model for temporal detection and localization which allows the training of deep neural networks using only counts of event occurrences as training labels. This powerful weakly-supervised framework alleviates the burden of the imprecise and time consuming process of annotating event locations in temporal data. Unlike existing methods, in which localization is explicitly achieved by design, our model learns localization implicitly as a byproduct of learning to count instances. This unique feature is a direct consequence of the model’s theoretical properties. We validate the effectiveness of our approach in a number of experiments (drum hit and piano onset detection in audio, digit detection in images) and demonstrate performance comparable to that of fully-supervised state-of-the-art methods, despite much weaker training requirements.

paragraphs: Training a detector usually requires knowing where events occur, but annotating those locations can be slow and imprecise. This paper proposes training deep neural networks using only the number of event occurrences in each example. The learning task therefore receives information about how many instances are present without requiring their locations as training labels.

The distinctive feature is that localization emerges implicitly from learning to count. The authors attribute this behavior to theoretical properties of their model. Rather than supplying location annotations, the count-based training objective and model structure together allow the system to learn where individual events occur. This connects a relatively coarse form of supervision to a more detailed prediction task.

The approach is evaluated on drum-hit detection and piano-onset detection in audio, as well as digit detection in images. The authors report performance comparable to fully supervised state-of-the-art methods despite the weaker labeling requirements. These results demonstrate that occurrence counts can supply enough supervision for useful localization in the evaluated tasks, potentially reducing the annotation burden associated with training such detectors.
summary.tldr: A count-trained neural model implicitly learns event locations and achieves performance comparable to fully supervised methods on the evaluated detection tasks.

title: Weakly-Supervised Temporal Localization via Occurrence Count Learning

abstract: Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) are a powerful deep learning approach for graph-structured data. Recently, GCNs and subsequent variants have shown superior performance in various application areas on real-world datasets. Despite their success, most of the current GCN models are shallow, due to the \emph{over-smoothing} problem. In this paper, we study the problem of designing and analyzing deep graph convolutional networks. We propose the GCNII, an extension of the vanilla GCN model with two simple yet effective techniques: \emph{Initial residual} and \emph{Identity mapping}. We provide theoretical and empirical evidence that the two techniques effectively relieves the problem of over-smoothing. Our experiments show that the deep GCNII model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on various semi- and full-supervised tasks.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks learn from graph-structured data, but adding layers can cause over-smoothing: node representations become too similar to remain useful. This helps explain why many successful graph convolutional models are shallow. The paper studies how to design deeper networks while relieving this obstacle.

The authors propose GCNII, an extension of the standard graph convolutional network with two techniques: initial residual and identity mapping. These modifications form the core of the architecture. The paper provides both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence that together they effectively reduce the over-smoothing problem, giving support for using greater depth.

Experiments show that deep GCNII models outperform leading methods on a variety of semi-supervised and fully supervised tasks. The results connect the architectural changes to improved predictive performance in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a relatively simple route to deeper graph convolutional models, with analysis explaining why the added techniques help and experiments showing that the resulting depth can be useful.
summary.tldr: GCNII uses initial residual and identity mapping to relieve over-smoothing and improve deep graph convolutional networks.

title: Simple and Deep Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: This paper studies a problem of learning surface mesh via implicit functions in an emerging field of deep learning surface reconstruction, where implicit functions are popularly implemented as multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) with rectified linear units (ReLU). To achieve meshing from the learned implicit functions, existing methods adopt the de-facto standard algorithm of marching cubes; while promising, they suffer from loss of precision learned in the MLPs, due to the discretization nature of marching cubes. Motivated by the knowledge that a ReLU based MLP partitions its input space into a number of linear regions, we identify from these regions analytic cells and faces that are associated with zero-level isosurface of the implicit function, and characterize the conditions under which the identified faces are guaranteed to connect and form a closed, piecewise planar surface. We propose a naturally parallelizable algorithm of analytic marching to exactly recover the mesh captured by a learned MLP. Experiments on deep learning mesh reconstruction verify the advantages of our algorithm over existing ones.

paragraphs: Neural surface reconstruction can represent a shape implicitly, using a network whose zero-valued locations define the surface. Turning this representation into an explicit mesh commonly uses marching cubes. Because that procedure discretizes space, it can lose precision already present in the learned network. This paper asks how to recover the represented mesh analytically.

The approach uses the structure of multilayer perceptrons with ReLU activations: they divide their input space into regions where the function is linear. The authors identify cells and faces within those regions associated with the zero-level surface. They also characterize conditions under which the faces connect into a closed surface made from planar pieces.

Their analytic marching algorithm uses this structure to recover exactly the mesh captured by the learned network and is naturally parallelizable. Experiments in neural mesh reconstruction verify advantages over existing approaches. Exact recovery here concerns the network's represented surface; the guarantee that the extracted faces form a closed surface depends on the characterized conditions.
summary.tldr: Analytic marching exploits a ReLU network's linear regions to recover its represented surface mesh without marching cubes' discretization loss.

title: Analytic Marching: An Analytic Meshing Solution from Deep Implicit Surface Networks

abstract: We provide a computational complexity analysis for the Sinkhorn algorithm that solves the entropic regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) problem between two measures of possibly different masses with at most $n$ components. We show that the complexity of the Sinkhorn algorithm for finding an $\varepsilon$-approximate solution to the UOT problem is of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^2/ \varepsilon)$. To the best of our knowledge, this complexity is better than the best known complexity upper bound of the Sinkhorn algorithm for solving the Optimal Transport (OT) problem, which is of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^2/\varepsilon^2)$. Our proof technique is based on the geometric convergence rate of the Sinkhorn updates to the optimal dual solution of the entropic regularized UOT problem and scaling properties of the primal solution. It is also different from the proof technique used to establish the complexity of the Sinkhorn algorithm for approximating the OT problem since the UOT solution does not need to meet the marginal constraints of the measures.

paragraphs: Unbalanced optimal transport compares measures that may have different total masses. This paper analyzes the computational cost of using the Sinkhorn algorithm for an entropy-regularized version of that problem. Each measure has at most n components, and the analysis asks how work grows as the desired approximation error ε decreases.

The authors establish a complexity bound of approximately n²/ε, with logarithmic factors suppressed. They contrast this with the cited best known Sinkhorn upper bound for standard optimal transport, approximately n²/ε² under the same notation. The distinction is in the dependence on accuracy: the unbalanced bound grows more slowly as ε becomes smaller.

The proof combines geometric convergence of the updates toward the optimal dual solution with scaling properties of the primal solution. It differs from the analysis for standard transport because the unbalanced solution need not satisfy exact marginal constraints. The result provides a computational guarantee for the unbalanced problem and explains how its mathematical structure supports a different proof and a better stated accuracy dependence.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes a roughly n²/ε Sinkhorn complexity bound for unbalanced optimal transport using convergence and scaling properties.

title: On Unbalanced Optimal Transport: An Analysis of Sinkhorn Algorithm

abstract: Abstract Interpretability allows the domain-expert to directly evaluate the model’s relevance and reliability, a practice that offers assurance and builds trust. In the healthcare setting, interpretable models should implicate relevant biological mechanisms independent of technical factors like data pre-processing. We define personalized interpretability as a measure of sample-specific feature attribution, and view it as a minimum requirement for a precision health model to justify its conclusions. Some health data, especially those generated by high-throughput sequencing experiments, have nuances that compromise precision health models and their interpretation. These data are compositional, meaning that each feature is conditionally dependent on all other features. We propose the Deep Compositional Data Analysis (DeepCoDA) framework to extend precision health modelling to high-dimensional compositional data, and to provide personalized interpretability through patient-specific weights. Our architecture maintains state-of-the-art performance across 25 real-world data sets, all while producing interpretations that are both personalized and fully coherent for compositional data.

paragraphs: Some health measurements, particularly those produced by high-throughput sequencing, are compositional: interpreting one feature depends on the other features in the sample. This dependence complicates both prediction and explanation. An attribution that ignores it may fail to respect the structure of the data being analyzed.

DeepCoDA addresses this issue with a framework for high-dimensional compositional health data. It also targets personalized interpretability, defined here as attributing a model's conclusion to features for an individual sample. The architecture uses patient-specific weights to provide these individualized explanations while maintaining coherence with the compositional nature of the inputs.

Across 25 real-world datasets, the authors report performance at the state of the art together with personalized, compositionally coherent interpretations. The contribution is therefore a combination of predictive modeling and explanations appropriate to the measurement structure. This matters for precision health because domain experts need to assess the relevance and reliability of a particular patient's prediction, including whether its interpretation reflects biology rather than technical preprocessing choices.
summary.tldr: DeepCoDA combines competitive prediction on compositional health data with patient-specific explanations that respect dependencies among features.

title: DeepCoDA: personalized interpretability for compositional health data

abstract: In this work, we investigate the application of Taylor expansions in reinforcement learning. In particular, we propose Taylor Expansion Policy Optimization, a policy optimization formalism that generalizes prior work as a first-order special case. We also show that Taylor expansions intimately relate to off-policy evaluation. Finally, we show that this new formulation entails modifications which improve the performance of several state-of-the-art distributed algorithms.
originalAbstract: In this work, we investigate the application of Taylor expansions in reinforcement learning. In particular, we propose Taylor Expansion Policy Optimization, a policy optimization formalism that generalizes prior work as a first-order special case. We also show that Taylor expansions intimately relate to off-policy evaluation. Finally, we show that this new formulation entails modifications which improve the performance of several state-of-the-art distributed algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper investigates Taylor expansions as a mathematical framework for reinforcement learning. Taylor expansions describe changes through successive orders of approximation. Here, the authors use that perspective to formulate policy optimization: the process of improving the rule that determines an agent's actions.

Their Taylor Expansion Policy Optimization framework includes prior work as a first-order special case. This gives existing policy optimization ideas a place within a broader formulation, making the order of approximation part of the conceptual picture. The authors also establish a close relationship between Taylor expansions and off-policy evaluation, which concerns evaluating a policy using experience associated with a different policy.

The contribution has an algorithmic consequence as well as a theoretical one. The new formulation leads to modifications that improve several state-of-the-art distributed reinforcement learning algorithms. The stated findings therefore connect a general mathematical treatment of policy improvement to practical algorithm changes, while also linking policy optimization with the separate task of off-policy evaluation.
summary.tldr: Taylor Expansion Policy Optimization generalizes prior policy optimization, connects it to off-policy evaluation, and yields improvements to several distributed algorithms.

title: Taylor Expansion Policy Optimization

abstract: We consider a deep ReLU / Leaky ReLU student network trained from the output of a fixed teacher network of the same depth, with Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). The student network is \emph{over-realized}: at each layer $l$, the number $n_l$ of student nodes is more than that ($m_l$) of teacher. Under mild conditions on dataset and teacher network, we prove that when the gradient is small at every data sample, each teacher node is \emph{specialized} by at least one student node \emph{at the lowest layer}. For two-layer network, such specialization can be achieved by training on any dataset of \emph{polynomial} size $\mathcal{O}( K^{5/2} d^3 \epsilon^{-1})$. until the gradient magnitude drops to $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon/K^{3/2}\sqrt{d})$. Here $d$ is the input dimension, $K = m_1 + n_1$ is the total number of neurons in the lowest layer of teacher and student. Note that we require a specific form of data augmentation and the sample complexity includes the additional data generated from augmentation. To our best knowledge, we are the first to give polynomial sample complexity for student specialization of training two-layer (Leaky) ReLU networks with finite depth and width in teacher-student setting, and finite complexity for the lowest layer specialization in multi-layer case, without parametric assumption of the input (like Gaussian). Our theory suggests that teacher nodes with large fan-out weights get specialized first when the gradient is still large, while others are specialized with small gradient, which suggests inductive bias in training. This shapes the stage of training as empirically observed in multiple previous works. Experiments on synthetic and CIFAR10 verify our findings. The code is released in \url{https://github.com/facebookresearch/luckmatters}.

Our theory suggests that teacher nodes with large fan-out weights get specialized first when the gradient is still large, while others are specialized with small gradient, which suggests inductive bias in training. This shapes the stage of training as empirically observed in multiple previous works. Experiments on synthetic and CIFAR10 verify our findings. The code is released in \url{https://github.com/facebookresearch/luckmatters}.

paragraphs: The paper studies a student neural network trained by stochastic gradient descent to reproduce a fixed teacher's outputs. Both networks have the same depth and use ReLU or Leaky ReLU activations, but the student has more nodes at every layer. The question is whether student nodes specialize to individual teacher nodes.

Under conditions on the dataset and teacher, the authors prove that a small gradient at every sample implies that each lowest-layer teacher node has at least one specialized student node. For two-layer networks, they establish polynomial sample complexity with a specified gradient threshold. The result requires a particular data augmentation procedure, and the sample count includes those additional examples.

The analysis covers finite network widths and input dimension without requiring a parametric input distribution such as a Gaussian. It also suggests that teacher nodes with larger outgoing weights specialize earlier, while others require smaller gradients. Synthetic and CIFAR10 experiments support the findings, connecting this conditional theory to observed stages of training.
summary.tldr: Under stated data and gradient conditions, wider student networks specialize to lowest-layer teacher nodes, with polynomial sample complexity established for two-layer networks.

title: Student Specialization in Deep Rectified Networks With Finite Width and Input Dimension

abstract: We are interested in how to design reinforcement learning agents that provably reduce the sample complexity for learning new tasks by transferring knowledge from previously-solved ones. The availability of solutions to related problems poses a fundamental trade-off: whether to seek policies that are expected to immediately achieve high (yet sub-optimal) performance in the new task or whether to seek information to quickly identify an optimal solution, potentially at the cost of poor initial behaviour. In this work, we focus on the second objective when the agent has access to a generative model of state-action pairs. First, given a set of solved tasks containing an approximation of the target one, we design an algorithm that quickly identifies an accurate solution by seeking the state-action pairs that are most informative for this purpose. We derive PAC bounds on its sample complexity which clearly demonstrate the benefits of using this kind of prior knowledge. Then, we show how to learn these approximate tasks sequentially by reducing our transfer setting to a hidden Markov model and employing spectral methods to recover its parameters. Finally, we empirically verify our theoretical findings in simple simulated domains.

paragraphs: Previous reinforcement learning tasks can help an agent approach a new one, but transfer has two possible aims: perform reasonably well immediately or gather information that quickly identifies an optimal solution. This paper focuses on the second aim, assuming access to a generative model for sampling state-action pairs.

Given previously solved tasks that include an approximation of the target task, the proposed algorithm seeks the state-action pairs most informative for identifying an accurate solution. The authors derive probably approximately correct sample-complexity bounds that demonstrate how this prior knowledge can reduce the amount of sampling required.

The paper also addresses how to obtain the approximate tasks over time. It reduces the sequential transfer setting to a hidden Markov model and uses spectral methods to recover its parameters. Experiments in simple simulated domains support the theoretical findings. Together, the results connect purposeful information gathering with a mechanism for accumulating transferable task knowledge, under the specified sampling access and relationship between prior tasks and the target.
summary.tldr: With generative-model access and suitable prior tasks, informative sampling can reduce the sample complexity of identifying a solution to a new reinforcement learning task.

title: Sequential Transfer in Reinforcement Learning with a Generative Model

abstract: We present GradientDICE for estimating the density ratio between the state distribution of the target policy and the sampling distribution in off-policy reinforcement learning. GradientDICE fixes several problems of GenDICE (Zhang et al., 2020), the current state-of-the-art for estimating such density ratios. Namely, the optimization problem in GenDICE is not a convex-concave saddle-point problem once nonlinearity in optimization variable parameterization is introduced to ensure positivity, so primal-dual algorithms are not guaranteed to find the desired solution. However, such nonlinearity is essential to ensure the consistency of GenDICE even with a tabular representation. This is a fundamental contradiction, resulting from GenDICE’s original formulation of the optimization problem. In GradientDICE, we optimize a different objective from GenDICE by using the Perron-Frobenius theorem and eliminating GenDICE’s use of divergence, such that nonlinearity in parameterization is not necessary for GradientDICE, which is provably convergent under linear function approximation.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning uses data collected under a distribution that can differ from the states visited by the policy being evaluated. GradientDICE estimates the density ratio between these distributions. That ratio describes their relative weighting and is the central estimation target of this paper.

The authors identify a conflict in the earlier GenDICE formulation. Ensuring positivity requires a nonlinear parameterization, even for consistency with a tabular representation. Yet introducing that nonlinearity destroys the convex-concave saddle-point structure that would support standard primal-dual convergence guarantees. Consequently, those optimization algorithms are not guaranteed to reach the desired solution.

GradientDICE changes the objective itself, drawing on the Perron-Frobenius theorem and removing the divergence used by GenDICE. This avoids the need for the problematic nonlinear parameterization. The authors prove convergence with linear function approximation. The contribution is therefore a reformulation that resolves the identified conflict and provides a convergence guarantee in a clearly specified representation setting.
summary.tldr: GradientDICE reformulates off-policy density-ratio estimation to avoid a parameterization conflict and guarantees convergence with linear function approximation.

title: GradientDICE: Rethinking Generalized Offline Estimation of Stationary Values

abstract: We investigate the capacity control provided by dropout in various machine learning problems. First, we study dropout for matrix completion, where it induces a distribution-dependent regularizer that equals the weighted trace-norm of the product of the factors. In deep learning, we show that the distribution-dependent regularizer due to dropout directly controls the Rademacher complexity of the underlying class of deep neural networks. These developments enable us to give concrete generalization error bounds for the dropout algorithm in both matrix completion as well as training deep neural networks.
originalAbstract: We investigate the capacity control provided by dropout in various machine learning problems. First, we study dropout for matrix completion, where it induces a distribution-dependent regularizer that equals the weighted trace-norm of the product of the factors. In deep learning, we show that the distribution-dependent regularizer due to dropout directly controls the Rademacher complexity of the underlying class of deep neural networks. These developments enable us to give concrete generalization error bounds for the dropout algorithm in both matrix completion as well as training deep neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper asks how dropout controls the complexity of the models it trains. Its emphasis is on identifying an explicit mathematical effect of dropout and connecting that effect to generalization. The authors study two settings: filling in missing entries of a matrix and training deep neural networks.

For matrix completion, they show that dropout induces a regularizer that depends on the data distribution. This regularizer equals a weighted trace norm of the product of the matrix factors. The result gives a concrete description of the preference introduced by dropout in the completed matrix, rather than leaving its effect as an unspecified consequence of randomness during training.

For deep networks, the authors connect dropout's distribution-dependent regularizer directly to Rademacher complexity, a measure of the expressive capacity of a function class. That connection supports explicit generalization error bounds. Taken together, the results provide theoretical capacity-control explanations in both settings, linking a training procedure to mathematical quantities that constrain the gap between fitting observed data and predicting beyond it.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies explicit dropout regularizers and uses them to derive generalization bounds for matrix completion and deep neural networks.

title: Dropout: Explicit Forms and Capacity Control

abstract: We consider the sample complexity of learning with adversarial robustness. Most prior theoretical results for this problem have considered a setting where different classes in the data are close together or overlapping. We consider, in contrast, the well-separated case where there exists a classifier with perfect accuracy and robustness, and show that the sample complexity narrates an entirely different story. Specifically, for linear classifiers, we show a large class of well-separated distributions where the expected robust loss of any algorithm is at least $\Omega(\frac{d}{n})$, whereas the max margin algorithm has expected standard loss $O(\frac{1}{n})$. This shows a gap in the standard and robust losses that cannot be obtained via prior techniques. Additionally, we present an algorithm that, given an instance where the robustness radius is much smaller than the gap between the classes, gives a solution with expected robust loss is $O(\frac{1}{n})$. This shows that for very well-separated data, convergence rates of $O(\frac{1}{n})$ are achievable, which is not the case otherwise. Our results apply to robustness measured in any $\ell_p$ norm with $p > 1$ (including $p = \infty$).

paragraphs: A perfectly accurate and robust classifier can exist without being easy to learn from limited data. This paper investigates that distinction for linear classification when the classes are well separated. Such a setting removes overlap between classes as the explanation for difficulty, allowing the authors to isolate the sample requirements of adversarial robustness.

For a large class of separated distributions, the expected robust loss of any learning algorithm is at least of order d divided by n, where d is dimension and n is sample size. By comparison, the max-margin algorithm achieves expected ordinary classification loss of order one divided by n. Robust learning can therefore retain a dimension-dependent penalty even when perfect robustness is achievable.

The authors also give an algorithm attaining expected robust loss of order one divided by n when the allowed perturbation radius is much smaller than the gap between classes. Their results apply to robustness measured in any lp norm with p greater than one, including infinity. The findings make the relative size of separation and perturbations central to robust learning rates.
summary.tldr: Separated classes can still make robust learning sample-intensive, while sufficiently large separation relative to perturbations permits faster rates.

title: Sample Complexity of Robust Linear Classification on Separated Data

abstract: We consider a general statistical estimation problem wherein binary labels across different observations are not independent conditioning on their feature vectors, but dependent, capturing settings where e.g. these observations are collected on a spatial domain, a temporal domain, or a social network, which induce dependencies. We model these dependencies in the language of Markov Random Fields and, importantly, allow these dependencies to be substantial, i.e. do not assume that the Markov Random Field capturing these dependencies is in high temperature. As our main contribution we provide algorithms and statistically efficient estimation rates for this model, giving several instantiations of our bounds in logistic regression, sparse logistic regression, and neural network regression settings with dependent data. Our estimation guarantees follow from novel results for estimating the parameters (i.e. external fields and interaction strengths) of Ising models from a single sample.

paragraphs: Many estimation problems involve observations whose labels remain dependent even after their features are known. Spatial proximity, temporal relationships, or social connections can create this situation. The paper studies binary labels with such dependencies, addressing a setting where treating observations as conditionally independent would miss part of the data-generating structure.

The authors represent dependencies using Markov random fields and allow them to be substantial. In particular, they do not require the field to be in a high-temperature regime. They provide algorithms and statistically efficient estimation rates, then specialize their bounds to logistic regression, sparse logistic regression, and neural network regression with dependent data.

The guarantees rely on new results for estimating Ising-model parameters from a single sample, including both external fields and interaction strengths. These results supply the mathematical foundation for the broader estimation framework. The contribution is therefore both methodological and theoretical: it offers learning procedures together with guarantees that explicitly accommodate label dependence, rather than restricting the analysis to weakly interacting observations.
summary.tldr: A Markov-random-field framework provides statistically efficient estimation guarantees for binary-label data with substantial dependencies.

title: Statistical Estimation from Dependent Data

abstract: We investigate the problem of best-policy identification in discounted Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) when the learner has access to a generative model. The objective is to devise a learning algorithm returning the best policy as early as possible. We first derive a problem-specific lower bound of the sample complexity satisfied by any learning algorithm. This lower bound corresponds to an optimal sample allocation that solves a non-convex program, and hence, is hard to exploit in the design of efficient algorithms. We then provide a simple and tight upper bound of the sample complexity lower bound, whose corresponding nearly-optimal sample allocation becomes explicit. The upper bound depends on specific functionals of the MDP such as the sub-optimality gaps and the variance of the next-state value function, and thus really captures the hardness of the MDP. Finally, we devise KLB-TS (KL Ball Track-and-Stop), an algorithm tracking this nearly-optimal allocation, and provide asymptotic guarantees for its sample complexity (both almost surely and in expectation). The advantages of KLB-TS against state-of-the-art algorithms are discussed and illustrated numerically.

This lower bound corresponds to an optimal sample allocation that solves a non-convex program, and hence, is hard to exploit in the design of efficient algorithms. We then provide a simple and tight upper bound of the sample complexity lower bound, whose corresponding nearly-optimal sample allocation becomes explicit. paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify the best policy in a discounted Markov decision process using as few samples as possible. The learner has access to a generative model that supplies samples of the environment. The central decision is how to allocate sampling effort so that the best policy can be identified quickly.

The authors first derive a lower bound on the samples any learning algorithm requires for the particular problem. Its optimal allocation is described by a non-convex optimization problem, making it difficult to use directly. They then derive a simple, tight upper bound on that lower bound, yielding an explicit allocation that is nearly optimal.

The allocation reflects properties such as the gaps between optimal and suboptimal choices and the variance of next-state values. Consequently, it responds to the difficulty of the specific environment. Their KLB-TS algorithm tracks this allocation, with asymptotic sample-complexity guarantees both almost surely and in expectation. Numerical comparisons illustrate its advantages against existing algorithms.
summary.tldr: KLB-TS adaptively tracks an explicit, nearly optimal sampling allocation to identify the best policy efficiently.

title: Adaptive Sampling for Best Policy Identification in Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Even with a still image, humans can ratiocinate various visual cause-and-effect descriptions before, at present, and after, as well as beyond the given image. However, it is challenging for models to achieve such task–the visual event ratiocination, owing to the limitations of time and space. To this end, we propose a novel multi-modal model, Hypergraph-Enhanced Graph Reasoning. First it represents the contents from the same modality as a semantic graph and mines the intra-modality relationship, therefore breaking the limitations in the spatial domain. Then, we introduce the Graph Self-Attention Enhancement. On the one hand, this enables semantic graph representations from different modalities to enhance each other and captures the inter-modality relationship along the line. On the other hand, it utilizes our built multi-modal hypergraphs in different moments to boost individual semantic graph representations, and breaks the limitations in the temporal domain. Our method illustrates the case of "two heads are better than one" in the sense that semantic graph representations with the help of the proposed enhancement mechanism are more robust than those without. Finally, we re-project these representations and leverage their outcomes to generate textual cause-and-effect descriptions. Experimental results show that our model achieves significantly higher performance in comparison with other state-of-the-arts.

paragraphs: Visual event reasoning asks a model to produce cause-and-effect descriptions that extend beyond what a still image directly shows. The descriptions may concern earlier events, the present situation, or what happens afterward. This paper addresses the challenge of connecting information across both spatial relationships and different moments.

Hypergraph-Enhanced Graph Reasoning first represents content within each modality as a semantic graph, allowing it to model relationships inside that modality. Its Graph Self-Attention Enhancement then lets graph representations from different modalities strengthen one another. Multimodal hypergraphs associated with different moments provide additional information to enhance each semantic graph.

The model re-projects these enhanced representations and uses them to generate textual cause-and-effect descriptions. The authors report that the enhancement produces more robust representations than versions without it and that the complete model significantly outperforms compared state-of-the-art methods. The approach matters because it combines within-modality relationships, cross-modality relationships, and information organized across moments in the representation used for event description.
summary.tldr: Semantic graphs and multimodal hypergraphs jointly strengthen representations for generating cause-and-effect descriptions beyond a still image.

title: Two Heads are Better Than One: Hypergraph-Enhanced Graph Reasoning for Visual Event Ratiocination

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is inefficient on long-horizon tasks due to sparse rewards and its policy can be fragile to slightly perturbed environments. We address these challenges via a curriculum of tasks with coupled environments, generated by two policies trained jointly with RL: (1) a co-operative planning policy recursively decomposing a hard task into a coarse-to-fine sub-task tree; and (2) an adversarial policy modifying the environment in each sub-task. They are complementary to acquire more informative feedback for RL: (1) provides dense reward of easier sub-tasks while (2) modifies sub-tasks’ environments to be more challenging and diverse. Conversely, they are trained by RL’s dense feedback on sub-tasks so their generated curriculum keeps adaptive to RL’s progress. The sub-task tree enables an easy-to-hard curriculum for every policy: its top-down construction gradually increases sub-tasks the planner needs to generate, while the adversarial training between the environment and RL follows a bottom-up traversal that starts from a dense sequence of easier sub-tasks allowing more frequent environment changes. We compare EAT-C with RL/planning targeting similar problems and methods with environment generators or adversarial agents. Extensive experiments on diverse tasks demonstrate the advantages of our method on improving RL’s efficiency and generalization.

paragraphs: Long-horizon reinforcement learning can provide too little reward feedback, while learned behavior can be sensitive to small environmental changes. EAT-C addresses both problems by generating a curriculum that changes the task structure and its environments together. The curriculum is learned jointly with the agent, allowing it to respond to the agent’s progress.

A cooperative planning policy recursively divides a difficult task into a tree of easier subtasks. These subtasks provide denser reward feedback. An adversarial policy then modifies their environments to make them more challenging and varied. Feedback from learning on the subtasks also trains the two curriculum-generating policies, connecting curriculum construction to what the agent currently handles.

The tree organizes increasing difficulty for all participating policies. Construction proceeds from coarse tasks toward finer subtasks, while adversarial training works upward from easier subtasks where environmental changes can occur more frequently. Across diverse experimental tasks, the authors report improved learning efficiency and generalization compared with methods addressing related planning, reinforcement learning, and environment-generation problems. The evidence supports the benefit of coordinating decomposition with environmental challenge.
summary.tldr: EAT-C jointly learns task decomposition and adversarial environment changes to improve reinforcement learning efficiency and generalization.

title: EAT-C: Environment-Adversarial sub-Task Curriculum for Efficient Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper proposes an extension of a popular decentralized discrete-time learning procedure when repeating a static game called fictitious play (FP) (Brown, 1951; Robinson, 1951) to a dynamic model called discounted stochastic game (Shapley, 1953). Our family of discrete-time FP procedures is proven to converge to the set of stationary Nash equilibria in identical interest discounted stochastic games. This extends similar convergence results for static games (Monderer & Shapley, 1996a). We then analyze the continuous-time counterpart of our FP procedures, which include as a particular case the best-response dynamic introduced and studied by Leslie et al. (2020) in the context of zero-sum stochastic games. We prove the converge of this dynamics to stationary Nash equilibria in identical-interest and zero-sum discounted stochastic games. Thanks to stochastic approximations, we can infer from the continuous-time convergence some discrete time results such as the convergence to stationary equilibria in zero-sum and team stochastic games (Holler, 2020).

paragraphs: The paper extends fictitious play, a decentralized learning procedure for repeatedly playing a static game, to discounted stochastic games. This move introduces a dynamic setting in which the game evolves over time. The central question is whether the resulting learning procedures approach stationary Nash equilibria in the game classes studied.

For identical-interest discounted stochastic games, the authors prove that a family of discrete-time fictitious-play procedures converges to the set of stationary Nash equilibria. They also study continuous-time counterparts, including a previously introduced best-response dynamic as a special case. Their continuous-time convergence results cover both identical-interest and zero-sum discounted stochastic games.

The connection between continuous and discrete time is another part of the contribution. Using stochastic approximation, the authors derive some discrete-time convergence results from the continuous-time analysis, including results for zero-sum and team stochastic games. These findings extend equilibrium-learning guarantees beyond static games. Their scope remains tied to the specified game structures, and convergence to an equilibrium set does not assert a unique equilibrium.
summary.tldr: Extended fictitious-play and best-response procedures have stationary-equilibrium convergence guarantees in specified classes of discounted stochastic games.

title: Fictitious Play and Best-Response Dynamics in Identical Interest and Zero-Sum Stochastic Games

abstract: We present a new finite-sample analysis of Catoni’s M-estimator under adversarial contamination, where an adversary is allowed to corrupt a fraction of the samples arbitrarily. We make minimal assumptions on the distribution of the uncontaminated random variables, namely, we only assume the existence of a known upper bound $\upsilon_{\varepsilon} > 0$ on the $(1+\varepsilon)^{th}$ central moment of the random variables, namely, for $\varepsilon \in (0,1]$ \[ \mathbb{E}_{X_1 \sim \mathcal{D}} \Big| X_1 - \mu \Big|^{1+\varepsilon} \leq \upsilon_{\varepsilon}. \]{We} provide a lower bound on the minimax error rate for the mean estimation problem under adversarial corruption under this weak assumption, and establish that the proposed M-estimator achieves this lower bound (up to multiplicative constants). When the variance is infinite, the tolerance to contamination of any estimator reduces as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. We establish a tight upper bound that characterizes this bargain. To illustrate the usefulness of the derived robust M-estimator in an online setting, we present a bandit algorithm for the partially identifiable best arm identification problem that improves upon the sample complexity of the state of the art algorithms.

paragraphs: Estimating a mean becomes especially difficult when clean observations can have heavy tails and an adversary can arbitrarily corrupt some samples. This paper analyzes Catoni’s M-estimator under both challenges. For the uncontaminated distribution, it assumes only a known upper bound on a central moment of order one plus epsilon, with epsilon between zero and one.

The authors establish a lower bound on the worst-case mean estimation error under this assumption. They then show that the proposed estimator matches that bound up to multiplicative constants. This gives a minimax guarantee: within the analyzed setting, its error dependence cannot be substantially improved by choosing a different estimator.

The analysis also characterizes a fundamental tradeoff when variance is infinite. As epsilon approaches zero, any estimator’s tolerance to contamination decreases, and the authors provide a tight bound describing this relationship. Finally, they use the robust estimator in a bandit algorithm for partially identifiable best-arm selection, improving sample complexity over the stated existing methods.
summary.tldr: A robust Catoni estimator achieves minimax mean estimation rates under adversarial corruption and weak moment assumptions, up to constants.

title: Minimax M-estimation under Adversarial Contamination

abstract: Recently, neural architectures with all Multi-layer Perceptrons (MLPs) have attracted great research interest from the computer vision community. However, the inefficient mixing of spatial-channel information causes MLP-like vision models to demand tremendous pre-training on large-scale datasets. This work solves the problem from a novel knowledge distillation perspective. We propose a novel Spatial-channel Token Distillation (STD) method, which improves the information mixing in the two dimensions by introducing distillation tokens to each of them. A mutual information regularization is further introduced to let distillation tokens focus on their specific dimensions and maximize the performance gain. Extensive experiments on ImageNet for several MLP-like architectures demonstrate that the proposed token distillation mechanism can efficiently improve the accuracy. For example, the proposed STD boosts the top-1 accuracy of Mixer-S16 on ImageNet from 73.8% to 75.7% without any costly pre-training on JFT-300M. When applied to stronger architectures, e.g. CycleMLP-B1 and CycleMLP-B2, STD can still harvest about 1.1% and 0.5% accuracy gains, respectively.
originalAbstract: Recently, neural architectures with all Multi-layer Perceptrons (MLPs) have attracted great research interest from the computer vision community. However, the inefficient mixing of spatial-channel information causes MLP-like vision models to demand tremendous pre-training on large-scale datasets. This work solves the problem from a novel knowledge distillation perspective. We propose a novel Spatial-channel Token Distillation (STD) method, which improves the information mixing in the two dimensions by introducing distillation tokens to each of them. A mutual information regularization is further introduced to let distillation tokens focus on their specific dimensions and maximize the performance gain. Extensive experiments on ImageNet for several MLP-like architectures demonstrate that the proposed token distillation mechanism can efficiently improve the accuracy. For example, the proposed STD boosts the top-1 accuracy of Mixer-S16 on ImageNet from 73.8% to 75.7% without any costly pre-training on JFT-300M. The paper identifies inefficient mixing between these dimensions as a reason such models can require extensive pretraining. It approaches the problem through knowledge distillation, aiming to improve how these architectures exchange information.

The proposed Spatial-channel Token Distillation method introduces distillation tokens for both spatial and channel dimensions. A mutual information regularizer encourages the tokens to focus on their respective dimensions. Together, these components organize the distillation process around the two kinds of information mixing that the authors seek to improve.

ImageNet experiments across several MLP-like architectures show accuracy improvements. Mixer-S16 rises from 73.8% to 75.7% top-1 accuracy without costly JFT-300M pretraining. The authors also report gains of about 1.1 and 0.5 percentage points for CycleMLP-B1 and CycleMLP-B2. These results indicate that the mechanism can benefit both the highlighted Mixer model and stronger architectures, with the reported improvement varying by architecture.

title: Spatial-Channel Token Distillation for Vision MLPs

abstract: Many communication-efficient methods have been proposed for distributed learning, whereby gradient compression is used to reduce the communication cost. However, given recent advances in large batch optimization (e.g., large batch SGD and its variant LARS with layerwise adaptive learning rates), the compute power of each machine is being fully utilized. This means, in modern distributed learning, the per-machine computation cost is no longer negligible compared to the communication cost. In this paper, we propose new gradient compression methods for large batch optimization, JointSpar and its variant JointSpar-LARS with layerwise adaptive learning rates, that jointly reduce both the computation and the communication cost. To achieve this, we take advantage of the redundancy in the gradient computation, unlike the existing methods compute all coordinates of the gradient vector, even if some coordinates are later dropped for communication efficiency. JointSpar and its variant further reduce the training time by avoiding the wasted computation on dropped coordinates. While computationally more efficient, we prove that JointSpar and its variant also maintain the same convergence rates as their respective baseline methods. Extensive experiments show that, by reducing the time per iteration, our methods converge faster than state-of-the-art compression methods in terms of wall-clock time.

The paper introduces JointSpar and a layerwise adaptive variant, JointSpar-LARS, to reduce computation and communication together. Their central idea is to exploit redundancy in gradient computation so that coordinates destined to be dropped do not incur the same wasted calculation. This targets the total cost of a training iteration rather than treating communication as its only significant expense.

The authors prove that both methods preserve the convergence rates of their corresponding baseline algorithms. Experiments show faster convergence in elapsed time than the compared compression methods, attributed to shorter iterations. The distinction matters: an algorithm can retain its iteration-based convergence behavior while reaching a useful solution sooner by making each iteration less expensive.
summary.tldr: JointSpar reduces distributed training time by avoiding gradient computations for discarded coordinates while also reducing communication.

title: Communication-efficient Distributed Learning for Large Batch Optimization

abstract: Offline or batch reinforcement learning seeks to learn a near-optimal policy using history data without active exploration of the environment. To counter the insufficient coverage and sample scarcity of many offline datasets, the principle of pessimism has been recently introduced to mitigate high bias of the estimated values. While pessimistic variants of model-based algorithms (e.g., value iteration with lower confidence bounds) have been theoretically investigated, their model-free counterparts — which do not require explicit model estimation — have not been adequately studied, especially in terms of sample efficiency. To address this inadequacy, we study a pessimistic variant of Q-learning in the context of finite-horizon Markov decision processes, and characterize its sample complexity under the single-policy concentrability assumption which does not require the full coverage of the state-action space. In addition, a variance-reduced pessimistic Q-learning algorithm is proposed to achieve near-optimal sample complexity. Altogether, this work highlights the efficiency of model-free algorithms in offline RL when used in conjunction with pessimism and variance reduction.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from an existing dataset without exploring the environment for additional evidence. Sparse data and incomplete coverage can distort estimated action values. That assumption does not require the dataset to cover the entire state–action space, making the analysis relevant to the incomplete coverage that motivates offline learning.

The authors also propose a variance-reduced version of pessimistic Q-learning and establish near-optimal sample complexity. The result shows that explicit estimation of an environment model is not required to obtain this level of sample efficiency in the analyzed setting. Pessimism and variance reduction together provide the basis for the stronger model-free guarantee under the stated coverage assumption.
summary.tldr: Variance-reduced pessimistic Q-learning achieves near-optimal offline sample complexity under a coverage assumption that does not require all state–action pairs.

title: Pessimistic Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning: Towards Optimal Sample Complexity

abstract: Wasserstein gradient flows of maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) functionals with non-smooth Riesz kernels show a rich structure as singular measures can become absolutely continuous ones and conversely. In this paper we contribute to the understanding of such flows. We propose to approximate the backward scheme of Jordan, Kinderlehrer and Otto for computing such Wasserstein gradient flows as well as a forward scheme for so-called Wasserstein steepest descent flows by neural networks (NNs). Since we cannot restrict ourselves to absolutely continuous measures, we have to deal with transport plans and velocity plans instead of usual transport maps and velocity fields. Indeed, we approximate the disintegration of both plans by generative NNs which are learned with respect to appropriate loss functions. In order to evaluate the quality of both neural schemes, we benchmark them on the interaction energy. Here we provide analytic formulas for Wasserstein schemes starting at a Dirac measure and show their convergence as the time step size tends to zero. Finally, we illustrate our neural MMD flows by numerical examples.

paragraphs: This paper studies how probability distributions evolve under Wasserstein gradient flows driven by maximum mean discrepancy with non-smooth Riesz kernels. These flows can change a distribution's character: mass concentrated on singular sets can spread into a density, and the reverse can occur. That behavior makes it important to handle distributions beyond those already described by densities.

The authors develop neural approximations of two time-stepping approaches: the backward Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto scheme and a forward Wasserstein steepest descent scheme. Because singular measures must be allowed, the methods use transport plans and velocity plans instead of ordinary transport maps and velocity fields. Generative neural networks approximate the conditional pieces of those plans and are trained with suitable losses.

To assess the schemes, the authors use an interaction-energy benchmark. For Wasserstein schemes beginning at a Dirac measure, they derive analytic formulas and prove convergence as the time step tends to zero. Numerical examples then illustrate the neural MMD flows. The work combines computational constructions with analysis tailored to flows whose evolving mass may concentrate or spread.
summary.tldr: Generative neural networks approximate Wasserstein flow schemes using transport and velocity plans that can accommodate singular distributions.

title: Neural Wasserstein Gradient Flows for Discrepancies with Riesz Kernels

abstract: Compact representation of multimedia signals using implicit neural representations (INRs) has advanced significantly over the past few years, and recent works address their applications to video. Existing studies on video INR have focused on network architecture design as all video information is contained within network parameters. Here, we propose a new paradigm in efficient INR for videos based on the idea of strong lottery ticket (SLT) hypothesis (Zhou et al., 2019), which demonstrates the possibility of finding an accurate subnetwork mask, called supermask, for a randomly initialized classification network without weight training. Specifically, we train multiple supermasks with a hierarchical structure for a randomly initialized image-wise video representation model without weight updates. Different from a previous approach employing hierarchical supermasks (Okoshi et al., 2022), a trainable scale parameter for each mask is used instead of multiplying by the same fixed scale for all levels. This simple modification widens the parameter search space to sufficiently explore various sparsity patterns, leading the proposed algorithm to find stronger subnetworks. Moreover, extensive experiments on popular UVG benchmark show that random subnetworks obtained from our framework achieve higher reconstruction and visual quality than fully trained models with similar encoding sizes. Our study is the first to demonstrate the existence of SLTs in video INR models and propose an efficient method for finding them.

This paper explores whether useful video representations can instead be found inside a randomly initialized network by learning which parts to retain.

The approach learns multiple hierarchically organized supermasks for an image-wise video representation model while leaving its underlying weights unchanged. Each mask also receives its own trainable scale parameter. Compared with using the same fixed scale at every level, these adjustable scales enlarge the search space and allow exploration of more sparsity patterns.

The authors present this as evidence for strong lottery tickets in video representation models and provide a method for finding them. Learning remains essential to the approach: the optimized objects are the masks and their scales, rather than the original network weights.
summary.tldr: Learning hierarchical masks and scales within a fixed random network yields strong video representations without updating its underlying weights.

title: Is Overfitting Necessary for Implicit Video Representation?

abstract: We introduce new differentially private (DP) mechanisms for gradient-based machine learning (ML) with multiple passes (epochs) over a dataset, substantially improving the achievable privacy-utility-computation tradeoffs. We formalize the problem of DP mechanisms for adaptive streams with multiple participations and introduce a non-trivial extension of online matrix factorization DP mechanisms to our setting. This includes establishing the necessary theory for sensitivity calculations and efficient computation of optimal matrices. For some applications like $>\!\! 10,000$ SGD steps, applying these optimal techniques becomes computationally expensive. We thus design an efficient Fourier-transform-based mechanism with only a minor utility loss. Extensive empirical evaluation on both example-level DP for image classification and user-level DP for language modeling demonstrate substantial improvements over all previous methods, including the widely-used DP-SGD. Though our primary application is to ML, our main DP results are applicable to arbitrary linear queries and hence may have much broader applicability.

paragraphs: Training a machine learning model over multiple epochs means that the same records participate repeatedly in computation. This paper develops differentially private mechanisms for that setting, aiming to improve the balance among privacy, predictive utility, and computational cost. It formalizes adaptive streams with repeated participation and extends online matrix factorization mechanisms to handle them.

The extension includes theory for calculating sensitivity and procedures for efficiently computing optimal matrices. However, the optimal methods become computationally expensive in some applications, including training with more than 10,000 stochastic gradient steps. The authors therefore introduce a Fourier-transform-based mechanism that offers a more efficient option with only a minor loss in utility.

Evaluations cover example-level privacy for image classification and user-level privacy for language modeling. They report substantial improvements over previous methods, including DP-SGD, in these experiments. The theoretical results also apply to arbitrary linear queries, extending their scope beyond the primary training applications. The paper therefore combines an improved formulation of repeated participation with practical mechanisms for different computational demands.
summary.tldr: New matrix factorization and Fourier-based privacy mechanisms improve the privacy, utility, and computation tradeoffs of training over multiple epochs.

title: Multi-Epoch Matrix Factorization Mechanisms for Private Machine Learning

abstract: Generalization error always improves with more in-distribution data. However, it is an open question what happens as we add out-of-distribution (OOD) data. Intuitively, if the OOD data is quite different, it seems more data would harm generalization error, though if the OOD data are sufficiently similar, much empirical evidence suggests that OOD data can actually improve generalization error. We show a counter-intuitive phenomenon: the generalization error of a task can be a non-monotonic function of the amount of OOD data. Specifically, we prove that generalization error can improve with small amounts of OOD data, and then get worse than no OOD data with larger amounts. In other words, there is value in training on small amounts of OOD data. We analytically demonstrate these results via Fisher’s Linear Discriminant on synthetic datasets, and empirically demonstrate them via deep networks on computer vision benchmarks such as MNIST, CIFAR-10, CINIC-10, PACS and DomainNet. In the idealistic setting where we know which samples are OOD, we show that these non-monotonic trends can be exploited using an appropriately weighted objective of the target and OOD empirical risk. While its practical utility is limited, this does suggest that if we can detect OOD samples, then there may be ways to benefit from them. When we do not know which samples are OOD, we show how a number of go-to strategies such as data-augmentation, hyper-parameter optimization and pre-training are not enough to ensure that the target generalization error does not deteriorate with the number of OOD samples in the dataset.

paragraphs: Adding data from a different distribution can help a target task, but the benefit need not grow with the amount added. This paper proves that generalization error can first improve with a small amount of out-of-distribution data, then become worse than if none had been included.

The authors establish this non-monotonic behavior analytically using Fisher’s Linear Discriminant on synthetic datasets. They also demonstrate it empirically with deep networks on several computer vision benchmarks. The finding concerns the quantity of added data as well as its source: data that is useful in a small amount can become harmful in a larger amount.

They describe this as an idealized setting with limited practical utility. When those identities are unknown, data augmentation, hyperparameter optimization, and pretraining do not ensure protection against deterioration as more such samples are added. The results suggest possible value in detecting and weighting these samples, without guaranteeing that standard training practices will manage them successfully.
summary.tldr: Small amounts of out-of-distribution data can improve generalization even when larger amounts make it worse than using none.

title: The Value of Out-of-Distribution Data

abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are emerging as popular mesh-free solvers for partial differential equations (PDEs). Recent extensions decompose the domain, apply different PINNs to solve the problem in each subdomain, and stitch the subdomains at the interface. Thereby, they can further alleviate the problem complexity, reduce the computational cost, and allow parallelization. However, the performance of multi-domain PINNs is sensitive to the choice of the interface conditions. While quite a few conditions have been proposed, there is no suggestion about how to select the conditions according to specific problems. To address this gap, we propose META Learning of Interface Conditions (METALIC), a simple, efficient yet powerful approach to dynamically determine appropriate interface conditions for solving a family of parametric PDEs. Specifically, we develop two contextual multi-arm bandit (MAB) models. The first one applies to the entire training course, and online updates a Gaussian process (GP) reward that given the PDE parameters and interface conditions predicts the performance. We prove a sub-linear regret bound for both UCB and Thompson sampling, which in theory guarantees the effectiveness of our MAB. The second one partitions the training into two stages, one is the stochastic phase and the other deterministic phase; we update a GP reward for each phase to enable different condition selections at the two stages to further bolster the flexibility and performance. We have shown the advantage of METALIC on four bench-mark PDE families.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks can solve partial differential equations by dividing a domain into regions and assigning a network to each region. Conditions at the interfaces connect these regional solutions, but performance depends strongly on their selection. METALIC learns how to choose appropriate interface conditions across a family of parameterized equations.
