Experiments on four benchmark equation families demonstrate advantages for METALIC. The contribution makes interface selection responsive to both the equation being solved and, in the two-stage version, the phase of training.
summary.tldr: METALIC uses contextual bandits to adapt interface conditions for multi-domain physics-informed networks across equations and training stages.

title: Meta Learning of Interface Conditions for Multi-Domain Physics-Informed Neural Networks

abstract: Black box optimisation of an unknown function from expensive and noisy evaluations is a ubiquitous problem in machine learning, academic research and industrial production. An abstraction of the problem can be formulated as a kernel based bandit problem (also known as Bayesian optimisation), where a learner aims at optimising a kernelized function through sequential noisy observations. The existing work predominantly assumes feedback is immediately available; an assumption which fails in many real world situations, including recommendation systems, clinical trials and hyperparameter tuning. We consider a kernel bandit problem under stochastically delayed feedback, and propose an algorithm with $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\sqrt{\Gamma_k(T) T}+\mathbb{E}[\tau]\right)$ regret, where $T$ is the number of time steps, $\Gamma_k(T)$ is the maximum information gain of the kernel with $T$ observations, and $\tau$ is the delay random variable. This represents a significant improvement over the state of the art regret bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\Gamma_k(T)\sqrt{ T}+\mathbb{E}[\tau]\Gamma_k(T)\right)$ reported in (Verma et al., 2022). In particular, for very non-smooth kernels, the information gain grows almost linearly in time, trivializing the existing results. We also validate our theoretical results with simulations.

paragraphs: Optimizing an unknown function can require expensive, noisy evaluations whose results arrive after further decisions have already been made. Kernel bandits model this sequential search problem, but much existing analysis assumes immediate feedback. This paper studies the more realistic case in which feedback delays are random.

The proposed algorithm has a regret bound that, up to logarithmic factors, grows as the square root of maximum kernel information gain times the number of steps, plus the expected delay. Regret measures accumulated loss from choosing less effective actions. Crucially, expected delay enters additively, without being multiplied by information gain as in the prior bound discussed in the paper.

The improved dependence on information gain also strengthens the part of the bound unrelated to delay. This matters especially for very non-smooth kernels, where information gain can grow almost linearly and make earlier guarantees uninformative. Simulations support the theoretical results. The contribution is a sharper account of optimization performance when observations arrive stochastically late.
summary.tldr: A new kernel-bandit algorithm improves regret guarantees under random feedback delays, with expected delay contributing additively.

title: Delayed Feedback in Kernel Bandits

abstract: Compared with full client participation, partial client participation is a more practical scenario in federated learning, but it may amplify some challenges in federated learning, such as data heterogeneity. The lack of inactive clients’ updates in partial client participation makes it more likely for the model aggregation to deviate from the aggregation based on full client participation. Training with large batches on individual clients is proposed to address data heterogeneity in general, but their effectiveness under partial client participation is not clear. Motivated by these challenges, we propose to develop a novel federated learning framework, referred to as FedAMD, for partial client participation. The core idea is anchor sampling, which separates partial participants into anchor and miner groups. Each client in the anchor group aims at the local bullseye with the gradient computation using a large batch. Guided by the bullseyes, clients in the miner group steer multiple near-optimal local updates using small batches and update the global model. By integrating the results of the two groups, FedAMD is able to accelerate the training process and improve the model performance. Measured by $\epsilon$-approximation and compared to the state-of-the-art methods, FedAMD achieves the convergence by up to $O(1/\epsilon)$ fewer communication rounds under non-convex objectives. Empirical studies on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of FedAMD and demonstrate the superiority of the proposed algorithm: Not only does it considerably save computation and communication costs, but also the test accuracy significantly improves.

Large local batches have been proposed to address heterogeneity, but their usefulness under partial participation is less clear.

FedAMD divides participating clients into anchor and miner groups. Anchor clients compute large-batch gradients to establish local reference directions, described as bullseyes. The design gives large and small batches complementary roles within the same training framework.

summary.tldr: FedAMD combines large-batch anchor gradients with guided small-batch updates to improve federated learning under partial client participation.

title: Anchor Sampling for Federated Learning with Partial Client Participation

abstract: Can a mere next-token predictor faithfully model human thinking? Our work is aimed at crystallizing this intuitive concern, which is currently fragmented in the literature. First, we emphasize isolating the two phases of next-token prediction that are often conflated: autoregression during inference vs. teacher-forcing during training. We argue that the previously-identified problem of "exponential error accumulation" is a symptom of autoregressive inference. But more concerningly, we identify that teacher-forcing can let the model fit the training data by cheating, causing total in-distribution failure. We design a minimal planning task where empirically both the Transformer and the Mamba architecture fail in this manner - remarkably, despite the task being easy to learn. Overall, our work consolidates these and other essential arguments surrounding next-token prediction. We hope this effort can ground future discussions and inspire explorations beyond the next-token prediction paradigm.

paragraphs: Next-token prediction involves two distinct processes: training with teacher forcing and generating autoregressively at inference time. This paper argues that separating them is essential to understanding failure. Error accumulation during generation belongs to the inference process, while another failure can arise from how the model learns in the first place.

The authors identify cases where teacher forcing allows a model to fit training data through a shortcut described as cheating. The resulting fit can coexist with complete failure even on the same data distribution. To demonstrate this, they design a minimal planning task that is easy to learn, yet empirically causes both Transformer and Mamba models to fail in this way.

The example makes a focused point: successful fitting under teacher forcing need not establish that a model has learned the behavior required during generation. The paper consolidates this concern with other arguments about next-token prediction and encourages exploration beyond that paradigm. Its evidence identifies a concrete failure mode in the constructed task, rather than establishing that every next-token model must fail at planning or cannot represent human thinking.
summary.tldr: A minimal planning task shows how teacher-forcing shortcuts can let Transformer and Mamba models fit training data yet fail in distribution.

title: The Pitfalls of Next-Token Prediction

abstract: We introduce Genie, the first generative interactive environment trained in an unsupervised manner from unlabelled Internet videos. The model can be prompted to generate an endless variety of action-controllable virtual worlds described through text, synthetic images, photographs, and even sketches. At 11B parameters, Genie can be considered a foundation world model. It is comprised of a spatiotemporal video tokenizer, an autoregressive dynamics model, and a simple and scalable latent action model. Genie enables users to act in the generated environments on a frame-by-frame basis despite training without any ground-truth action labels or other domain specific requirements typically found in the world model literature. Further the resulting learned latent action space facilitates training agents to imitate behaviors from unseen videos, opening the path for training generalist agents of the future.

paragraphs: Genie learns to generate interactive virtual environments from unlabelled Internet videos. Users can prompt it with text or visual material, including synthetic images, photographs, and sketches, and then act within the generated world frame by frame. The central contribution is learning this controllability without ground-truth labels specifying which actions produced the training videos.

The 11-billion-parameter model combines three components: a spatiotemporal video tokenizer, an autoregressive dynamics model, and a latent action model. Together, these provide a representation of video, a model of how it unfolds, and a learned space of actions. The authors present the resulting system as a foundation world model capable of generating a wide variety of environments.

The learned action space also supports training agents to imitate behaviors shown in previously unseen videos. This extends the contribution beyond producing interactive scenes to using video as a source of behavioral learning. The abstract frames generalist agents as a future possibility opened by this capability, rather than an outcome already established by Genie.
summary.tldr: Genie learns action-controllable virtual worlds from unlabelled videos and provides latent actions that support imitation from unseen videos.

title: Genie: Generative Interactive Environments

abstract: Recent advancements in data-driven approaches, such as Neural Operator (NO), have demonstrated their effectiveness in reducing the solving time of Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). However, one major challenge faced by these approaches is the requirement for a large amount of high-precision training data, which needs significant computational costs during the generation process. To address this challenge, we propose a novel PDE dataset generation algorithm, namely Differential Operator Action in Solution space (DiffOAS), which speeds up the data generation process and enhances the precision of the generated data simultaneously. Specifically, DiffOAS obtains a few basic PDE solutions and then combines them to get solutions. It applies differential operators on these solutions, a process we call ’operator action’, to efficiently generate precise PDE data points. Theoretical analysis shows that the time complexity of DiffOAS method is one order lower than the existing generation method. Experimental results show that DiffOAS accelerates the generation of large-scale datasets with 10,000 instances by 300 times. Even with just 5% of the generation time, NO trained on the data generated by DiffOAS exhibits comparable performance to that using the existing generation method, which highlights the efficiency of DiffOAS.

paragraphs: Data-driven methods for partial differential equations can make solving these equations faster, but training them requires many accurate examples. Producing those examples can itself be computationally expensive. DiffOAS addresses this preparation cost by changing how training data are generated, with the stated aim of improving both generation speed and numerical precision.

The method starts with a small collection of basic PDE solutions and combines them to obtain additional solutions. It then applies differential operators to those solutions to produce PDE data points. This places the reusable solutions at the center of data generation, allowing the algorithm to build a larger dataset through combinations and operator evaluations.

The theoretical analysis finds a time complexity one order lower than the existing generation method. In the reported experiments, generating 10,000 instances is 300 times faster. A neural operator trained on DiffOAS data also achieves comparable performance using only 5% of the generation time. These results connect faster data preparation to the practical objective: training a useful PDE model.
summary.tldr: DiffOAS combines basic PDE solutions and applies differential operators to generate accurate training data much faster in the reported experiments.

title: Accelerating PDE Data Generation via Differential Operator Action in Solution Space

abstract: Learning the distribution of data on Riemannian manifolds is crucial for modeling data from non-Euclidean space, which is required by many applications in diverse scientific fields. Yet, existing generative models on manifolds suffer from expensive divergence computation or rely on approximations of heat kernel. These limitations restrict their applicability to simple geometries and hinder scalability to high dimensions. In this work, we introduce the Riemannian Diffusion Mixture, a principled framework for building a generative diffusion process on manifolds. Instead of following the denoising approach of previous diffusion models, we construct a diffusion process using a mixture of bridge processes derived on general manifolds without requiring heat kernel estimations. We develop a geometric understanding of the mixture process, deriving the drift as a weighted mean of tangent directions to the data points that guides the process toward the data distribution. We further propose a scalable training objective for learning the mixture process that readily applies to general manifolds. Our method achieves superior performance on diverse manifolds with dramatically reduced number of in-training simulation steps for general manifolds.

paragraphs: Some data naturally occupy curved spaces, so generating realistic samples requires respecting that geometry. Existing manifold-based generative methods can involve expensive divergence calculations or approximations of heat kernels. These requirements make complicated geometries and high-dimensional problems difficult to handle. This paper introduces Riemannian Diffusion Mixture to address those obstacles.

The framework constructs a generative process by combining bridge processes defined on general manifolds. These bridges guide the evolving sample toward data points without requiring heat-kernel estimates. The authors derive a geometric interpretation of the resulting drift: it is a weighted average of tangent directions toward the data. This describes how the process moves toward the target distribution while accounting for the surrounding geometry.

The paper also develops a scalable training objective for learning this mixture process on general manifolds. Reported experiments show superior performance across diverse manifolds while substantially reducing the number of simulation steps used during training. The contribution therefore links an interpretable geometric construction with a training procedure intended to make manifold generation more computationally practical.
summary.tldr: A mixture of geometric bridge processes enables manifold-aware generation without heat-kernel estimation and with fewer training simulation steps.

title: Generative Modeling on Manifolds Through Mixture of Riemannian Diffusion Processes

abstract: Data-parallel SGD is the de facto algorithm for distributed optimization, especially for large scale machine learning. Despite its merits, communication bottleneck is one of its persistent issues. Most compression schemes to alleviate this either assume noiseless communication links, or fail to achieve good performance on practical tasks. In this paper, we close this gap and introduce LASER: LineAr CompreSsion in WirEless DistRibuted Optimization. LASER capitalizes on the inherent low-rank structure of gradients and transmits them efficiently over the noisy channels. Whilst enjoying theoretical guarantees similar to those of the classical SGD, LASER shows consistent gains over baselines on a variety of practical benchmarks. In particular, it outperforms the state-of-the-art compression schemes on challenging computer vision and GPT language modeling tasks. On the latter, we obtain 50-64% improvement in perplexity over our baselines for noisy channels.

paragraphs: Distributed training often splits data across workers that must communicate gradient information. This communication can become a bottleneck, and wireless links introduce noise as well as a need for efficiency. The paper targets a gap in compression methods: many assume noise-free transmission, while others deliver weak results on practical learning tasks.

LASER uses the low-rank structure present in gradients to compress and transmit them over noisy channels. Low-rank structure means the gradient information admits a more compact representation. Exploiting that structure connects the compression scheme to the information being communicated, while the method explicitly addresses transmission noise.

The authors establish theoretical guarantees similar to classical stochastic gradient descent and report consistent improvements over baselines across practical benchmarks. Their evaluations include computer vision and GPT language modeling. For language modeling over noisy channels, they report perplexity improvements of 50%–64% relative to their baselines. The findings support compression designed jointly around gradient structure and noisy communication, with both optimization theory and downstream model performance informing the assessment.
summary.tldr: LASER exploits low-rank gradients to make distributed training effective over noisy wireless channels.

title: LASER: Linear Compression in Wireless Distributed Optimization

abstract: We introduce MusicFlow, a cascaded text-to-music generation model based on flow matching. Based on self-supervised representations to bridge between text descriptions and music audios, we construct two flow matching networks to model the conditional distribution of semantic and acoustic features. Additionally, we leverage masked prediction as the training objective, enabling the model to generalize to other tasks such as music infilling and continuation in a zero-shot manner. Experiments on MusicCaps reveal that the music generated by MusicFlow exhibits superior quality and text coherence despite being over $2\sim5$ times smaller and requiring $5$ times fewer iterative steps. Simultaneously, the model can perform other music generation tasks and achieves competitive performance in music infilling and continuation.

paragraphs: MusicFlow generates music from text descriptions through a cascade of two flow-matching networks. Self-supervised representations connect the written description with the audio, providing intermediate features for generation. The two networks model conditional distributions of semantic and acoustic features, separating these aspects of the text-to-music process.

The training objective uses masked prediction, asking the model to predict missing information. This also enables tasks involving partially available music, including filling gaps and continuing an existing piece. The authors report zero-shot generalization to these tasks, so the same framework supports more than generation from a text prompt alone.

On MusicCaps, MusicFlow produces music with better reported quality and text coherence while using a model roughly two to five times smaller and five times fewer iterative steps in the reported comparisons. It also achieves competitive infilling and continuation performance. The results connect compact, efficient generation with flexibility across several music tasks, rather than treating each task as a separate modeling problem.
summary.tldr: MusicFlow combines cascaded flow matching and masked prediction for efficient text-to-music generation, infilling, and continuation.

title: MusicFlow: Cascaded Flow Matching for Text Guided Music Generation

abstract: This paper enhances image-GPT (iGPT), one of the pioneering works that introduce autoregressive pretraining to predict the next pixels for visual representation learning. Two simple yet essential changes are made. First, we shift the prediction target from raw pixels to semantic tokens, enabling a higher-level understanding of visual content. Second, we supplement the autoregressive modeling by instructing the model to predict not only the next tokens but also the visible tokens. This pipeline is particularly effective when semantic tokens are encoded by discriminatively trained models, such as CLIP. We introduce this novel approach as D-iGPT. Extensive experiments showcase that D-iGPT excels as a strong learner of visual representations: A notable achievement is its compelling performance on the ImageNet-1K dataset — by training on publicly available datasets, D-iGPT unprecedentedly achieves 90.0% top-1 accuracy with a vanilla ViT-H. Additionally, D-iGPT shows strong generalization on the downstream task. Code is available at https://github.com/OliverRensu/D-iGPT.

paragraphs: Image-GPT applies autoregressive learning to images by predicting upcoming pixels. This paper revisits that approach with two changes intended to produce stronger visual representations. The first replaces raw-pixel prediction with prediction of semantic tokens, shifting the learning target toward higher-level visual content instead of individual pixel values.

The second change adds prediction of visible tokens alongside prediction of the next tokens. The resulting method, D-iGPT, therefore supplements the sequential prediction task with an additional objective over content already visible to the model. The authors report that the approach is particularly effective when its semantic tokens come from discriminatively trained models such as CLIP.

Extensive experiments support D-iGPT as a strong visual representation learner. Using publicly available training datasets and a vanilla ViT-H, it reaches 90.0% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K. The paper also reports strong generalization on a downstream task. These findings support revising both what an autoregressive image model predicts and which token positions contribute to its learning objective.
summary.tldr: D-iGPT strengthens autoregressive visual learning by predicting semantic and visible tokens, reaching 90.0% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with a vanilla ViT-H.

title: Rejuvenating image-GPT as Strong Visual Representation Learners

abstract: This work introduces a Byzantine resilient solution for learning low-dimensional linear representation. Our main contribution is the development of a provably Byzantine-resilient AltGDmin algorithm for solving this problem in a federated setting. We argue that our solution is sample-efficient, fast, and communicationefficient. In solving this problem, we also introduce a novel secure solution to the federated subspace learning meta-problem that occurs in many different applications.
originalAbstract: This work introduces a Byzantine resilient solution for learning low-dimensional linear representation. paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn a low-dimensional linear representation in a federated setting. The aim is to obtain a compact shared representation through distributed learning while making the procedure resilient to Byzantine behavior. Here, resilience concerns whether the learning method can withstand participants that do not behave as the algorithm expects.

The central contribution is a version of the AltGDmin algorithm with a mathematical guarantee of Byzantine resilience for this representation-learning problem. The authors also argue that their solution uses samples efficiently, runs quickly, and limits communication. These are distinct considerations: a distributed method needs to manage the data it requires, the computation it performs, and the information exchanged among participants.

As part of this work, the authors introduce a secure solution to federated subspace learning, a component problem that they identify as relevant to many applications. The contribution therefore includes both the representation-learning algorithm and a more broadly applicable subspace-learning procedure. Its stated scope is low-dimensional linear representation learning, with robustness established for the proposed algorithm.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a provably Byzantine-resilient federated algorithm for low-dimensional linear representation learning and a secure federated subspace-learning procedure.

title: Byzantine Resilient and Fast Federated Few-Shot Learning

abstract: Sleep is a complex physiological process evaluated through various modalities recording electrical brain, cardiac, and respiratory activities. We curate a large polysomnography dataset from over 14,000 participants comprising over 100,000 hours of multi-modal sleep recordings. Leveraging this extensive dataset, we developed SleepFM, the first multi-modal foundation model for sleep analysis. We show that a novel leave-one-out approach for contrastive learning significantly improves downstream task performance compared to representations from standard pairwise contrastive learning. A logistic regression model trained on SleepFM’s learned embeddings outperforms an end-to-end trained convolutional neural network (CNN) on sleep stage classification (macro AUROC 0.88 vs 0.72 and macro AUPRC 0.72 vs 0.48) and sleep disordered breathing detection (AUROC 0.85 vs 0.69 and AUPRC 0.77 vs 0.61). Notably, the learned embeddings achieve 48% top-1 average accuracy in retrieving modality clip pairs from 90,000 candidates. This work demonstrates the value of holistic multi-modal sleep modeling to fully capture the richness of sleep recordings. SleepFM is open source and available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/sleepfm.

The objective is to learn representations that bring these different physiological measurements together.

Together, these findings support learning relationships across sleep-recording modalities as a useful source of task-relevant representations.
summary.tldr: SleepFM learns joint representations of brain, cardiac, and respiratory recordings that improve evaluated sleep-analysis tasks and cross-modality retrieval.

title: SleepFM: Multi-modal Representation Learning for Sleep Across Brain Activity, ECG and Respiratory Signals

abstract: Does the stethoscope in the picture make the adjacent person a doctor or a patient? This, of course, depends on the contextual relationship of the two objects. If it’s obvious, why don’t explanation methods for vision models use contextual information? In this paper, we (1) review the most popular methods of explaining computer vision models by pointing out that they do not take into account context information, (2) show examples of failures of popular XAI methods, (3) provide examples of real-world use cases where spatial context plays a significant role, (4) propose new research directions that may lead to better use of context information in explaining computer vision models, (5) argue that a change in approach to explanations is needed from *where* to *how*.

paragraphs: An object’s significance in an image can depend on its relationship with nearby objects. A stethoscope beside a person, for example, does not establish whether that person is a doctor or a patient without context. This position paper uses that observation to question explanations of vision models that identify relevant image regions without accounting for contextual relationships.

The authors review popular explanation methods and argue that they omit contextual information. They present examples of failures and real-world cases where spatial context plays a substantial role. These examples motivate a broader question about what an explanation needs to communicate: identifying an influential location may leave the relationship behind the model’s decision unexplained.

The paper proposes research directions for incorporating context into vision explanations and advocates a shift from locating evidence to explaining how it matters. This is a proposed change in the goals and design of explanation methods. Its contribution is an argument, supported by reviews and examples, that spatial relationships should play a more explicit role in explaining visual decisions.
summary.tldr: This position paper argues that vision explanations should account for contextual relationships and explain how visual evidence affects decisions.

title: Position: Do Not Explain Vision Models Without Context

abstract: Spatial sound reasoning is a fundamental human skill, enabling us to navigate and interpret our surroundings based on sound. In this paper we present BAT, which combines the spatial sound perception ability of a binaural acoustic scene analysis model with the natural language reasoning capabilities of a large language model (LLM) to replicate this innate ability. To address the lack of existing datasets of in-the-wild spatial sounds, we synthesized a binaural audio dataset using AudioSet and SoundSpaces 2.0. Next, we developed SpatialSoundQA, a spatial sound-based question-answering dataset, offering a range of QA tasks that train BAT in various aspects of spatial sound perception and reasoning. The acoustic front end encoder of BAT is a novel spatial audio encoder named Spatial Audio Spectrogram Transformer, or Spatial-AST, which by itself achieves strong performance across sound event detection, spatial localization, and distance estimation. By integrating Spatial-AST with LLaMA-2 7B model, BAT transcends standard Sound Event Localization and Detection (SELD) tasks, enabling the model to reason about the relationships between the sounds in its environment. Our experiments demonstrate BAT’s superior performance on both spatial sound perception and reasoning, showcasing the immense potential of LLMs in navigating and interpreting complex spatial audio environments.

paragraphs: BAT combines a model for spatial hearing with a large language model to answer questions about an acoustic environment. The aim extends beyond recognizing which sounds are present: the system also reasons about their spatial relationships. This brings sound perception and language-based reasoning into a single approach.

To supply training material, the authors synthesize binaural audio using AudioSet and SoundSpaces 2.0, addressing a shortage of suitable recordings from natural environments. They also create SpatialSoundQA, a question-answering dataset covering several aspects of spatial sound perception and reasoning. The acoustic component, Spatial-AST, processes audio and achieves strong results on identifying sound events, locating them, and estimating their distances.

The complete system connects Spatial-AST to LLaMA-2 7B. This combination allows BAT to reason about relationships among sounds beyond standard sound detection and localization tasks. The reported experiments show superior performance on both perception and reasoning. The contribution is therefore both a spatial-audio learning resource and a model architecture demonstrating how acoustic information can support language-based interpretation of an environment.
summary.tldr: BAT connects a spatial audio encoder to a language model to perceive sounds and reason about their relationships.

title: BAT: Learning to Reason about Spatial Sounds with Large Language Models

abstract: We propose and investigate probabilistic guarantees for the adversarial robustness of classification algorithms. While traditional formal verification approaches for robustness are intractable and sampling-based approaches do not provide formal guarantees, our approach is able to efficiently certify a probabilistic relaxation of robustness. The key idea is to sample an $\epsilon$-net and invoke a local robustness oracle on the sample. Remarkably, the size of the sample needed to achieve probably approximately global robustness guarantees is independent of the input dimensionality, the number of classes, and the learning algorithm itself. Our approach can, therefore, be applied even to large neural networks that are beyond the scope of traditional formal verification. Experiments empirically confirm that it characterizes robustness better than state-of-the-art sampling-based approaches and scales better than formal methods.

While traditional formal verification approaches for robustness are intractable and sampling-based approaches do not provide formal guarantees, our approach is able to efficiently certify a probabilistic relaxation of robustness. The key idea is to sample an $\epsilon$-net and invoke a local robustness oracle on the sample. Remarkably, the size of the sample needed to achieve probably approximately global robustness guarantees is independent of the input dimensionality, the number of classes, and the learning algorithm itself. paragraphs: Certifying a classifier's resistance to adversarial changes can be computationally difficult. Sampling is more manageable, but sampling-based assessments alone do not provide the formal guarantees sought here. This paper develops a probabilistic relaxation of global robustness that aims to combine efficient evaluation with a precise guarantee.

The method samples an epsilon-net and applies a local robustness oracle to the sampled inputs. These local checks support a probably approximately global statement. A central theoretical result is that the required sample size does not depend on input dimensionality, the number of classes, or the learning algorithm. This is a claim about sample requirements, rather than a claim that every part of verification has identical cost across models.

The approach can therefore be applied to large neural networks beyond the reach of traditional formal verification. Experiments show better robustness characterization than the compared sampling methods and better scaling than formal methods. Its value lies in certifying the stated probabilistic relaxation, which makes a broader robustness guarantee computationally accessible.
summary.tldr: Sampling combined with local robustness checks yields formal probabilistic global guarantees with sample requirements independent of input dimension and class count.

title: Probably Approximately Global Robustness Certification

abstract: De novo peptide sequencing is a fundamental computational technique for ascertaining amino acid sequences of peptides directly from tandem mass spectrometry data, eliminating the need for reference databases. Cutting-edge models encode the observed mass spectra into latent representations from which peptides are predicted auto-regressively. However, the issue of missing fragmentation, attributable to factors such as suboptimal fragmentation efficiency and instrumental constraints, presents a formidable challenge in practical applications. To tackle this obstacle, we propose a novel computational paradigm called $\underline{\textbf{L}}$atent $\underline{\textbf{I}}$mputation before $\underline{\textbf{P}}$rediction (LIPNovo). LIPNovo is devised to compensate for missing fragmentation information within observed spectra before executing the final peptide prediction. Rather than generating raw missing data, LIPNovo performs imputation in the latent space, guided by the theoretical peak profile of the target peptide sequence. The imputation process is conceptualized as a set-prediction problem, utilizing a set of learnable peak queries to reason about the relationships among observed peaks and directly generate the latent representations of theoretical peaks through optimal bipartite matching. In this way, LIPNovo manages to supplement missing information during inference and thus boosts performance. Despite its simplicity, experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that LIPNovo outperforms state-of-the-art methods by large margins. Code is available at https://github.com/usr922/LIPNovo.

paragraphs: De novo peptide sequencing reconstructs amino acid sequences directly from tandem mass spectra, without relying on a reference database. A major difficulty is that an observed spectrum may lack fragmentation information because of imperfect fragmentation or instrument constraints. A model that predicts directly from the available spectrum must therefore work with an incomplete account of the peptide.

LIPNovo adds an imputation stage before sequence prediction. It fills in missing information within the model's internal representation rather than synthesizing raw spectral measurements. Guided by the target peptide's theoretical peak profile, it treats the problem as predicting a set: learnable peak queries reason about observed peaks, while optimal bipartite matching associates predicted representations with theoretical peaks.

This design gives the final prediction stage an enriched representation that can supplement missing evidence during inference. Experiments on three benchmark datasets report large improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The stated result supports the paper's central computational choice: reconstruct useful latent information before asking the model to commit to an amino acid sequence.
summary.tldr: LIPNovo reconstructs missing spectral information in latent space before peptide prediction, yielding large reported gains on three benchmarks.

title: Latent Imputation before Prediction: A New Computational Paradigm for De Novo Peptide Sequencing

abstract: With rapid advancements in machine learning, first-order algorithms have emerged as the backbone of modern optimization techniques, owing to their computational efficiency and low memory requirements. Recently, the connection between accelerated gradient methods and damped heavy-ball motion, particularly within the framework of Hamiltonian dynamics, has inspired the development of innovative quantum algorithms for continuous optimization. One such algorithm, Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD), leverages quantum tunneling to escape saddle points and local minima, facilitating the discovery of global solutions in complex optimization landscapes. However, QHD faces several challenges, including slower convergence rates compared to classical gradient methods and limited robustness in highly non-convex problems due to the non-local nature of quantum states. Furthermore, the original QHD formulation primarily relies on function value information, which limits its effectiveness. Inspired by insights from high-resolution differential equations that have elucidated the acceleration mechanisms in classical methods, we propose an enhancement to QHD by incorporating gradient information, leading to what we call gradient-based QHD. This gradient-based QHD achieves faster convergence and significantly increases the likelihood of identifying global solutions. Numerical simulations on challenging problem instances demonstrate that this gradient-based QHD outperforms existing quantum and classical methods by at least an order of magnitude.

paragraphs: Quantum Hamiltonian Descent uses quantum dynamics, including tunneling, to move through difficult optimization landscapes and escape local traps. Its original formulation mainly uses function values. The paper identifies slow convergence relative to classical gradient methods and limited robustness on highly non-convex problems as challenges for this approach.

The authors propose incorporating gradient information into Quantum Hamiltonian Descent. Their motivation comes from high-resolution differential equations that help explain acceleration in classical optimization. Gradients provide information about how an objective changes, adding directional guidance to the quantum optimization process. The resulting method is called gradient-based QHD and is intended to improve both convergence and the chance of reaching a global solution.

Numerical simulations on challenging problem instances report faster convergence, a substantially greater likelihood of finding global solutions, and performance exceeding existing quantum and classical methods by at least an order of magnitude. These are findings from the simulated instances described in the abstract. The central contribution is showing how gradient information can strengthen a quantum optimization method whose original design relies primarily on objective values.
summary.tldr: Adding gradient information to Quantum Hamiltonian Descent improves convergence and global-solution discovery in numerical simulations.

title: Quantum Optimization via Gradient-Based Hamiltonian Descent

abstract: While popular optimization methods such as SGD, AdamW, and Lion depend on steepest descent updates in either $\ell_2$ or $\ell_\infty$ norms, there remains a critical gap in handling the non-Euclidean structure observed in modern deep networks training. In this work, we address this need by introducing a new accelerated $\ell_p$ steepest descent algorithm, called Stacey, which uses interpolated primal-dual iterate sequences to effectively navigate non-Euclidean smooth optimization tasks. In addition to providing novel theoretical guarantees for the foundations of our algorithm, we empirically compare our approach against these popular methods on tasks including image classification and language model (LLM) pretraining, demonstrating both faster convergence and higher final accuracy. We further evaluate different values of $p$ across various models and datasets, underscoring the importance and efficiency of non-Euclidean approaches over standard Euclidean methods. Code can be found at https://github.com/xinyuluo8561/Stacey.

paragraphs: An optimizer's choice of geometry affects which update direction counts as steepest. This paper notes that widely used methods such as SGD, AdamW, and Lion rely on steepest-descent updates associated with either the l2 or l-infinity norm. It investigates a broader family of l-p geometries to address non-Euclidean structure encountered in deep-network training.

The proposed optimizer, Stacey, is an accelerated l-p steepest-descent algorithm. It uses interpolated primal and dual iterate sequences to navigate smooth optimization problems in this geometry. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for the algorithm's foundations, connecting the update design with an analysis of nonconvex optimization.

Experiments compare Stacey with SGD, AdamW, and Lion on image classification and language-model pretraining, reporting faster convergence and higher final accuracy. The study also varies p across models and datasets, examining how the choice of geometry affects training. These results support treating the norm underlying steepest descent as a useful optimization choice, with empirical benefits for the tasks evaluated.
summary.tldr: Stacey extends accelerated steepest descent to l-p geometries, reporting faster convergence and higher accuracy in image classification and language-model pretraining.

title: Stacey: Promoting Stochastic Steepest Descent via Accelerated $\ell_p$-Smooth Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: Embedding probability distributions into reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) has enabled powerful nonparametric methods such as the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), a statistical distance with strong theoretical and computational properties. At its core, the MMD relies on kernel mean embeddings to represent distributions as mean functions in RKHS. However, it remains unclear if the mean function is the only meaningful RKHS representation. Inspired by generalised quantiles, we introduce the notion of kernel quantile embeddings (KQEs). We then use KQEs to construct a family of distances that: (i) are probability metrics under weaker kernel conditions than MMD; (ii) recover a kernelised form of the sliced Wasserstein distance; and (iii) can be efficiently estimated with near-linear cost. Through hypothesis testing, we show that these distances offer a competitive alternative to MMD and its fast approximations.

paragraphs: The paper investigates a different way to represent probability distributions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. A familiar approach represents each distribution through a kernel mean embedding and compares these representations using maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD. The authors ask whether useful representations can also be built from generalized quantiles.

They introduce kernel quantile embeddings and use them to define a family of distances between distributions. These distances satisfy the requirements of probability metrics under weaker conditions on the kernel than MMD requires. The construction also recovers a kernelized version of sliced Wasserstein distance, connecting the new representation to another approach to distribution comparison.

The proposed distances can be estimated with near-linear computational cost. In hypothesis-testing experiments, they provide a competitive alternative to MMD and its fast approximations. The contribution therefore combines a broader theoretical choice of representations with a computationally practical comparison method. The empirical claim is competitiveness in the reported tests, while the theoretical results explain why the resulting distances have valid metric properties.
summary.tldr: Kernel quantile embeddings yield efficiently estimated distribution distances with metric guarantees under weaker kernel conditions than MMD.

title: Kernel Quantile Embeddings and Associated Probability Metrics

abstract: Modern deep neural networks exhibit heterogeneity across numerous layers of various types such as residuals, multi-head attention, etc., due to varying structures (dimensions, activation functions, etc.), distinct representation characteristics, which impact predictions. We develop a general layer-wise quantization framework with tight variance and code-length bounds, adapting to the heterogeneities over the course of training. We then apply a new layer-wise quantization technique within distributed variational inequalities (VIs), proposing a novel Quantized Optimistic Dual Averaging (QODA) algorithm with adaptive learning rates, which achieves competitive convergence rates for monotone VIs. We empirically show that QODA achieves up to a $150$% speedup over the baselines in end-to-end training time for training Wasserstein GAN on $12+$ GPUs.

paragraphs: Neural-network layers differ in dimensions, activation functions, structure, and the representations they learn. These differences also evolve during training. This paper develops a quantization framework that adapts to such layer-level variation, rather than treating the information handled by every layer as interchangeable.

The framework provides tight bounds on quantization variance and code length. These quantities describe two connected concerns: the variability introduced by quantization and the length of its encoded representation. The authors then apply a new layer-wise technique to distributed variational inequalities, introducing Quantized Optimistic Dual Averaging, or QODA, with adaptive learning rates.

For monotone variational inequalities, QODA achieves competitive convergence rates. Its practical evaluation trains a Wasserstein GAN using more than twelve GPUs and reports up to a 150% speedup over the baselines in end-to-end training time. The theoretical result is tied to the monotone setting, while the speedup is an empirical result from the evaluated training setup. Together, they connect adaptive layer-wise compression with both optimization analysis and measured training efficiency.
summary.tldr: QODA combines adaptive layer-wise quantization with distributed optimization, providing convergence results and reported multi-GPU training speedups.

title: Layer-wise Quantization for Quantized Optimistic Dual Averaging

abstract: For continuous action spaces, actor-critic methods are widely used in online reinforcement learning (RL). However, unlike RL algorithms for discrete actions, which generally model the optimal value function using the Bellman optimality operator, RL algorithms for continuous actions typically model Q-values for the current policy using the Bellman operator. These algorithms for continuous actions rely exclusively on policy updates for improvement, which often results in low sample efficiency. This study examines the effectiveness of incorporating the Bellman optimality operator into actor-critic frameworks. Experiments in a simple environment show that modeling optimal values accelerates learning but leads to overestimation bias. To address this, we propose an annealing approach that gradually transitions from the Bellman optimality operator to the Bellman operator, thereby accelerating learning while mitigating bias. Our method, combined with TD3 and SAC, significantly outperforms existing approaches across various locomotion and manipulation tasks, demonstrating improved performance and robustness to hyperparameters related to optimality. The code for this study is available at https://github.com/motokiomura/annealed-q-learning.

paragraphs: In continuous-action reinforcement learning, actor-critic methods typically learn action values for their current policy. Improvements then depend on updating that policy. This paper investigates whether learning toward optimal action values can accelerate the process, borrowing an idea commonly used in discrete-action algorithms: the Bellman optimality operator.

Experiments in a simple environment reveal a tradeoff. Modeling optimal values speeds learning, but also introduces overestimation bias, meaning that estimated values become overly optimistic. The authors respond with an annealing method that gradually changes the learning update from the Bellman optimality operator to the Bellman operator for the current policy. The transition aims to retain faster learning while reducing the associated bias.

The method is combined with TD3 and SAC and evaluated on locomotion and manipulation tasks. The authors report significant performance improvements over existing approaches and robustness to hyperparameters associated with optimality. The findings support changing the value-learning target over time as a useful way to balance learning speed and estimation bias within established actor-critic frameworks.
summary.tldr: Gradually shifting from optimal-value updates to current-policy updates improves reported actor-critic learning speed while mitigating overestimation bias.

title: Gradual Transition from Bellman Optimality Operator to Bellman Operator in Online Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is a powerful ability that emerges in transformer models, enabling them to learn from context without weight updates. Recent work has established emergent ICL as a transient phenomenon that can sometimes disappear after long training times. In this work, we sought a mechanistic understanding of these transient dynamics. Firstly, we find that—after the disappearance of ICL—the asymptotic strategy is a remarkable hybrid between in-weights and in-context learning, which we term “context-constrained in-weights learning” (CIWL). CIWL is in competition with ICL, and eventually replaces it as the dominant strategy of the model (thus leading to ICL transience). However, we also find that the two competing strategies actually share sub-circuits, which gives rise to cooperative dynamics as well. For example, in our setup, ICL is unable to emerge quickly on its own, and can only be enabled through the simultaneous slow development of asymptotic CIWL. CIWL thus both cooperates and competes with ICL, a phenomenon we term “strategy coopetition”. We propose a minimal mathematical model that reproduces these key dynamics and interactions. Informed by this model, we were able to identify a setup where ICL is truly emergent and persistent.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a transformer learn from its context without updating its weights, but this ability can sometimes disappear during extended training. The paper investigates the mechanisms behind that transience. It identifies a later dominant strategy called context-constrained in-weights learning, a hybrid that combines information stored in the weights with constraints supplied by the context.

This hybrid strategy competes with in-context learning and eventually replaces it in the studied setting. Yet the strategies also share sub-circuits, creating cooperation during their development. In the authors' setup, in-context learning cannot emerge quickly by itself; it depends on the simultaneous slower development of the hybrid strategy. The same strategy therefore helps enable in-context learning before displacing it.

The authors call this relationship strategy coopetition and construct a minimal mathematical model reproducing the main interactions and training dynamics. Guided by that model, they identify a setup where in-context learning emerges and persists. The findings explain transience through interactions among learned strategies, while demonstrating that disappearance is not inevitable in every setup.
summary.tldr: Shared circuitry lets a competing learning strategy first enable and later displace in-context learning in the studied setting.

title: Strategy Coopetition Explains the Emergence and Transience of In-Context Learning

abstract: Video understanding is a complex challenge that requires effective modeling of spatial-temporal dynamics. With the success of image foundation models (IFMs) in image understanding, recent approaches have explored parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) to adapt IFMs for video. However, most of these methods tend to process spatial and temporal information separately, which may fail to capture the full intricacy of video dynamics. In this paper, we propose MoMa, an efficient adapter framework that achieves full spatial-temporal modeling by integrating Mamba’s selective state space modeling into IFMs. We propose a novel SeqMod operation to inject spatial-temporal information into pre-trained IFMs, without disrupting their original features. By incorporating SeqMod into a Divide-and-Modulate architecture, MoMa enhances video understanding while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on multiple video benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MoMa, achieving superior performance with reduced computational cost. Codes will be released upon publication.

paragraphs: Adapting an image foundation model to video requires handling how visual content changes over time. Parameter-efficient methods can reuse an image model's capabilities, but many process spatial and temporal information separately. The paper argues that this separation may miss some of the interactions that make video dynamics difficult to understand.

MoMa introduces an adapter framework that integrates Mamba's selective state space modeling into image foundation models. Its SeqMod operation injects spatial-temporal information while preserving the original pretrained features. SeqMod is placed within a Divide-and-Modulate architecture, allowing the adaptation mechanism to model space and time together while maintaining computational efficiency.

The reported experiments cover multiple video benchmarks and show superior performance with reduced computational cost. These results support the value of joint spatial-temporal adaptation when transferring image models to video recognition. The main contribution is a way to add dynamic information to existing visual features efficiently, connecting the strengths of pretrained image representations with a mechanism designed to capture the relationships that unfold across video.
summary.tldr: MoMa uses Mamba-based adapters to add joint spatial-temporal modeling to image foundation models for efficient video recognition.

title: MoMa: Modulating Mamba for Adapting Image Foundation Models to Video Recognition

abstract: Aligning Large Language Models to integrate and reflect human values, especially for tasks that demand intricate human oversight, is arduous since it is resource-intensive and time-consuming to depend on human expertise for context-specific guidance. Prior work has utilized predefined sets of rules or principles to steer the behavior of models (Bai et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2023). However, these principles tend to be generic, making it challenging to adapt them to each individual input query or context. In this work, we present Situated-PRInciples (SPRI), a framework requiring minimal or no human effort that is designed to automatically generate guiding principles in real-time for each input query and utilize them to align each response. We evaluate SPRI on three tasks, and show that 1) SPRI can derive principles in a complex domain-specific task that leads to on-par performance as expert-crafted ones; 2) SPRI-generated principles lead to instance-specific rubrics that outperform prior LLM-as-a-judge frameworks; 3) using SPRI to generate synthetic SFT data leads to substantial improvement on truthfulness.

paragraphs: Guiding language models with human values can require substantial expert effort when instructions must fit a particular context. Fixed sets of principles offer reusable guidance, but their generality can make them difficult to adapt to individual queries. SPRI addresses this by automatically generating principles for each input in real time.

The generated principles then guide the corresponding response. The framework is designed to require minimal or no human effort, making context-specific guidance part of the model’s workflow. Its central contribution is the creation of principles situated in the immediate task, so that the guidance can reflect the requirements of an individual instance.

The paper evaluates three uses. In a complex domain-specific task, generated principles yield performance comparable to expert-written ones. Instance-specific evaluation rubrics outperform prior language-model judging frameworks, and using SPRI to create synthetic supervised fine-tuning data substantially improves truthfulness. These results show benefits across response guidance, evaluation, and training-data generation in the studied tasks, supporting automated contextual principles as a useful alignment mechanism.
summary.tldr: SPRI generates principles tailored to each query, with reported benefits for expert-level guidance, response evaluation, and truthfulness training.

title: SPRI: Aligning Large Language Models with Context-Situated Principles

abstract: The LoRA method has achieved notable success in reducing GPU memory usage by applying low-rank updates to weight matrices. Yet, one simple question remains: can we push this reduction even further? Furthermore, is it possible to achieve this while improving performance and reducing computation time? Answering these questions requires moving beyond the conventional weight-centric approach. In this paper, we present a state-based fine-tuning framework that shifts the focus from weight adaptation to optimizing forward states, with LoRA acting as a special example. Specifically, state-based tuning introduces parameterized perturbations to the states within the computational graph, allowing us to control states across an entire residual block. A key advantage of this approach is the potential to avoid storing large intermediate states in models like transformers. Empirical results across multiple architectures—including ViT, RoBERTa, LLaMA2-7B, and LLaMA3-8B—show that our method further reduces memory consumption and computation time while simultaneously improving performance. Moreover, as a result of memory reduction, we explore the feasibility to train 7B/8B models on consumer-level GPUs like Nvidia 3090, without model quantization. The code is available at an anonymous GitHub repository

paragraphs: LoRA reduces fine-tuning memory by learning low-rank changes to model weights. This paper asks whether further savings can come from changing the object being optimized. Its framework focuses on forward states, the intermediate values produced during computation, and treats LoRA as a special case of this broader approach.

State-based tuning introduces parameterized perturbations within the computational graph. These perturbations allow control over states across an entire residual block. A key potential benefit is avoiding storage of large intermediate states in architectures such as transformers. This matters because reducing the number of trainable weights is only one route to lowering the memory needed during adaptation.

Experiments on ViT, RoBERTa, LLaMA2-7B, and LLaMA3-8B report lower memory consumption and computation time alongside improved performance. The authors also explore whether the savings make training 7B and 8B models feasible on consumer GPUs such as the Nvidia 3090 without quantization. That exploration points toward broader hardware accessibility while retaining the abstract's qualified claim about feasibility.
summary.tldr: State-based fine-tuning controls intermediate model states to reduce memory and computation beyond LoRA while improving performance in reported experiments.

title: From Weight-Based to State-Based Fine-Tuning: Further Memory Reduction on LoRA with Parallel Control

abstract: Recent studies have raised significant concerns regarding the vulnerability of Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) to maliciously injected or perturbed input images, which can mislead their responses. Existing defense methods show that such vision attacks are sensitive to image modifications especially cropping, using majority voting across responses of modified images as corrected responses. However, these modifications often result in partial images and distort the semantics, which reduces response quality on clean images after voting. Instead of directly using responses from partial images for voting, we investigate using them to supervise (guide) the LVLM’s responses to the original images at inference time. We propose a black-box, training-free method called DPS (Defense through Partial-Perception Supervision). In this approach, the model is prompted using the responses generated by a model that perceives only a partial image. With DPS, the model can adjust its response based on partial image understanding when under attack, while confidently maintaining its original response for clean input. Empirical experiments show our method outperforms the baseline, cutting the average attack success rate by 76.3% across six datasets on three popular models.

Instead of directly using responses from partial images for voting, we investigate using them to supervise (guide) the LVLM’s responses to the original images at inference time. We propose a black-box, training-free method called DPS (Defense through Partial-Perception Supervision). In this approach, the model is prompted using the responses generated by a model that perceives only a partial image. With DPS, the model can adjust its response based on partial image understanding when under attack, while confidently maintaining its original response for clean input. Empirical experiments show our method outperforms the baseline, cutting the average attack success rate by 76.3% across six datasets on three popular models.

paragraphs: Malicious changes to input images can cause large vision-language models to produce misleading responses. Image modifications such as cropping can disrupt these attacks, but they also remove context. Existing defenses that vote across answers to modified images therefore risk degrading answers on clean inputs, because an answer based on an incomplete image may miss its intended meaning.

Defense through Partial-Perception Supervision, or DPS, uses partial-image answers as guidance for answering the original image. At inference time, a model's response to a partial view becomes part of the prompt used to guide the full-image response. The method is black-box and training-free. Its design lets the model use partial understanding to revise an attacked response while retaining access to the original visual context.

Across six datasets and three popular models, experiments report a 76.3% reduction in average attack success rate compared with the baseline. The authors also describe the method as maintaining its original response confidently on clean inputs. The result supports partial perception as a useful source of supervision for defending full-image reasoning.
summary.tldr: DPS uses partial-image responses to guide full-image answers without training, reducing average attack success by 76.3% in the reported evaluation.

title: Defending LVLMs Against Vision Attacks Through Partial-Perception Supervision

abstract: Activities in numerous evolving systems can be represented as dynamic graphs in snapshot form at different time intervals, i.e., discrete-time dynamic graphs (DTDGs). Existing methods show impressive advances in capturing historical temporal evolution patterns in DTDGs, but they focus on addressing an offline learning setting, where models are trained using historical snapshots once and then evaluated to all subsequent graph snapshots without further updating. This fails to capture 1) the nature of evolving complexities across graph snapshots and 2) the distribution shift in the testing graph snapshots. To address these problems, we propose PromptDyG, a novel framework that leverages unsupervised test-time Prompt adaptation for Dynamic Graph learning under a live-update online setting. The key insight is that an expressive dynamic graph prompt can be learned on a frozen backbone via minimization of feature-wise, label-free entropy to efficiently and continuously model the evolving patterns. We show theoretically that this unsupervised prompt adaptation can guarantee a larger similarity margin between positive and negative pairs, facilitating more accurate dynamic predictions. It is further confirmed by our extensive empirical results on six benchmark datasets that show consistent and significant improvements of PromptDyG over state-of-the-art baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/mala-lab/PromptDyG.

A model trained once on historical snapshots can struggle when later snapshots develop new patterns or shift away from the training distribution. PromptDyG addresses this problem in a live-update setting, allowing adaptation as new graph snapshots arrive.

It updates that prompt by minimizing feature-wise entropy without labels, making adaptation possible without supervised feedback on the new snapshots. The prompt provides an adjustable component through which the system can continuously respond to changing graph patterns.

Together, the analysis and results support prompt adaptation as an efficient way to update predictions for evolving graphs while retaining a fixed underlying model.
summary.tldr: PromptDyG adapts prompts without labels as graph snapshots evolve, improving predictions while keeping the backbone frozen.

title: PromptDyG: Test-Time Prompt Adaptation on Dynamic Graphs

abstract: The web is littered with images, once created for human consumption and now increasingly interpreted by agents using vision-language models (VLMs). These agents make visual decisions at scale, deciding what to click, recommend, or buy. Yet, we know little about the structure of their visual preferences. We introduce a framework for studying this by placing VLMs in controlled image-based choice tasks and systematically perturbing their inputs. Our key idea is to treat the agent’s decision function as a latent visual utility that can be inferred through revealed preference: choices between systematically edited images. Starting from common images, such as product photos, we propose methods for visual prompt optimization, adapting text optimization methods to iteratively propose and apply visually plausible modifications using an image generation model (such as in composition, lighting, or background). We then evaluate which edits increase selection probability. Through large-scale experiments on frontier VLMs, we demonstrate that optimized edits significantly shift choice probabilities in head-to-head comparisons. We develop an automatic interpretability pipeline to explain these preferences, identifying consistent visual themes that drive selection. We argue that this approach offers a practical and efficient way to surface visual vulnerabilities, safety concerns that might otherwise be discovered implicitly in the wild, supporting more proactive auditing and governance of image-based AI agents.

title: Visual Persuasion: What Influences Decisions of Vision-Language Models?

abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) typically solve reasoning-intensive tasks by generating long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces, leading to substantial inference overhead. We identify a reproducible inference-time phenomenon, termed Self-Compression: when multiple independent and answerable questions are presented within a single prompt, the model spontaneously produces shorter reasoning traces for each question. This phenomenon arises from multi-question contextual pressure during generation and consistently manifests across models and benchmarks. Building on this observation, we propose ConPress (Learning from Contextual Pressure, a lightweight self-supervised fine-tuning approach. ConPress constructs multi-question prompts to induce self-compression, samples the resulting model outputs, and parses and filters per-question traces to obtain concise yet correct reasoning trajectories. These trajectories are directly used for supervised fine-tuning, internalizing compressed reasoning behavior in single-question settings without external teachers, manual pruning, or reinforcement learning. With only 8k fine-tuning examples, ConPress reduces reasoning token usage by 59% on MATH500 and 33% on AIME25, while maintaining competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: ConPress starts from an observed behavior of large reasoning models: when several independent, answerable questions appear in one prompt, the model tends to produce shorter reasoning for each. The authors call this self-compression and report that it recurs across models and benchmarks. They attribute it to pressure created by sharing the prompt context across questions.

The training method turns that behavior into examples. It constructs multi-question prompts, samples the model's responses, then separates and filters the reasoning for individual questions to retain concise, correct trajectories. Supervised fine-tuning on those trajectories teaches the model to use compressed reasoning even when it later receives a single question.

This process requires no external teacher, manual trace pruning, or reinforcement learning. With 8,000 fine-tuning examples, the reported reasoning-token reductions are 59% on MATH500 and 33% on AIME25, with competitive accuracy. The findings suggest that a model's own context-induced behavior can supply useful training data for reducing reasoning overhead; competitive accuracy does not imply that accuracy is identical in every setting.
summary.tldr: ConPress trains on concise reasoning elicited by multi-question prompts, reducing reasoning-token use while maintaining competitive accuracy.

title: ConPress: Learning Efficient Reasoning from Multi-Question Contextual Pressure

abstract: The Shapley value is a ubiquitous framework for attribution in machine learning, encompassing feature importance, data valuation, and causal inference. However, its exact computation is generally intractable, necessitating efficient approximation methods. While the most effective and popular estimators leverage the paired sampling heuristic to reduce estimation error, the theoretical mechanism driving this improvement has remained opaque. In this work, we provide an elegant and fundamental justification for paired sampling: we prove that the Shapley value depends exclusively on the odd component of the set function, and that paired sampling orthogonalizes the regression objective to filter out the irrelevant even component. Leveraging this insight, we propose OddSHAP, a novel consistent estimator that performs polynomial regression solely on the odd subspace. By utilizing the Fourier basis to isolate this subspace and employing a proxy model to identify high-impact interactions, OddSHAP overcomes the combinatorial explosion of higher-order approximations. Through an extensive benchmark, we find that OddSHAP achieves state-of-the-art estimation accuracy at larger sampling budgets.

paragraphs: Shapley values assign credit to contributors, supporting tasks such as feature attribution and data valuation. Computing them exactly is generally intractable, so practical methods estimate them from sampled evaluations. Pairing samples often reduces estimation error, but the reason this common technique works has lacked a clear theoretical explanation.

The paper proves that Shapley values depend exclusively on the odd component of the underlying set function. It further shows that paired sampling makes the regression objective orthogonal to the irrelevant even component, filtering that component out. This identifies which mathematical structure an estimator needs to recover and which structure can be excluded.

The resulting estimator, OddSHAP, fits a polynomial only within the odd subspace. A Fourier basis isolates that subspace, while a proxy model identifies influential interactions to avoid the combinatorial growth associated with higher-order approximations. OddSHAP is consistent, and the reported benchmarks show state-of-the-art estimation accuracy at larger sampling budgets. That sampling-budget qualification is part of the empirical finding.
summary.tldr: OddSHAP estimates Shapley values using only the mathematically relevant odd component, achieving leading accuracy at larger sampling budgets.

title: An Odd Estimator for Shapley Values

abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization has emerged as essential for aligning video diffusion models with human preferences, but faces a critical computational bottleneck: training a 14B parametered model typically demands hundreds of GPU days per experiment. Existing efficiency methods reduce costs through sliding window subsampling training timesteps, but fundamentally compromise optimization, exhibiting severe instability and failing to reach full trajectory performance. We present Flash-GRPO, a single-step training framework that outperforms full trajectory training in alignment quality under low computational budgets while substantially improving training efficiency. Flash-GRPO addresses two critical challenges: iso-temporal grouping eliminates timestep-confounded variance by enforcing prompt-wise temporal consistency, decoupling policy performance from timestep difficulty; temporal gradient rectification neutralizes the time-dependent scaling factor that causes vastly inconsistent gradient magnitudes across timesteps. Experiments on 1.3B to 14B parameter models validate Flash-GRPO’s effectiveness, demonstrating substantial training acceleration with consistent stability and state-of-the-art alignment quality.

paragraphs: Aligning video diffusion models with human preferences through Group Relative Policy Optimization can require substantial computation. Existing approaches save work by sampling training timesteps within sliding windows, but the paper reports instability and weaker optimization than full-trajectory training. Flash-GRPO introduces a single-step training framework designed to make this alignment process more efficient while maintaining stable updates.

Its first component, iso-temporal grouping, keeps timesteps consistent within each prompt's comparison group. This separates differences in policy performance from differences caused by timestep difficulty. Its second component, temporal gradient rectification, removes a time-dependent scaling factor responsible for large variations in gradient magnitude. The two mechanisms address distinct sources of inconsistency when learning from selected diffusion steps.

Experiments on models ranging from 1.3B to 14B parameters report substantial training acceleration, consistent stability, and state-of-the-art alignment quality. Under low computational budgets, Flash-GRPO outperforms full-trajectory training in alignment quality. That budget condition is central to the comparison: the finding concerns how effectively the methods use limited training resources.
summary.tldr: Flash-GRPO stabilizes single-step video diffusion alignment and outperforms full-trajectory training in alignment quality under low computational budgets.

title: Flash-GRPO: Efficient Alignment for Video Diffusion via One-Step Policy Optimization

abstract: Scheduling problems arise from repeatedly selecting one item from a set of candidates based on their states. These problems often reduce to assigning priority scores and choosing the highest-ranked item. In this work, we propose a factorized scheduling principle (FSP) framework to learn interpretable and transferable scheduling rules. The FSP framework represents system states as condition distributions and decomposes a global scheduling principle into additive univariate and pairwise components with identifiability constraints. The scheduling principle enables the framework to maintain a simple priority-based structure during deployment. This principle is learned by using a policy-based objective combined with a temporal-difference signal defined on the condition distribution. Experiments on synthetic and realistic scheduling tasks demonstrate the FSP framework’s strong performance, interpretability, and zero-shot generalization across different system scales.
