paragraphs: Many scheduling problems repeatedly choose one item from a set of candidates. A priority rule makes this decision by scoring candidates and selecting the highest-ranked one. The Factorized Scheduling Principle framework aims to learn such rules while keeping their structure interpretable and allowing them to transfer between systems of different sizes.

The framework describes system states through condition distributions. It then expresses the scheduling principle as a sum of components involving individual conditions and pairs of conditions, subject to identifiability constraints. This decomposition exposes separate contributions and interactions instead of placing the entire decision inside an undivided function. Deployment still uses a simple priority-based decision structure.

Training combines a policy-based objective with a temporal-difference signal defined over the condition distribution. Experiments on synthetic and realistic scheduling tasks report strong performance, interpretability, and zero-shot generalization across system scales. The findings support learning a structured scheduling rule whose components remain inspectable and whose usefulness can extend to differently sized systems without additional training.
summary.tldr: Factorized Scheduling Principle learns interpretable priority rules that show zero-shot transfer across different system sizes.

title: Factorized Scheduling Principle: Learning Interpretable and Transferable Policies via Structured Additive Functions

abstract: Although upper bound guarantees for bilevel optimization have been widely studied, progress on lower bounds has been limited due to the complexity of the bilevel structure. In this work, we focus on the smooth nonconvex-strongly-convex setting and develop new hard instances that yield nontrivial lower bounds under deterministic and stochastic first-order oracle models. In the deterministic case, we prove that any first-order zero-respecting algorithm requires at least $\Omega(\kappa^{3/2}\epsilon^{-2})$ oracle calls to find an $\epsilon$-accurate stationary point, improving the optimal lower bounds known for single-level nonconvex optimization and for nonconvex-strongly-convex min-max problems. In the stochastic case, we show that at least $\Omega(\kappa^{5/2}\epsilon^{-4})$ stochastic oracle calls are necessary, again strengthening the best known bounds in related settings. Our results expose substantial gaps between current upper and lower bounds for bilevel optimization and suggest that even simplified regimes, such as those with quadratic lower-level objectives, warrant further investigation toward understanding the optimal complexity of bilevel optimization under standard first-order oracles.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization contains one optimization problem inside another. This paper studies the smooth setting where the upper-level problem is nonconvex and the lower-level problem is strongly convex. It asks how much first-order information algorithms must obtain in difficult cases, complementing upper bounds that describe how quickly particular algorithms can succeed.

The bounds strengthen known lower bounds in related single-level nonconvex and nonconvex–strongly-convex min-max settings. They also reveal substantial remaining gaps between available upper and lower bounds for bilevel optimization. The authors highlight even quadratic lower-level objectives as deserving further investigation, indicating that the best achievable complexity remains unresolved despite the new impossibility results.
summary.tldr: New hard instances establish stronger first-order complexity lower bounds for smooth nonconvex–strongly-convex bilevel optimization.

title: Lower Complexity Bounds for Nonconvex-Strongly-Convex Bilevel Optimization with First-Order Oracles

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are typically deterministic in nature and lack intrinsic mechanisms to quantify epistemic uncertainty, which reflects the model’s lack of knowledge or ignorance of its own representations. We theoretically motivate negative log-density of an embedding as a proxy for the epistemic uncertainty, where low-density regions signify model ignorance. The proposed method REPVLM computes the probability density on the hyperspherical manifold of the VLM embeddings using Riemannian Flow Matching. We empirically demonstrate that REPVLM achieves near-perfect correlation between uncertainty and prediction error, significantly outperforming existing baselines. Beyond classification, we also demonstrate that the model also provides a scalable metric for out-of-distribution detection and automated data curation.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can produce a prediction without indicating how much relevant knowledge it lacks. This paper targets that epistemic uncertainty by examining the model’s embeddings, the internal representations used to encode inputs. The central idea is that an embedding in a low-density region can signal a gap in the model’s knowledge.

The authors theoretically motivate negative log-density as a proxy for this uncertainty: lower estimated density corresponds to greater uncertainty. Their method, REPVLM, estimates density using Riemannian Flow Matching on the hyperspherical space occupied by the embeddings. Accounting for this geometry makes the density model correspond to the space where the representations actually reside.

In the reported experiments, REPVLM’s uncertainty estimates have near-perfect correlation with prediction error and substantially outperform existing baselines. The authors also demonstrate applications to detecting inputs outside the expected distribution and to automated data curation. These findings support embedding density as a useful empirical uncertainty signal, with the near-perfect relationship being a reported experimental result rather than a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: REPVLM estimates density in vision-language embedding space to quantify uncertainty, reporting near-perfect correlation with prediction error in its experiments.

title: Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification for Pre-trained VLMs via Riemannian Flow Matching

abstract: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) have emerged as a promising approach for generative modeling in discrete spaces. By generating sequences in any order and allowing for parallel decoding, they enable fast inference and strong performance on non-causal tasks. However, this flexibility comes with a training complexity trade-off: MDMs train on an exponentially large set of masking patterns, which is not only computationally expensive, but also creates a train–test mismatch between the random masks used in training and the highly structured masks induced by inference-time unmasking. In this work, we propose Progressive UnMAsking (PUMA), a simple modification of the forward masking process that aligns training-time and inference-time masking patterns, thereby focusing optimization on inference-aligned masks and speeding up training. Empirically, PUMA speeds up pretraining at the 125M scale by $\approx 2.3 \times$ and offers complementary advantages on top of common recipes like autoregressive initialization. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/PUMA.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion models learn to fill missing tokens and can generate in flexible orders, including updating several positions together. That flexibility creates a large training burden: there are exponentially many possible masking patterns. Random training masks also differ from the structured patterns encountered as an inference procedure progressively fills a sequence.

Progressive UnMAsking, or PUMA, modifies the forward masking process to bring those two pattern distributions into closer alignment. Training focuses on masks that correspond more closely to the model's eventual unmasking behavior. The approach therefore changes which reconstruction problems the model practices, directing optimization toward situations relevant to generation.

At the 125-million-parameter scale, the reported experiments show approximately 2.3-fold faster pretraining. PUMA also provides complementary benefits when combined with common recipes such as autoregressive initialization. These findings support training-mask selection as a useful source of efficiency: some of the cost of masked diffusion comes from the breadth and mismatch of training patterns, and aligning them with inference can reduce that burden in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: PUMA aligns training masks with inference-time unmasking patterns, delivering approximately 2.3-fold faster pretraining at the evaluated 125M scale.

title: Stop Training for the Worst: Progressive Unmasking Accelerates Masked Diffusion Training

abstract: We study optimal experimental design for multinomial logit (MNL) bandits, where an agent repeatedly selects a subset of $K$ items from a ground set of size $N$ and observes single-choice feedback. Unlike linear or generalized linear bandits, MNL bandits have a combinatorial action space, which makes classical optimal design approaches and naive optimization over all subsets computationally intractable. We propose a computationally efficient optimal design framework for MNL models that achieves both statistical efficiency and scalability through two complementary approaches: (i) an exact or certified-approximate reformulation of the design oracle as a $0$-$1$ mixed-integer linear program (MILP) with solver-certified early stopping, and (ii) a fully polynomial-time lifted design that replaces the nonlinear objective with a tractable surrogate. Using the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence theorem, we establish near G-optimality guarantees and characterize the induced statistical-computational trade-offs. As an application, we develop a best assortment identification algorithm for MNL bandits with linear utilities and non-uniform revenues, and prove an instance-dependent sample complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\frac{d \log N}{\Delta^2}\big)$, where $d$ is the feature dimension, $N$ is the number of arms, and $\Delta$ is the minimum revenue gap.

We propose a computationally efficient optimal design framework for MNL models that achieves both statistical efficiency and scalability through two complementary approaches: (i) an exact or certified-approximate reformulation of the design oracle as a $0$-$1$ mixed-integer linear program (MILP) with solver-certified early stopping, and (ii) a fully polynomial-time lifted design that replaces the nonlinear objective with a tractable surrogate. paragraphs: In multinomial logit bandits, an agent presents a subset of items and observes a single choice. Designing informative experiments is difficult because the number of possible subsets grows combinatorially. This paper seeks experiments that are statistically informative while remaining computationally feasible, avoiding direct optimization over every possible assortment.

The framework offers two complementary approaches. One reformulates the design oracle as a binary mixed-integer linear program, allowing exact solutions or certified approximations with solver-certified early stopping. The other replaces the nonlinear design objective with a tractable surrogate and runs in fully polynomial time. Using the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence theorem, the authors establish near G-optimality guarantees and describe the resulting trade-offs between information quality and computational cost.

The framework also supports an algorithm for identifying the best assortment when utilities are linear and revenues differ across items. Its proved instance-dependent sample complexity scales as d log N divided by the squared minimum revenue gap, up to suppressed logarithmic factors. This connects experimental design to the number of observations needed to distinguish the best assortment.
summary.tldr: The paper develops scalable experimental designs for multinomial logit bandits and proves sample-complexity guarantees for identifying the best assortment.

title: Optimal Design for Multinomial Logit Model with Applications to Best Assortment Identification

abstract: The long-standing tension between Pre- and Post-Norm remains an open problem in Transformer architecture, reflecting a fundamental trade-off between training stability and representational capacity. Prior attempts to combine their strengths have made progress, but often show limited robustness across training settings, restricting their broader applicability. We revisit this dilemma, showing that single-stream architectures struggle to reconcile Pre-Norm’s stable identity-gradient propagation with Post-Norm’s normalization of the main residual path. To address this structural tension, we propose SiameseNorm, a simple yet effective two-stream architecture that remains compatible with Pre-Norm training recipes. SiameseNorm couples Pre-Norm-like and Post-Norm-like streams through shared residual blocks, allowing each residual block to receive optimization signals from both pathways with negligible overhead. Extensive experiments on 400M and 1.3B dense language models, 15B MoE models, Vision Transformers, and Diffusion Transformers show that SiameseNorm consistently improves performance while maintaining strong training stability across architectures and modalities. abstract: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable, yet their safety lags behind. This creates a gap between what agents can do and should do. This gap widens as agents engage in multi-turn interactions and employ diverse tools, introducing new risks overlooked by existing benchmarks. To systematically scale safety testing in multi-turn, tool-realistic settings, we propose a principled taxonomy that transforms single-turn harmful tasks into multi-turn attack sequences. Using this taxonomy, we construct MT-AgentRisk (Multi-Turn Agent Risk Benchmark), the first benchmark to evaluate tool-using agent safety under multi-turn, harmful-distribution settings. Our experiments reveal substantial safety degradation: the Attack Success Rate (ASR) increases by 16% on average across open and closed models in multi-turn settings. To close this gap, we propose ToolShield, a training-free, tool-agnostic, self-exploration defense: when encountering a new tool, the agent autonomously generates test cases, executes them to observe downstream effects, and distills safety experiences for deployment. Experiments show that ToolShield effectively reduces ASR by 30% on average in multi-turn interactions.

summary.tldr: MT-AgentRisk exposes increased safety failures across multiple turns, while ToolShield reduces attacks through training-free exploration of tool behavior.

title: Unsafer in Many Turns: Benchmarking and Defending Multi-Turn Safety Risks in Tool-Using Agents

abstract: In-context learning is fundamental to modern Large Language Models (LLMs); however, prevailing architectures impose a rigid and fixed contextual structure by assigning linear or constant positional indices. The rigid position information poses the full burden of organizing the input structure to attention layers, thus reducing the amount of attention that could be allocated for more critical information. To address this, we propose RePo, a novel mechanism that alleviates the burden for attention layers via context re-positioning. Unlike conventional approaches, RePo utilizes a differentiable module, $f_\phi$, to assign token positions that capture contextual dependencies, rather than replying on pre-defined order. By continually pre-training on the OLMo-2 1B & 7B models, we demonstrate that RePo consistently enhances performance on tasks involving noisy contexts, structured data, and longer context length, while maintaining competitive performance on general short-context tasks. Analysis reveals that RePo successfully allocates more attention mass to distant but relevant information, assigns positions in a dense and non-linear space, and captures the intrinsic structure of the input context.

paragraphs: Language models normally receive position information based on a predetermined ordering. RePo argues that this rigid structure leaves attention layers responsible for discovering how the input's pieces relate to one another. That organizational burden can reduce the attention available for identifying the information most relevant to a task.

RePo introduces a differentiable module that assigns token positions according to contextual dependencies. The authors apply this mechanism through continued pretraining of OLMo-2 models with one billion and seven billion parameters.

The resulting models improve consistently on tasks involving noisy context, structured data, and longer contexts, while remaining competitive on general short-context tasks. Analysis finds that relevant but distant information receives more attention and that the learned positions occupy a dense, nonlinear space. These observations support the proposed mechanism: changing positional structure can help the model organize context and direct attention toward useful relationships that ordinary sequence distance does not adequately express.
summary.tldr: RePo learns context-dependent token positions to improve how language models use noisy, structured, and long inputs.

title: RePo: Language Models with Context Re-Positioning

abstract: Regression is a cornerstone of statistics and machine learning, with applications spanning science, engineering, and economics. While quantum algorithms for regression have attracted considerable attention, most existing work has focused on linear regression, leaving many more complex yet practically important variants unexplored. In this work, we present a unified quantum framework for accelerating a broad class of regression tasks—including linear and multiple regression, Lasso, Ridge, Huber, $\ell_p$-, and $\delta_p$-type regressions—achieving up to a quadratic improvement in the number of samples $m$ over the best classical algorithms. This speedup is achieved by a non-trivial quantization of the recent classical breakthrough of Jambulapati et al. (2024), where we construct a full quantum pipeline that strategically employs quantum leverage score approximation to initialize and refine Multiscale Leverage Score Overestimates, enabling efficient importance sampling via the preparation of multiple state copies. For problems of dimension $n$, sparsity $r < n$, and error parameter $\epsilon$, our algorithm solves the problem in $\widetilde{O}(r\sqrt{mn}/\epsilon + \mathrm{poly}(n,1/\epsilon))$ quantum time, demonstrating both the applicability and the efficiency of quantum computing in accelerating regression tasks.

paragraphs: This paper develops a quantum framework for several regression problems, extending beyond the linear regression setting that has dominated earlier quantum work. Its sample-dependent term scales with the square root of the sample count, while an additional term depends polynomially on dimension and inverse error. Consequently, the claimed acceleration concerns a particular complexity dependence; it does not imply an unconditional quadratic reduction in total runtime for every regression problem.
summary.tldr: A unified quantum regression framework offers up to quadratic improvement in sample-count dependence across several regression families.

title: Accelerating Regression Tasks with Quantum Algorithms

abstract: Prompt learning for vision-language models (VLMs) primarily follows end-to-end or decoupled routes to balance base and new task performance, but suffers a fundamental bottleneck: sample-wise optimization within task-specific feature spaces traps models in local optima, hindering global optimality. To address this, we identify a key insight that VLMs can be prompted within a Coupled Prompt Field-a shared space where base and new tasks are mutually constrained-and present AlignedNorm, which enforces the field coupling. By dynamically aligning the norms of prompts to VLMs’ native scale, our method enables joint optimization of both tasks. Without complex designs, our method matches leading decoupled approaches on 15 datasets across 4 experimental settings, offering both a new perspective and a practical solution to the local-optima dilemma in prompt learning.

paragraphs: Prompt learning adapts vision-language models through trainable prompts while trying to balance performance on base and new tasks. The authors argue that optimizing individual samples within separate task-specific feature spaces creates a bottleneck: optimization can become trapped in local solutions that obstruct better joint performance.

AlignedNorm approaches this problem through a Coupled Prompt Field, a shared space in which base and new tasks constrain one another. Its central mechanism dynamically adjusts prompt norms—their magnitudes—to match the vision-language model’s native scale. This alignment enforces coupling between the tasks and enables their joint optimization without introducing a complex architecture.

Across 15 datasets and four experimental settings, the method matches leading decoupled approaches. The reported result supports norm alignment as a practical way to balance the two task groups with a relatively simple mechanism. The shared-space perspective also offers an explanation for why prompt scale matters: it participates in coordinating optimization across tasks. The empirical comparison establishes competitive performance, rather than a general guarantee that optimization always reaches a global optimum.
summary.tldr: AlignedNorm dynamically aligns prompt magnitudes to jointly optimize base and new tasks, matching leading approaches across the reported evaluations.

title: AlignedNorm: Prompting Vision–Language Models via Coupled Prompt Field

abstract: GUI grounding maps natural language instructions to the correct interface elements, serving as the perception foundation for GUI agents. Existing approaches predominantly rely on fine-tuning multimodal large language models (MLLMs) using large-scale GUI datasets to predict target element coordinates, which is data-intensive and generalizes poorly to unseen interfaces. Recent attention-based alternatives exploit localization signals in MLLMs attention mechanisms without task-specific fine-tuning, but suffer from low reliability due to the lack of explicit and complementary spatial anchors in GUI images. To address this limitation, we propose Trifuse, an attention-based grounding framework that explicitly integrates complementary spatial anchors. Trifuse integrates attention, OCR-derived textual cues, and icon-level caption semantics via a Consensus-SinglePeak (CS) fusion strategy that enforces cross-modal agreement while retaining sharp localization peaks. Extensive evaluations on four grounding benchmarks demonstrate that Trifuse achieves strong performance without task-specific fine-tuning, substantially reducing the reliance on expensive annotated data. Moreover, ablation studies reveal that incorporating OCR and caption cues consistently improves attention-based grounding performance across different backbones, highlighting its effectiveness as a general framework for GUI grounding.

paragraphs: GUI grounding connects an instruction to the interface element it refers to. Attention-based methods can locate elements without task-specific fine-tuning, but their localization signals can be unreliable. Trifuse strengthens those signals by adding explicit spatial evidence from interface text and icon descriptions, reducing reliance on large annotated GUI datasets.

The framework combines model attention, text cues obtained through optical character recognition, and semantic captions for icons. Its Consensus-SinglePeak fusion strategy encourages agreement among these sources while preserving sharp localization peaks. This addresses two linked needs: corroborating the likely target and retaining a precise location instead of spreading support broadly across the screen.

Evaluations on four grounding benchmarks report strong performance without task-specific fine-tuning. Ablation studies also show that adding OCR and caption information consistently improves attention-based grounding across different model backbones. These findings support complementary spatial anchors as a general way to strengthen attention-based localization, with the reported benefits extending beyond a single underlying model architecture.
summary.tldr: Trifuse combines attention, recognized text, and icon captions to improve GUI grounding without task-specific fine-tuning.

title: Trifuse: Enhancing Attention-Based GUI Grounding via Multimodal Fusion

abstract: Many real-world datasets contain hidden structure that cannot be detected by simple linear correlations between input features. For example, latent factors may influence the data in a coordinated way, even though their effect is invisible to covariance-based methods such as PCA. In practice, nonlinear neural networks often succeed in extracting such hidden structure in unsupervised and self-supervised learning. However, constructing a minimal high-dimensional model where this advantage can be rigorously analyzed has remained an open theoretical challenge. We introduce a tractable high-dimensional spiked model with two latent factors: one visible to covariance, and one statistically dependent yet uncorrelated, appearing only in higher-order moments. PCA and linear autoencoders fail to recover the latter, while a minimal nonlinear autoencoder provably extracts both. We analyze both the population risk, and empirical risk minimization. Our model also provides a tractable example where self-supervised test loss is poorly aligned with representation quality: nonlinear autoencoders recover latent structure that linear methods miss, even though their reconstruction loss is higher.

paragraphs: A representation can capture useful hidden structure even when its reconstruction error looks worse. This paper constructs a mathematically tractable example of that mismatch, while explaining why nonlinear autoencoders can discover patterns that principal component analysis, or PCA, cannot detect.

The proposed high-dimensional model contains two latent factors. One affects covariance, the statistical structure that PCA uses. The other is statistically dependent yet uncorrelated, so its presence becomes visible only through higher-order moments. This distinction gives the researchers a controlled setting in which linear and nonlinear methods have different access to the underlying structure.

The authors prove that a minimal nonlinear autoencoder extracts both factors, whereas PCA and linear autoencoders fail to recover the second. They analyze both population risk and learning through empirical risk minimization. In this model, the nonlinear autoencoder can recover richer latent structure despite having higher reconstruction loss. The result shows why self-supervised test loss can be a misleading measure of representation quality, even in a setting that permits rigorous analysis.
summary.tldr: A tractable model proves that nonlinear autoencoders can recover structure missed by PCA even while having worse reconstruction loss.

title: A Solvable High-Dimensional Model Where Nonlinear Autoencoders Learn Structure Invisible to PCA While Test Loss Misaligns With Generalization

abstract: Covariance matrices serve as compact descriptors of feature distributions in many machine-learning pipelines, including domain adaptation and Gaussian embeddings. Under a centered Gaussian approximation, the unregularized Wasserstein-2 optimal transport (OT) discrepancy admits a closed form on covariances given by the Bures–Wasserstein (BW) objective on the symmetric positive definite (SPD) cone. We propose ITSPACE (Iterative Transport for Stable Proximal Alignment of Covariance Embeddings), a proximal majorization-minimization method that directly optimizes this exact BW objective through closed-form updates in a square-root factorization. In exact arithmetic, each iteration satisfies a sufficient-decrease inequality for the BW objective; under inexact polar computations, we provide an explicit certificate-gap bound controlling deviations from exact descent. The resulting iterations preserve PSD structure by construction and naturally support rank-restricted factors, making ITSPACE well-suited as a lightweight inner-loop primitive in settings where adaptation must be performed from unlabeled target batches under strict step and compute budgets. Across real-world covariance-alignment benchmarks, ITSPACE reaches low-BW-gap solutions substantially faster than BW-gradient descent, methods based on other covariance geometries, and entropically regularized sample-OT baselines.

Its contribution combines efficient empirical alignment with carefully qualified guarantees about objective descent.
summary.tldr: ITSPACE efficiently aligns covariance representations through structure-preserving updates with exact-arithmetic descent guarantees and bounds for inexact computation.

title: ITSPACE: Monotone Gaussian Optimal Transport Updates

abstract: Modern deep-learning models have achieved remarkable success in time-series forecasting. Yet, their performance degrades in long-term prediction due to error accumulation in autoregressive inference, where predictions are recursively used as inputs. While classical error correction mechanisms (ECMs) have long been used in statistical methods, their applicability to deep learning models remains limited or ineffective. In this work, we revisit the error accumulation problem in deep time-series forecasting and investigate the role and necessity of ECMs in this new context. We propose a simple, architecture-agnostic error correction model that can be integrated with any existing forecaster without requiring retraining. By explicitly decomposing predictions into trend and seasonal components and training the corrector to adjust each separately, we introduce the Universal Error Corrector with Seasonal–Trend Decomposition (UEC-STD), which significantly improves correction accuracy and robustness across 4 backbones and 10 datasets. Our findings provide a practical tool for enhancing forecasts while offering new insights into mitigating autoregressive errors in deep time-series models.

paragraphs: Long-range forecasts can deteriorate when a model repeatedly feeds its own predictions back as inputs. Errors from earlier steps then influence later predictions. This paper revisits error correction for deep time-series models, examining how an idea used in classical statistical forecasting can become useful in modern forecasting systems.

The proposed Universal Error Corrector with Seasonal–Trend Decomposition separates predictions into trend and seasonal components. It trains a corrector to adjust each component separately, allowing correction to address these different parts of the forecast explicitly. The corrector is architecture-agnostic and can be attached to an existing forecaster without retraining that forecaster, although the correction model itself is trained.

Experiments across four forecasting backbones and ten datasets show significant improvements in correction accuracy and robustness. These findings support treating correction as a separate learned component that can improve existing forecasting systems. The seasonal–trend decomposition supplies the structure for that correction, helping address accumulated autoregressive errors through distinct adjustments to the forecast’s components.
summary.tldr: UEC-STD improves forecasts by separately correcting trend and seasonal components without requiring the underlying forecaster to be retrained.

title: Reviving Error Correction in Modern Deep Time-Series Forecasting

abstract: This paper tackles the challenging problem of developing a proactive copyright protection mechanism that cuts off unauthorized use of diffusion bridge models. Existing studies largely fall into post-hoc attribution (e.g., watermarking and fingerprinting) or degradation-only defenses, which offer only indirect and limited preventive effect. We therefore propose GoodDiffusion, inspired by backdoor mechanisms, to enforce model-level use-time control by internalizing authorization into the generative process through a selectively permissive, otherwise closed behavior. Specifically, GoodDiffusion preserves high-quality generation for authorized queries carrying valid signatures, yet refuses to generate for unauthorized inputs. We further empirically show that naive static-signature designs (like conventional backdoor injection) are fundamentally fragile, since a surrogate signature can be efficiently recovered via gradient-based optimization. To strengthen security, we introduce a Learnable Signature Network (LSN) that assigns sample-specific signatures conditioned on each input. This breaks the universality of signatures and prevents a surrogate from transferring across inputs. Extensive experiments validate that GoodDiffusion effectively blocks unauthorized use while maintaining strong generation quality for authorized users.

Specifically, GoodDiffusion preserves high-quality generation for authorized queries carrying valid signatures, yet refuses to generate for unauthorized inputs. We further empirically show that naive static-signature designs (like conventional backdoor injection) are fundamentally fragile, since a surrogate signature can be efficiently recovered via gradient-based optimization. To strengthen security, we introduce a Learnable Signature Network (LSN) that assigns sample-specific signatures conditioned on each input. paragraphs: GoodDiffusion addresses copyright protection by making authorization part of how a diffusion bridge model generates outputs. The aim is to control unauthorized use when it happens. The paper contrasts this approach with watermarking and fingerprinting, which support attribution after use, and defenses that primarily reduce output quality.

The proposed mechanism draws inspiration from backdoors: a signature carried by an input determines whether generation is permitted. Queries with valid signatures retain high-quality generation, while unauthorized inputs are refused. This makes selective access a behavior built into the model’s generative process.

A central finding concerns the weakness of using a fixed signature. The authors empirically show that gradient-based optimization can efficiently recover a substitute signature in naive static-signature designs. Such a substitute undermines authorization because it can provide an alternative way to activate generation.

GoodDiffusion therefore introduces a Learnable Signature Network that produces signatures specific to each input. By removing the shared signature across inputs, this design prevents a recovered substitute from transferring between them. The reported experiments show effective blocking of unauthorized use alongside strong generation quality for authorized users. Together, these findings support input-dependent signatures as a way to strengthen access control while preserving useful generation for permitted queries.
summary.tldr: GoodDiffusion builds authorization into diffusion bridge models using input-specific signatures, with experiments showing effective blocking of unauthorized use while preserving authorized generation quality.

title: GoodDiffusion: Proactive Copyright Protection for Diffusion Bridge Models via Learnable Sample-specific Signatures

abstract: We prove the conjecture stated in Appendix F.3 of Zhu et al.: among all conversion rules that map a Rényi Differential Privacy (RDP) profile $\tau \mapsto \rho(\tau)$ to a valid hypothesis-testing trade-off $f$ (or equivalently, an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-Differential Privacy curve), the rule based on the intersection of single-order RDP privacy regions is optimal. This optimality holds simultaneously for all valid RDP profiles and for all Type I error levels $\alpha$. Concretely, we show that in the space of trade-off functions, the tightest possible bound is $f_{\rho(\cdot)}(\alpha) = \sup_{\tau \geq 0.5} f_{\tau,\rho(\tau)}(\alpha)$: the pointwise maximum of the single-order bounds for each RDP privacy region. Our proof unifies and sharpens the insights of Balle et al., Asoodeh et al., and Zhu et al.. Our analysis relies on a precise geometric characterization of the RDP privacy region, leveraging its convexity and the fact that its boundary is determined exclusively by Bernoulli mechanisms. Our results establish that the "intersection-of-RDP-privacy-regions" rule is not only valid, but optimal: no other black-box conversion can uniformly dominate it in the Blackwell sense, marking the fundamental limit of what can be inferred about a mechanism’s privacy solely from its RDP guarantees.
originalAbstract: We prove the conjecture stated in Appendix F.3 of Zhu et al.: among all conversion rules that map a Rényi Differential Privacy (RDP) profile $\tau \mapsto \rho(\tau)$ to a valid hypothesis-testing trade-off $f$ (or equivalently, an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-Differential Privacy curve), the rule based on the intersection of single-order RDP privacy regions is optimal. This optimality holds simultaneously for all valid RDP profiles and for all Type I error levels $\alpha$. Concretely, we show that in the space of trade-off functions, the tightest possible bound is $f_{\rho(\cdot)}(\alpha) = \sup_{\tau \geq 0.5} f_{\tau,\rho(\tau)}(\alpha)$: the pointwise maximum of the single-order bounds for each RDP privacy region. Our proof unifies and sharpens the insights of Balle et al., Asoodeh et al., and Zhu et al.. Our analysis relies on a precise geometric characterization of the RDP privacy region, leveraging its convexity and the fact that its boundary is determined exclusively by Bernoulli mechanisms. Our results establish that the "intersection-of-RDP-privacy-regions" rule is not only valid, but optimal: no other black-box conversion can uniformly dominate it in the Blackwell sense, marking the fundamental limit of what can be inferred about a mechanism’s privacy solely from its RDP guarantees.

paragraphs: Rényi differential privacy describes privacy through a profile indexed by Rényi order. Another representation expresses privacy as a trade-off between errors in a hypothesis test. This paper asks how tightly the second representation can be inferred when the only available information is the first.

The authors prove that intersecting the privacy regions associated with individual Rényi orders gives an optimal conversion. Equivalently, at each Type I error level, one takes the strongest of the corresponding single-order trade-off bounds. The result applies simultaneously to every valid Rényi privacy profile and every such error level, resolving the stated conjecture.

The proof uses the convex geometry of Rényi privacy regions and a characterization of their boundaries through Bernoulli mechanisms. Its practical meaning is a limit on information recovery: no other black-box conversion can uniformly improve this rule in the stated Blackwell sense using only the same Rényi guarantees. Stronger conclusions about a particular mechanism would therefore require information beyond its Rényi privacy profile.
summary.tldr: Intersecting single-order Rényi privacy regions yields the optimal black-box conversion from an RDP profile to a hypothesis-testing privacy trade-off.

title: Optimal conversion from Rényi Differential Privacy to $f$-Differential Privacy

abstract: The rapid rise of generative AI has made multimodal fake news increasingly realistic and pervasive, posing severe threats to public trust and social stability. Existing detection methods rely heavily on manipulation-specific models and large-scale labeled data, resulting in poor generalization to emerging manipulation types. We observed that the essence of manipulated misinformation lies in its intrinsic conflicts, i.e., semantic or physical inconsistencies either across modalities or with common world knowledge. Inspired by this observation, we propose Conflict-Oriented REasoning (CORE) framework, an effective paradigm that learns to endows multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with explicit conflict-capturing capability. To this end, CORE first constructs the Conflict Attribution Corpus (CAC) with fine-grained annotations of conflict factors and sources, providing essential data support for subsequent conflict perception training. By performing conflict-oriented representation enhancement and reasoning based on CAC, CORE achieves robust and generalizable conflict detection, effectively and rapidly adapting to unseen manipulation types with a few samples or in even zero-shot settings. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CORE surpasses state-of-the-art models by 9.7%, 14.1%, and 11.8% in accuracy on the DGM$^4$, MMFakeBench, and MDSM benchmarks, respectively.

CORE also adapts to unseen manipulation types with few examples or in zero-shot settings. These results support the usefulness of conflict-focused supervision for generalization, with the reported benefits tied to the evaluated benchmarks and adaptation settings.
summary.tldr: CORE trains multimodal models to identify inconsistencies, improving manipulation detection and adaptation to unseen manipulation types.

title: CORE: Conflict-Oriented Reasoning for General Multimodal Manipulation Detection

abstract: Can we train LLMs to introspect, i.e. to faithfully describe their own behaviors in natural language? Prior work has shown some, limited, success. However, it is difficult to scale introspection training due to a lack of ground-truth labels. In this work, we study an approach to introspection training which side-steps this data bottleneck. Given a target model $M$, our method works by fine-tuning models $M_i$ from $M$ with implanted behaviors $b_i$ (such as downplaying medical problems); the $(M_i, b_i)$ pairs serve as labeled introspection training data. We then train an introspection adapter (IA): a LoRA adapter jointly optimized across the fine-tunes $M_i$ which causes them to verbalize their implanted behaviors. This IA induces faithful introspection in fine-tunes of $M$ that were trained in very different ways from the $M_i$, as well as in $M$ itself. This is surprising because the IA was never trained on $M$. To demonstrate the utility of IAs, we use them to successfully audit misaligned models introduced in prior work. IAs can also be used to detect fine-tuning API attacks which train models to comply with encrypted harmful requests. Notably, IAs are more effective when applied to larger models. Overall, our results suggest that IAs are a scalable, effective, and practically useful approach to LLM introspection training.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether language models can be trained to describe their own learned behaviors faithfully. A major obstacle is obtaining reliable labels for what a model has learned. The authors create such labels by fine-tuning copies of a target model with deliberately implanted behaviors, producing pairs of models and known behavioral descriptions.

They then jointly train a LoRA introspection adapter across these modified models so that each verbalizes its implanted behavior. The adapter also induces faithful reports in other fine-tunes trained through substantially different procedures and in the original target model itself. Transfer to the original model is especially notable because the adapter was never trained on that model directly.

The authors demonstrate applications by auditing previously introduced misaligned models and detecting fine-tuning API attacks involving encrypted harmful requests. They also find that adapters work better on larger models. These results suggest that deliberately constructed behavioral labels can support scalable introspection training, with demonstrated transfer beyond the models used to train the adapter and practical value for the reported auditing tasks.
summary.tldr: Adapters trained on deliberately implanted behaviors help language models describe learned behaviors and support audits of misaligned models.

title: Introspection Adapters: Training LLMs to Report Their Learned Behaviors

abstract: Providing non-conservative uncertainty quantification for function estimates derived from noisy observations remains a fundamental challenge in statistical machine learning, particularly for applications in safety-critical domains. In this work, we propose novel non-asymptotic probabilistic uniform error bounds for kernel-based regression. Compared to related bounds in the literature that are restricted to (conditionally) independent sub-Gaussian noise, our bounds allow to consider a broad class of non-Gaussian distributions, such as sub-Gaussian, bounded, sub-exponential, and variance/moment-bounded noise. Moreover, our results apply to correlated and uncorrelated noise. We compare our proposed error bounds with existing results in terms of the induced uncertainty region and their performance in safe control, demonstrating the tightness of the proposed bounds.

paragraphs: Kernel regression estimates an unknown function from noisy observations. To use those estimates confidently, one also needs bounds on how far they may be from the true function. This paper develops probabilistic error bounds that hold uniformly across the function's domain, rather than describing uncertainty only at an individual evaluation point.

The bounds are non-asymptotic, meaning they address finite amounts of data. Their main expansion is in the noise conditions they accommodate. Related results discussed in the paper require conditionally independent sub-Gaussian noise, whereas these bounds cover several distribution classes, including bounded, sub-exponential, and variance- or moment-bounded noise. They also apply to both correlated and uncorrelated noise, broadening the settings in which uncertainty can be quantified.

The authors compare the resulting uncertainty regions with existing bounds and examine their performance in safe control. These comparisons demonstrate the tightness of the proposed bounds. The contribution matters because uncertainty regions that are unnecessarily wide can restrict useful decisions, while narrow regions need mathematical support under the noise conditions actually being modeled.
summary.tldr: New finite-data kernel-regression error bounds accommodate broader noise distributions and correlations while providing tight uncertainty regions.

title: On Uniform Error Bounds for Kernel Regression under Non-Gaussian Noise

abstract: As the computational demands for pre-training Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to surge, the need for efficient training paradigms becomes critical. Despite the vast resources already invested in existing pre-trained checkpoints, these assets often remain under-leveraged due to architectural limitations. We introduce an "orthogonal growth" strategy designed to "recycle" these checkpoints by strategically expanding their parameters prior to continued training. Our method focuses on optimizing converged Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models through two dimensions: interpositional layer copying for increased depth and noisy expert duplication for expanded width. Through extensive scaling laws analysis, we demonstrate a strong positive correlation between the "sunk cost" (prior investment) and the final model accuracy. Empirical results on models up to 70B parameters and 1T tokens show that our recycling approach yields a 10.6% accuracy improvement compared to training from scratch under identical extra compute budgets. This work provides a cost-effective blueprint for sustainable large-scale LLM development.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how to reuse the computation already invested in pretrained language models when building larger ones. Its starting point is a converged mixture-of-experts model. Rather than leaving the checkpoint at its original size, the proposed strategy expands its architecture and then continues training, carrying previous learning into a larger model.

The expansion proceeds along two dimensions. Interpositional layer copying increases depth, while duplicating experts with added noise increases width. The authors call this orthogonal growth. Together, these operations provide a way to enlarge an existing mixture-of-experts checkpoint instead of requiring the larger architecture to learn everything from an untrained starting point.

Scaling-law analysis finds a strong positive correlation between prior training investment and final accuracy. Experiments involving models up to 70 billion parameters and one trillion tokens report a 10.6% accuracy improvement over training from scratch with the same additional compute budget. That comparison concerns new computation after checkpoint reuse; it does not equate the total historical computation invested in the two approaches.
summary.tldr: Expanding pretrained mixture-of-experts models in depth and width improves reported accuracy over training from scratch under equal additional compute budgets.

title: Beyond Sunk Costs: Boosting LLM Pre-training Efficiency via Orthogonal Growth of Mixture-of-Experts

abstract: Few-shot molecular property prediction (FSMPP) is essential in drug discovery and materials design, where high-quality labeled data are often scarce and expensive to obtain. Despite the promising performance of existing methods, especially context-aware methods, they still face two-fold severe challenges with ${\rm \textit{insufficient structural context modeling}}$ & ${\rm \textit{redundant auxiliary context learning}}$, leading to inadequate context graph exploration and ineffective information utilization for effective molecule representation learning. To address these, in this paper, we propose a novel framework by learning on ${\rm \mathbf{\underline{Re}}}$ational and ${\rm \mathbf{\underline{C}}}$ompact c${\rm \mathbf{\underline{o}}}$ntext ${\rm \mathbf{\underline{G}}}$raph, named ReCoG, to comprehensively exploit the context graph for expressive molecular property prediction. Specifically, the proposed ReCoG contains two core modules: a (1) cross-property relational learning module to better model the structural and relational context information, and a (2) context graph information bottleneck module to adaptively suppress irrelevant auxiliary signals for compact context information utilization, followed by a detailed theoretical demonstration regarding the importance of joint relational and compact knowledge extraction in context graphs.

Specifically, the proposed ReCoG contains two core modules: a (1) cross-property relational learning module to better model the structural and relational context information, and a (2) context graph information bottleneck module to adaptively suppress irrelevant auxiliary signals for compact context information utilization, followed by a detailed theoretical demonstration regarding the importance of joint relational and compact knowledge extraction in context graphs.

paragraphs: Molecular property prediction often has to work with few labeled examples because obtaining reliable labels is expensive. Context-aware methods try to compensate by learning from related information, but that context can be poorly organized or contain redundant auxiliary signals. ReCoG addresses both problems: extracting useful relationships and limiting information that distracts from the prediction task.

Its cross-property relational learning module models structural and relational context more fully. A separate context-graph information bottleneck adaptively suppresses irrelevant auxiliary signals. These modules serve complementary purposes. Richer relational modeling expands what the representation can learn from the context graph, while compression concentrates that information on what is relevant to molecular property prediction.

The paper also provides a theoretical discussion of why relational and compact knowledge extraction should be considered jointly. Its stated contribution is a framework for making context more expressive without allowing auxiliary information to remain indiscriminately influential. For few-shot prediction, this matters because the method aims to use scarce supervision more effectively through better organized and more selective contextual learning.
summary.tldr: ReCoG combines cross-property relational learning with an information bottleneck to make molecular context more useful for few-shot prediction.

title: ReCoG: Relational and Compact Context Graph Learning for Few-shot Molecular Property Prediction

abstract: Federated learning enables on-device training without centralizing data, yet existing systems still struggle to provide explanations that are both locally faithful and globally consistent under strict privacy and bandwidth constraints. Prior approaches either keep explanations siloed across clients, transmit heavy or sensitive artifacts, or replace expressive task models with interpretable surrogates that sacrifice accuracy. We propose xFedAlign, a model-agnostic framework that decouples task optimization in parameter space from explanation coordination in a compact group space. Each client distills a lightweight surrogate to produce private, per-class top-k attribution artifacts, which are robustly aggregated by the server into a Global Explanation Prior that softly aligns client explanations without constraining task learning. Across image, text, and tabular benchmarks with IID and non-IID partitions, xFedAlign matches FedAvg accuracy while consistently reducing explanation drift and improving deletion and insertion AUC relative to Local-XAI, FedAttr-Agg, and Fed-XAI, with only a few kilobytes of additional communication per round. Privacy and robustness evaluations further demonstrate reduced membership inference advantage and increased resistance to attribution poisoning, enabling consistent and trustworthy explanations in federated learning.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains models across devices without collecting their data centrally. Explaining those models introduces another coordination problem: explanations should reflect each client’s model while remaining consistent across clients. Existing approaches can leave explanations isolated, require substantial or sensitive communication, or sacrifice predictive accuracy by replacing expressive models with simpler ones.

xFedAlign separates task-model training from explanation coordination. Each client distills a lightweight surrogate and produces compact, private attribution summaries containing its top-ranked contributions for each class. The server robustly aggregates these summaries into a Global Explanation Prior. This prior softly aligns local explanations without constraining learning of the task model.

Across image, text, and tabular benchmarks with both similar and heterogeneous client distributions, xFedAlign matches FedAvg accuracy while reducing explanation drift and improving deletion and insertion AUC against the stated explanation baselines. Communication increases by only a few kilobytes per round. Additional evaluations show reduced membership-inference advantage and greater resistance to attribution poisoning, supporting the framework’s explanation consistency, privacy, and robustness in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: xFedAlign coordinates compact explanation summaries across federated clients, improving explanation consistency while matching FedAvg accuracy in the reported benchmarks.

title: Explainable Federated Learning via Global–Local Attribution Alignment

abstract: Label Distribution Learning (LDL) models supervision as an instance-wise probability distribution, enabling fine-grained learning under inherent ambiguity, but its success relies on high-fidelity label distributions that are costly to obtain and thus often noisy. Motivated by privacy-sensitive applications, we study Federated Label Distribution Learning (Fed-LDL), where data isolation further induces heterogeneous annotation quality across clients, making local updates unevenly reliable and breaking sample-size-based aggregation (e.g., FedAvg). To address this trust dilemma, we propose FedQual, a quality-aware Fed-LDL framework with two coupled mechanisms: (i) quality-adaptive client training guided by a global semantic anchor that calibrates low-quality clients while preserving high-quality autonomy, and (ii) reliability-aware server aggregation that reweights client contributions by effective reliable information rather than raw sample size. To enable rigorous evaluation, we construct four new Fed-LDL benchmarks (FER-LDL, FI-LDL, PIPAL-LDL, and KADID-LDL) with controlled annotation quality disparity. We further provide a theoretical guarantee showing that under heterogeneous supervision quality, client-specific calibration is strictly better than any uniform calibration. Experiments on the proposed benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of FedQual.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning represents each example’s supervision as probabilities across labels, making room for ambiguity. Obtaining reliable distributions is expensive, so annotation quality can vary. In federated learning, isolated clients may have very different supervision quality, making the quantity of their data a poor guide to the reliability of their updates.

FedQual responds at both the client and server. A global semantic anchor guides client training, providing stronger calibration for low-quality clients while preserving autonomy for high-quality ones. The server then weights contributions according to effective reliable information instead of raw sample counts. The authors construct four benchmarks with controlled annotation-quality differences and report effective performance across them. They also provide a theoretical guarantee that, under heterogeneous supervision quality, client-specific calibration is strictly better than any uniform calibration. The contribution establishes quality disparity as a distinct federated-learning concern and offers a coordinated response: adapt assistance to each client and adjust how much its updates influence the shared model.
summary.tldr: FedQual adapts client training and server aggregation to annotation reliability in federated label distribution learning.

title: Trustworthy Federated Label Distribution Learning under Annotation Quality Disparity

abstract: Offline Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pipelines such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) train on a pre-collected preference dataset, which makes them vulnerable to preference poisoning attack. We study label flip attacks against log-linear DPO. We first illustrate that flipping one preference label induces a parameter-independent shift in the DPO gradient. Using this key property, we can then convert the targeted poisoning problem into a structured binary sparse approximation problem. To solve this problem, we develop two attack methods: Binary-Aware Lattice Attack (BAL-A) and Binary Matching Pursuit Attack (BMP-A). BAL-A embeds the binary flip selection problem into a binary-aware lattice and applies Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovász reduction and Babai’s nearest plane algorithm; we provide sufficient conditions that enforce binary coefficients and recover the minimum-flip objective. BMP-A adapts binary matching pursuit to our non-normalized gradient dictionary and yields coherence-based recovery guarantees and robustness (impossibility) certificates for $K$-flip budgets. Experiments on synthetic dictionaries and the Stanford Human Preferences dataset validate the theory and highlight how dictionary geometry governs attack success.

paragraphs: Offline preference training relies on an already collected dataset, making corrupted preference labels a potential vulnerability. This paper studies targeted label flips specifically for log-linear Direct Preference Optimization. Its starting observation is that reversing one preference label changes the training gradient by an amount that does not depend on the model parameters.

That property lets the authors express poisoning as a structured problem of selecting a sparse set of binary choices. They develop a lattice-based method, BAL-A, and a matching-pursuit method, BMP-A. For the lattice approach, they give sufficient conditions for enforcing binary coefficients and recovering the minimum-flip objective. These are conditional guarantees rather than a claim that recovery always succeeds.

For BMP-A, the analysis connects recovery to dictionary coherence and provides certificates showing when attacks are impossible within a specified flip budget. Experiments on synthetic dictionaries and the Stanford Human Preferences dataset support the theory. The results highlight the geometry of the available gradient shifts as a determinant of attack success and robustness.
summary.tldr: For log-linear DPO, preference-label poisoning becomes a structured binary selection problem with conditional recovery and robustness guarantees.

title: Efficient Preference Poisoning Attack on Offline RLHF

abstract: Transformers serve as the foundation of most modern large language models. To mitigate the quadratic complexity of standard full attention, various efficient attention mechanisms, such as linear and hybrid attention, have been developed. A fundamental gap remains: their expressive power relative to full attention lacks a rigorous theoretical characterization. In this work, we theoretically characterize the performance differences among these attention mechanisms. Our theory applies to all linear attention variants that can be formulated as a recurrence, including Mamba, DeltaNet, etc. Specifically, we establish an expressiveness hierarchy: for the sequential function composition-a multi-step reasoning task that must occur within a model’s forward pass, an $(L+1)$-layer full attention network is sufficient, whereas any hybrid network interleaving $L-1$ layers of full attention with a substantially larger number ($2^{3L^2}$) of linear attention layers cannot solve it. This result demonstrates a clear separation in expressive power between the two types of attention. Our work provides the first provable separation between hybrid attention and standard full attention, offering a theoretical perspective for understanding the fundamental capabilities and limitations of different attention mechanisms.

paragraphs: Efficient attention mechanisms reduce the computational burden of full attention, but efficiency alone does not establish whether they can perform the same computations. This paper studies that question theoretically, focusing on sequential function composition: a reasoning task in which several dependent operations must be completed within a single forward pass.

The authors establish a separation based on network depth and attention type. A full-attention network with L+1 layers is sufficient for the task. By contrast, a hybrid network containing L−1 full-attention layers cannot solve it even when those layers are interleaved with 2^(3L²) linear-attention layers. The analysis covers linear-attention variants expressible as recurrences, including Mamba and DeltaNet.

The significance is that an enormous increase in recurrent linear-attention depth cannot compensate for the specified reduction in full-attention layers on this task. This provides a rigorous expressiveness hierarchy for the studied computation. Its scope is a theoretical separation on sequential composition, rather than a claim that full attention performs better on every practical language-model task.
summary.tldr: A theoretical separation shows that vastly more linear-attention layers cannot replace a small number of full-attention layers for a particular multi-step reasoning task.

title: A Provable Expressiveness Hierarchy in Hybrid Linear-Full Attention

abstract: Reliable Docker-based environment construction is a dominant bottleneck for scaling execution-grounded training and evaluation of software engineering agents. We introduce DockSmith, a specialized agentic Docker builder designed to address this challenge. DockSmith treats environment construction not merely as a preprocessing step, but as a core agentic capability that exercises long-horizon tool use, dependency reasoning, and failure recovery, yielding supervision that transfers beyond Docker building itself. DockSmith is trained on large-scale, execution-grounded Docker-building trajectories produced by a SWE-Factory–style pipeline augmented with a loop-detection controller and a cross-task success memory. Training a 30B-A3B model on these trajectories achieves open-source state-of-the-art performance on Multi-Docker-Eval, with 39.72% Fail-to-Pass and 58.28% Commit Rate. Moreover, DockSmith improves out-of-distribution performance on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and Terminal-Bench 2.0, demonstrating the broader agentic benefits of environment construction. Our model and Docker-building trajectories are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/JiaranZhang/DockSmith.

DockSmith treats environment construction not merely as a preprocessing step, but as a core agentic capability that exercises long-horizon tool use, dependency reasoning, and failure recovery, yielding supervision that transfers beyond Docker building itself. Training a 30B-A3B model on these trajectories achieves open-source state-of-the-art performance on Multi-Docker-Eval, with 39.72% Fail-to-Pass and 58.28% Commit Rate. Moreover, DockSmith improves out-of-distribution performance on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and Terminal-Bench 2.0, demonstrating the broader agentic benefits of environment construction. Our model and Docker-building trajectories are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/JiaranZhang/DockSmith.

paragraphs: Software engineering agents need working execution environments to train and be evaluated reliably. Constructing those environments can itself demand substantial reasoning about dependencies, tool use, and recovery from failures. DockSmith treats Docker environment building as an agent capability worth training directly, with skills that may also transfer to broader software tasks.

The training data consists of large-scale Docker-building trajectories grounded in actual execution. The generation pipeline includes a controller for detecting loops and a memory of successes across tasks. These additions support the production of trajectories for training a 30B-A3B model, making environment construction both the immediate task and a source of supervision for longer-horizon agent behavior.

On Multi-Docker-Eval, DockSmith achieves 39.72% Fail-to-Pass and a 58.28% Commit Rate, which the authors report as open-source state-of-the-art performance. They also report improvements on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 outside the training distribution. Those results support the claim that learning to construct environments can benefit capabilities beyond Docker building itself.
summary.tldr: DockSmith trains an agent on executed Docker-building trajectories, improving environment construction and performance on broader software-agent benchmarks.

title: DOCKSMITH: Scaling Reliable Coding Environments via an Agentic Docker Builder

abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a promising paradigm for solving workflow-structured tasks through expert collaboration. However, the data required for such collaboration are often distributed across organizations and cannot be centrally pooled due to privacy, intellectual property, and compliance constraints. Federated Learning preserves data locality, but existing federated paradigms typically treat clients as independent and fail to model workflow dependencies that are crucial for coherent multi-stage collaboration. We introduce FedWave, a federated and workflow-aware framework that enables LLM-based experts to solve sequential tasks under data-locality constraints. FedWave combines a Value Chain Layer to model inter-stage dependencies, federated LoRA adaptation to preserve role-specific expertise, a shared Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router for input-conditioned expert fusion, and a Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) stage based on router-induced preferences. Experiments across workflow datasets and LLM backbones show that FedWave outperforms federated baselines and remains competitive with centralized multi-agent systems while preserving data locality.

paragraphs: Language-model agents can collaborate as specialists across stages of a workflow, but the training data for those roles may belong to different organizations. Privacy, intellectual-property, and compliance constraints can prevent pooling that data. Federated learning keeps data local, yet conventional approaches often treat participating clients independently and overlook dependencies between workflow stages.

FedWave incorporates those dependencies into federated collaboration. A Value Chain Layer models relationships between stages, while federated LoRA adaptation maintains role-specific expertise. A shared mixture-of-experts router combines experts according to the input. A subsequent Direct Preference Optimization stage uses preferences induced by that router.

The framework therefore connects local specialist adaptation with coordination across the sequence of tasks. Experiments across workflow datasets and language-model backbones show improvements over federated baselines while remaining competitive with centralized multi-agent systems. These results support workflow-aware learning when data must stay distributed: preserving local data access can coexist with useful coordination between experts whose contributions depend on earlier and later stages.
summary.tldr: FedWave combines federated specialist adaptation with workflow-aware routing to coordinate LLM agents while keeping training data local.

title: Weaving in the Clouds: Achieving Synergistic Collaboration among LLM Agents via Federated Learning

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has received increasing attention and adoption in real-world use cases. Most of these systems follow a train-then-fix paradigm, where trained agents do not learn while interacting with the world until performance degrades and retraining becomes necessary. In this position paper, we argue that deploying an agent that is incapable of optimality, but receives an evaluative reward signal, is inherently a continual RL problem. We identify four sources of non-stationarity after deployment that necessitate never-ending learning, and highlight why the best deployed agents never stop adapting. We analyze successful examples of continual RL in the real world, and present the community with the advantages and measures to move away from the current train-then-fix paradigm.

paragraphs: This paper challenges the common practice of training a reinforcement learning agent, fixing its behavior during deployment, and retraining only after performance deteriorates. The authors argue that deployment should instead be understood as an ongoing learning problem when an agent cannot achieve optimality and continues to receive rewards that evaluate its behavior.

Their argument centers on non-stationarity: conditions relevant to the agent change after deployment. The paper identifies four sources of such change and argues that they require learning to continue indefinitely. Under this perspective, feedback received during real-world interaction is part of the learning process throughout operation, rather than merely a signal that another separate training cycle is due.

The authors analyze successful real-world examples of continual reinforcement learning and discuss advantages and measures for moving away from the prevailing deployment pattern. Their position connects the structure of the problem to the design of deployed systems: if performance remains improvable and evaluative feedback remains available, adaptation should remain active. The paper advocates this shift as a direction for reinforcement learning practice.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that deployed reward-guided agents unable to achieve optimality should keep learning as conditions change.

title: Position: Deployed Reinforcement Learning should be Continual

abstract: Current approaches to aligning large language models (LLMs) aggregate diverse human preferences into a single reward signal, effectively optimizing for a hypothetical “average user” who represents no real person particularly well. This position paper argues that LLMs should learn personalized, individual preferences rather than aggregated ones. We show that aggregation masks critical information about preference diversity, individual values, and contextual dependencies, which is a limitation both theoretically grounded in social choice theory and empirically evident across demographic groups. We analyze the rich structure that human preferences encode, survey technical approaches to personalization, and systematically address counterarguments on scalability, shared standards, and manipulation risk. While personalization introduces genuine safety challenges including filter bubbles, value lock-in, and psychological manipulation, we argue these are manageable through bounded personalization frameworks that preserve universal safety constraints while accommodating legitimate individual variation. We conclude with a concrete research and policy agenda for developing preference-aware models that respect both individual autonomy and collective safety.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that combining diverse human preferences into one reward signal loses information needed to serve individuals well. The resulting target is a hypothetical average user. The authors connect this problem to social choice theory and empirical differences across demographic groups, emphasizing that preferences also depend on personal values and context.

The paper analyzes the structure of human preferences and surveys technical approaches to learning them individually. It also examines objections involving scalability, shared standards, and manipulation. The proposed direction is preference-aware models that can accommodate legitimate differences among people while retaining constraints that protect collective safety.

The authors acknowledge that personalization creates risks, including filter bubbles, entrenched values, and psychological manipulation. They argue these risks are manageable through bounded personalization that preserves universal safety constraints. That is a proposed way to govern personalization, rather than a claim that the risks disappear. The paper concludes with a research and policy agenda aimed at reconciling individual autonomy with shared protections.
summary.tldr: LLMs should learn individual preferences within shared safety boundaries because aggregated rewards obscure meaningful differences among users.

title: Position: Large Language Models Should Learn Personalized Rather Than Aggregated Human Preferences

abstract: Recent advances in text-to-speech (TTS) technology have enabled systems to generate speech that is often indistinguishable from human speech, bringing benefits to accessibility, content creation, and human-computer interaction. However, current evaluation practices are increasingly inadequate for capturing the full range of capabilities, limitations, and societal impacts of modern TTS systems. This position paper introduces the concept of Responsible Evaluation and argues that it is essential and urgent for the next phase of TTS development, structured through three progressive levels: (1) ensuring the faithful and accurate reflection of a model’s true capabilities and limitations, with more robust, discriminative, and comprehensive objective and subjective scoring methodologies; (2) enabling comparability, standardization, and transferability through standardized benchmarks, transparent reporting, and transferable evaluation metrics; and (3) assessing governance, fairness, and security concerns around data provenance, disparities, misuse, spoofing, and traceability. Through this concept, we critically examine current evaluation practices, identify systemic shortcomings, and propose actionable recommendations. We hope this concept will not only foster more reliable TTS technology but also guide its development toward ethically sound and societally beneficial applications.

Through this concept, we critically examine current evaluation practices, identify systemic shortcomings, and propose actionable recommendations. paragraphs: This position paper argues that evaluating synthetic speech requires a broader framework as generated voices become increasingly humanlike. Natural-sounding output alone does not capture a system’s capabilities, weaknesses, or societal consequences. The authors introduce responsible evaluation as a way to organize these requirements and guide the next phase of text-to-speech development.

Their framework has three progressive levels. First, objective measurements and human judgments should accurately distinguish capabilities and limitations. Second, standardized benchmarks, transparent reporting, and transferable metrics should enable meaningful comparisons. Third, evaluation should address governance, fairness, and security, including the origins of training data, disparities, misuse, impersonation through spoofing, and traceability.

The authors use this framework to critique current practices, identify systemic shortcomings, and offer recommendations. Its value lies in connecting the quality of a measurement to the decisions it supports: a score should represent the model faithfully, remain useful across comparisons, and address consequences beyond speech quality. The proposed direction aims to support reliable technology and socially beneficial applications.
summary.tldr: The authors propose evaluating text-to-speech through faithful capability measurement, comparable reporting, and explicit assessment of societal and security concerns.

abstract: The performance of graph based clustering methods critically depends on the quality of the distance function used to compute similarities between pairs of neighboring nodes. In this paper we learndistance functions by training binary classifiers with margins. Theclassifiers are defined over the product space of pairs of points and aretrained to distinguish whether two points come from the same class or not. The signed margin is used as the distance value. Our main contribution is a distance learning method DistBoost, which combines boosting hypotheses over the product space with a weak learner based on partitioning the original feature space. Each weak hypothesis is a Gaussian mixture model computed using a semi-supervised constrained EM algorithm, which is trained using both unlabeled and labeled data. We also consider SVM and decision trees boosting as margin based classifiers in the product space. We experimentally compare the margin based distance functions with other existing metric learning methods, and with existing techniques for the directincorporation of constraints into various clustering algorithms. Clustering performance is measured on some benchmark databases from the UCI repository, a sample from the MNIST database, and a data set of color images of animals. In most cases the DistBoostalgorithm significantly and robustly outperformed its competitors.
