paragraphs: Graph-based clustering depends heavily on the distance function used to compare neighboring points. This paper learns that function through binary classification of point pairs. A classifier predicts whether two points belong to the same class, and its signed margin supplies the distance value used in clustering.

The main method, DistBoost, combines boosted hypotheses over pairs of points with a weak learner that partitions the original feature space. Each weak hypothesis is a Gaussian mixture model fitted through a semi-supervised constrained expectation-maximization procedure. This allows both labeled and unlabeled data to contribute. The paper also considers SVMs and boosted decision trees as margin-based classifiers of pairs.

Experiments compare the learned distances with other metric learning methods and approaches that insert constraints directly into clustering algorithms. Evaluations include UCI datasets, a sample of MNIST, and animal color images. DistBoost significantly and robustly outperforms its competitors in most reported cases, supporting the usefulness of learning pairwise relationships for these clustering tasks.
summary.tldr: DistBoost learns clustering distances from boosted pairwise classifiers and significantly outperforms competitors in most reported experiments.

title: Boosting margin based distance functions for clustering
A new approach to data driven clustering

abstract: We1 present a new actor-critic learning model in which a Bayesian class of non-parametric critics, using Gaussian process temporal difference learning is used. Such critics model the state-action value function as a Gaussian process, allowing Bayes’ rule to be used in computing the posterior distribution over state-action value functions, conditioned on the observed data. Appropriate choices of the prior covariance (kernel) between stateaction values and of the parametrization of the policy allow us to obtain closed-form expressions for the posterior distribution of the gradient of the average discounted return with respect to the policy parameters. The posterior mean, which serves as our estimate of the policy gradient, is used to update the policy, while the posterior covariance allows us to gauge the reliability of the update.

Appropriate choices of the prior covariance (kernel) between stateaction values and of the parametrization of the policy allow us to obtain closed-form expressions for the posterior distribution of the gradient of the average discounted return with respect to the policy parameters. The posterior mean, which serves as our estimate of the policy gradient, is used to update the policy, while the posterior covariance allows us to gauge the reliability of the update.

paragraphs: Actor-critic learning connects a policy that chooses actions with a critic that evaluates them. This paper develops a Bayesian version in which the critic represents uncertainty about the value of taking an action in a state. Its central aim is to turn that uncertainty into information about how to update the policy.

The critic uses Gaussian process temporal difference learning to model state-action values. After observations arrive, Bayes’ rule produces a posterior distribution over possible value functions. With suitable choices of the covariance kernel and policy parameterization, the authors derive closed-form expressions for the posterior distribution of the policy gradient, which describes how the average discounted return changes with the policy parameters.

The posterior mean supplies the gradient estimate used to update the policy. The posterior covariance provides a measure of how reliable that update is. This couples a proposed direction of improvement with an assessment of uncertainty about that direction. The closed-form result depends on the specified compatibility between the kernel and policy representation, rather than applying automatically to every actor-critic design.
summary.tldr: Bayesian critics yield policy-gradient estimates and uncertainty measures, with closed-form posteriors under suitable kernel and policy choices.

title: Bayesian actor-critic algorithms

abstract: Clustering with advice (often known as constrained clustering) has been a recent focus of the data mining community. Success has been achieved incorporating advice into the k-means framework, as well as spectral clustering. Although the theory community has explored inconsistent advice, it has not yet been incorporated into spectral clustering. Extending work of De Bie and Cristianini, we set out a framework for finding minimum normalized cuts, subject to inconsistent advice. Our results suggest that the framework will be successful in many situations.

Although the theory community has explored inconsistent advice, it has not yet been incorporated into spectral clustering. paragraphs: Clustering with advice supplements the data with guidance about how groups should be formed. Such guidance can be inconsistent, creating a challenge for methods that must reconcile the clustering objective with the supplied advice. This paper brings that problem into spectral clustering, where the authors identify a gap between earlier theoretical work on inconsistency and existing clustering methods.

The proposed framework seeks minimum normalized cuts subject to inconsistent advice. Normalized cut supplies the graph-partitioning objective, while the advice adds information about the desired grouping. Bringing both into one framework makes inconsistency part of the clustering problem being addressed. The work extends an existing approach by De Bie and Cristianini.

The authors' results suggest that the framework can succeed in many situations. That is a qualified assessment of its promise, rather than a universal guarantee for every collection of conflicting advice. The contribution is the explicit incorporation of inconsistent guidance into a normalized-cut framework, broadening the kinds of supervision that spectral clustering can attempt to accommodate.
summary.tldr: The paper extends normalized-cut spectral clustering to incorporate inconsistent advice, with results suggesting usefulness across many situations.

title: Spectral clustering with inconsistent advice

abstract: We present a new algorithm for minimizing a convex loss-function subject to regularization. Our framework applies to numerous problems in machine learning and statistics; notably, for sparsity-promoting regularizers such as l_1 or l_{1,\infty} norms it enables efficient computation of sparse solutions. Our approach is based on the trust-region framework with non smooth objectives, which allows us to build on known results to provide convergence analysis. We avoid the computational overheads associated with the conventional Hessian approximation used by trust-region methods by instead using a simple separable quadratic approximation. This approximation also enables use of proximity operators for tackling non smooth regularizers. We illustrate the versatility of our resulting algorithm by specializing it to three mixed-norm regression problems: group lasso [36], group logistic regression [21], and multi-task lasso [19]. We experiment with both synthetic and real-world large-scale data�our method is seen to be competitive, robust, and scalable.

paragraphs: This paper develops an optimization algorithm for fitting models with a convex loss and regularization. Its framework includes penalties that encourage sparse solutions, where many model coefficients become zero. Such penalties are useful for selecting relevant inputs, but their lack of smoothness creates challenges for optimization methods built around smooth local approximations.

The authors adapt the trust-region framework to these nonsmooth objectives. Their main computational choice is a simple separable quadratic approximation in place of the conventional Hessian approximation. This avoids associated computational overhead and makes proximity operators available for handling nonsmooth regularizers. The trust-region formulation also allows the authors to build a convergence analysis using established results.

They specialize the framework to group lasso, group logistic regression, and multi-task lasso, showing how one optimization approach accommodates several mixed-norm regression problems. Experiments on synthetic and large real-world datasets report competitive, robust, and scalable behavior. The contribution combines an economical local approximation with a framework that supports both sparse modeling and convergence analysis.
summary.tldr: A trust-region algorithm uses simple quadratic approximations to solve sparse and mixed-norm regression problems efficiently.

title: A scalable trust-region algorithm with application to mixed-norm regression

abstract: We carefully study how well minimizing convex surrogate loss functions, corresponds to minimizing the misclassification error rate for the problem of binary classification with linear predictors. In particular, we show that amongst all convex surrogate losses, the hinge loss gives essentially the best possible bound, of all convex loss functions, for the misclassification error rate of the resulting linear predictor in terms of the best possible margin error rate. We also provide lower bounds for specific convex surrogates that show how different commonly used losses qualitatively differ from each other.
originalAbstract: We carefully study how well minimizing convex surrogate loss functions, corresponds to minimizing the misclassification error rate for the problem of binary classification with linear predictors. In particular, we show that amongst all convex surrogate losses, the hinge loss gives essentially the best possible bound, of all convex loss functions, for the misclassification error rate of the resulting linear predictor in terms of the best possible margin error rate. We also provide lower bounds for specific convex surrogates that show how different commonly used losses qualitatively differ from each other.

paragraphs: Binary classifiers are often trained by minimizing a convex surrogate loss, even though their eventual quality is judged by how often they assign the wrong label. This paper examines how well those two objectives align for linear predictors. Its focus is the classification error that can be guaranteed after minimizing a chosen surrogate.

The main result compares convex losses using the best achievable margin error as the reference quantity. Under this comparison, hinge loss provides essentially the strongest possible bound on the resulting linear predictor’s misclassification rate among convex surrogates. The qualification matters: the result concerns this particular guarantee for linear classification and does not assert that hinge loss wins every empirical comparison.

The authors also establish lower bounds for particular convex surrogate losses. These reveal qualitative differences between commonly used training objectives, showing that their classification guarantees need not be interchangeable. The paper’s contribution is a sharper theoretical account of how surrogate choice constrains the relationship between successful loss minimization and low classification error.
summary.tldr: For linear binary classifiers, hinge loss gives essentially the best convex-surrogate error bound in terms of achievable margin error.

title: Minimizing The Misclassification Error Rate Using a Surrogate Convex Loss
